abstract: An information-theoretic optimization principle is proposed for the development of each processing stage of a multilayered perceptual network. This principle of "maximum information preservation" states that the signal transformation that is to be realized at each stage is one that maximizes the information that the output signal values (from that stage) convey about the input signals values (to that stage), subject to certain constraints and in the presence of processing noise. The quantity being maximized is a Shannon information rate. I provide motivation for this principle and -- for some simple model cases -- derive some of its consequences, discuss an algorithmic implementation, and show how the principle may lead to biologically relevant neural architectural features such as topographic maps, map distortions, orientation selectivity, and extraction of spatial and temporal signal correlations. A possible connection between this information-theoretic principle and a principle of minimum entropy production in nonequilibrium thermodynamics is suggested.

paragraphs: The paper proposes that each stage of a perceptual network should preserve as much information about its input as possible. It expresses this goal by maximizing a Shannon information rate between the stage’s input and output. The optimization explicitly includes constraints and processing noise, so preservation is considered within the conditions the stage must operate under.

For simple model cases, the author derives consequences of this principle and discusses an algorithmic implementation. The analysis explores how an information-preservation objective could lead to biologically relevant features, including topographic maps, distortions of those maps, orientation selectivity, and extraction of spatial and temporal correlations.

This gives a common organizing question to several aspects of perceptual architecture: which transformation retains the most useful input information under the stated constraints and noise? The results are presented for simple cases, and the architectural implications are described as possibilities. The paper also suggests a connection with minimum entropy production in nonequilibrium thermodynamics, extending the proposed principle into a broader theoretical discussion.
summary.tldr: Maximizing information preservation under noise and constraints is proposed as an organizing principle for layered perceptual networks.

title: Towards an Organizing Principle for a Layered Perceptual Network

abstract: The pyloric Central Pattern Generator of the crustacean stomatogastric ganglion is a well-defined biological neural network. This 14-neuron network is modulated by many inputs. These inputs reconfigure the network to produce multiple output patterns by three simple mechanisms: 1) detennining which cells are active; 2) modulating the synaptic efficacy; 3) changing the intrinsic response properties of individual neurons. The importance of modifiable intrinsic response properties of neurons for network function and modulation is discussed.
originalAbstract: The pyloric Central Pattern Generator of the crustacean stomatogastric ganglion is a well-defined biological neural network. This 14-neuron network is modulated by many inputs. These inputs reconfigure the network to produce multiple output patterns by three simple mechanisms: 1) detennining which cells are active; 2) modulating the synaptic efficacy; 3) changing the intrinsic response properties of individual neurons. The importance of modifiable intrinsic response properties of neurons for network function and modulation is discussed.

paragraphs: The paper examines how biological inputs can change the behavior of an existing neural circuit. Its example is the pyloric central pattern generator in the crustacean stomatogastric ganglion, a defined network of 14 neurons. Many inputs modulate this circuit, allowing it to produce multiple patterns of output from the same underlying collection of cells.

The abstract identifies three mechanisms for this reconfiguration. Modulation can determine which neurons participate, change the efficacy of their synaptic connections, or alter how individual neurons respond intrinsically. These mechanisms affect different aspects of network operation: the active membership, the influence cells exert on one another, and the response behavior of the cells themselves.

The discussion emphasizes the third mechanism, the ability to modify a neuron's intrinsic response properties. Understanding the circuit's output therefore requires considering more than which cells are connected and how strong those connections are. The paper uses this small biological network to explain how adjustable cellular behavior contributes to flexibility in the function of the whole circuit.
summary.tldr: A 14-neuron biological circuit produces different outputs through changes in cell participation, synaptic efficacy, and intrinsic neuronal responses.

title: Mechanisms for Neuromodulation of Biological Neural Networks

abstract: This paper explores the effect of initial weight selection on feed-forward networks learning simple functions with the back-propagation technique. We first demonstrate. through the use of Monte Carlo techniques. that the magnitude of the initial condition vector (in weight space) is a very significant parameter in convergence time variability. In order to further understand this result. additional deterministic experiments were performed. The results of these experiments demon~trate the extreme sensitivity of back propagation to initial weight configuration.
originalAbstract: This paper explores the effect of initial weight selection on feed-forward networks learning simple functions with the back-propagation technique. We first demonstrate. through the use of Monte Carlo techniques. that the magnitude of the initial condition vector (in weight space) is a very significant parameter in convergence time variability. In order to further understand this result. additional deterministic experiments were performed. The results of these experiments demon~trate the extreme sensitivity of back propagation to initial weight configuration.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how a neural network’s starting weights affect learning with back-propagation. It studies feedforward networks learning simple functions, focusing on variation in the time needed to converge. The question is whether the initial state of the weights can explain substantial differences between otherwise comparable learning runs.

The authors first use Monte Carlo techniques to explore this variability. They find that the magnitude of the initial weight vector is a highly significant factor. This magnitude expresses the overall size of the starting weights, so the result identifies initialization scale as an important part of understanding how long learning takes.

Additional deterministic experiments examine the finding more closely and show extreme sensitivity to the initial weight configuration. Together, the experiments connect convergence behavior with both the overall size and the particular arrangement of starting weights. The practical meaning is that back-propagation’s behavior on these simple tasks depends strongly on where learning begins, making initialization a substantive experimental variable.
summary.tldr: Back-propagation’s convergence time depends strongly on the scale and configuration of a network’s initial weights.

title: Back Propagation is Sensitive to Initial Conditions

abstract: We introduce a framework for training architectures composed of several modules. This framework, which uses a statistical formulation of learning systems, provides a unique formalism for describing many classical connectionist algorithms as well as complex systems where several algorithms interact. It allows to design hybrid systems which combine the advantages of connectionist algorithms as well as other learning algorithms.
originalAbstract: We introduce a framework for training architectures composed of several modules. This framework, which uses a statistical formulation of learning systems, provides a unique formalism for describing many classical connectionist algorithms as well as complex systems where several algorithms interact. It allows to design hybrid systems which combine the advantages of connectionist algorithms as well as other learning algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how to train a learning system made of several interacting modules. Such an architecture raises a question beyond how any one component learns: how can different learning procedures be described together so that their cooperation becomes part of the system's design? The authors propose a common framework for this purpose.

Their approach uses a statistical formulation of learning systems. Within that formulation, they describe both established connectionist algorithms and more complex architectures in which several algorithms interact. A shared mathematical language makes the relationships among these learning procedures explicit, allowing individual methods and their combinations to be considered within the same account.

The framework also supports hybrid systems that combine connectionist methods with other learning algorithms. Its stated contribution is a way to design and describe such combinations so that they can draw on the advantages of their components. The emphasis is on organizing learning across an architecture, extending the scope of analysis from an isolated algorithm to a cooperating collection.
summary.tldr: A statistical framework gives interacting learning algorithms a common formalism for training modular and hybrid systems.

title: A Framework for the Cooperation of Learning Algorithms

abstract: Spoken language is one of the most natural, efficient, flexible, and econom(cid:173) ical means of communication among humans. As computers play an ever increasing role in our lives, it is important that we address the issue of providing a graceful human-machine interface through spoken language. In this paper, we will describe our recent efforts in moving beyond the scope of speech recognition into the realm of spoken-language understand(cid:173) ing. Specifically, we report on the development of an urban navigation and exploration system called VOYAGER, an application which we have used as a basis for performing research in spoken-language understanding.
originalAbstract: Spoken language is one of the most natural, efficient, flexible, and econom(cid:173) ical means of communication among humans. As computers play an ever increasing role in our lives, it is important that we address the issue of providing a graceful human-machine interface through spoken language. In this paper, we will describe our recent efforts in moving beyond the scope of speech recognition into the realm of spoken-language understand(cid:173) ing. Specifically, we report on the development of an urban navigation and exploration system called VOYAGER, an application which we have used as a basis for performing research in spoken-language understanding.

paragraphs: This paper describes work toward computer interfaces that support spoken-language understanding. Its motivation is the usefulness of speech in human communication: people communicate naturally and efficiently through spoken language, making it an attractive way to interact with computers. The research asks how speech technology can support a practical interaction rather than stop at recognizing spoken input.

The concrete application is VOYAGER, a system for urban navigation and exploration. The authors use this application as a basis for investigating spoken-language understanding. A navigation setting gives the research a particular purpose: spoken communication is connected to helping a user engage with information about an urban environment.

The contribution reported in the abstract is the development of this application and its role in moving the research beyond speech recognition. The distinction concerns the level of the task: recognizing speech supplies input, while understanding must connect that input to the application's purpose. VOYAGER provides a setting in which the authors can investigate that transition as part of building a spoken human-computer interface.
summary.tldr: VOYAGER uses urban navigation and exploration as a practical setting for developing spoken-language understanding beyond speech recognition.

title: From Speech Recognition to Spoken Language Understanding: The Development of the MIT SUMMIT and VOYAGER Systems

abstract: We introduce a method for the efficient design of a Boltzmann machine (or a Hopfield net) that computes an arbitrary given Boolean function f . This method is based on an efficient simulation of acyclic circuits with threshold gates by Boltzmann machines. As a consequence we can show that various concrete Boolean functions f that are relevant for classification problems can be computed by scalable Boltzmann machines that are guaranteed to converge to their global maximum configuration with high probability after constantly many steps.
originalAbstract: We introduce a method for the efficient design of a Boltzmann machine (or a Hopfield net) that computes an arbitrary given Boolean function f . This method is based on an efficient simulation of acyclic circuits with threshold gates by Boltzmann machines. As a consequence we can show that various concrete Boolean functions f that are relevant for classification problems can be computed by scalable Boltzmann machines that are guaranteed to converge to their global maximum configuration with high probability after constantly many steps.

paragraphs: This paper addresses how to construct a Boltzmann machine or Hopfield network that computes a specified Boolean function. A Boolean function maps binary inputs to a binary answer, making it a natural representation for classification decisions. The design problem is to turn that desired input-output behavior into an appropriate network efficiently.

The proposed method starts from an acyclic circuit made of threshold gates. Such a circuit has no feedback loops, and each gate produces its output by comparing its inputs against a threshold. The authors show how to simulate these circuits efficiently with Boltzmann machines, providing a systematic connection between a circuit description and a recurrent network implementation.

For several concrete Boolean functions relevant to classification, the construction yields scalable networks with a strong convergence guarantee. They reach their global maximum configuration with high probability after a constant number of steps. The significance is that the paper links network design to both correct computation and rapid convergence for these functions, rather than treating convergence as an unspecified consequence of running the network.
summary.tldr: A circuit-based construction produces Boltzmann machines for classification, with constant-step, high-probability convergence guarantees for several concrete functions.

title: A Method for the Efficient Design of Boltzmann Machines for Classiffication Problems

abstract: Network vision systems must make inferences from evidential informa(cid:173) tion across levels of representational abstraction, from low level invariants, through intermediate scene segments, to high level behaviorally relevant object descriptions. This paper shows that such networks can be realized as Markov Random Fields (MRFs). We show first how to construct an MRF functionally equivalent to a Hough transform parameter network, thus establishing a principled probabilistic basis for visual networks. Sec(cid:173) ond, we show that these MRF parameter networks are more capable and flexible than traditional methods. In particular, they have a well-defined probabilistic interpretation, intrinsically incorporate feedback, and offer richer representations and decision capabilities.
originalAbstract: Network vision systems must make inferences from evidential informa(cid:173) tion across levels of representational abstraction, from low level invariants, through intermediate scene segments, to high level behaviorally relevant object descriptions. This paper shows that such networks can be realized as Markov Random Fields (MRFs). We show first how to construct an MRF functionally equivalent to a Hough transform parameter network, thus establishing a principled probabilistic basis for visual networks. Sec(cid:173) ond, we show that these MRF parameter networks are more capable and flexible than traditional methods. In particular, they have a well-defined probabilistic interpretation, intrinsically incorporate feedback, and offer richer representations and decision capabilities.

paragraphs: Visual interpretation requires connecting evidence at different levels, from basic image properties to scene regions and meaningful object descriptions. This paper argues that Markov random fields can provide a common probabilistic framework for networks that connect these representations. The aim is to make inference across levels mathematically coherent.

The authors first construct a Markov random field that performs the same function as a Hough-transform parameter network. Establishing this equivalence gives an existing visual-network computation a probabilistic interpretation. It provides a concrete connection between a familiar parameter-based recognition mechanism and a broader framework for representing relationships among variables.

The paper then argues that these probabilistic parameter networks offer greater flexibility than traditional methods. They incorporate feedback intrinsically and support richer representations and decision capabilities. Feedback matters here because inference can involve interaction across levels of description. The contribution is both a translation of an existing network into probabilistic terms and an argument for extending what such networks can represent and decide.
summary.tldr: Markov random fields give visual parameter networks a probabilistic foundation with feedback and richer representational capabilities.

title: Markov Random Fields Can Bridge Levels of Abstraction

abstract: Hinton [6] proposed that generalization in artificial neural nets should improve if nets learn to represent the domain's underlying regularities. Abu-Mustafa's hints work [1] shows that the outputs of a backprop net can be used as inputs through which domain(cid:173) specific information can be given to the net. We extend these ideas by showing that a backprop net learning many related tasks at the same time can use these tasks as inductive bias for each other and thus learn better. We identify five mechanisms by which multitask backprop improves generalization and give empirical evidence that multi task backprop generalizes better in real domains.
originalAbstract: Hinton [6] proposed that generalization in artificial neural nets should improve if nets learn to represent the domain's underlying regularities. Abu-Mustafa's hints work [1] shows that the outputs of a backprop net can be used as inputs through which domain(cid:173) specific information can be given to the net. We extend these ideas by showing that a backprop net learning many related tasks at the same time can use these tasks as inductive bias for each other and thus learn better. We identify five mechanisms by which multitask backprop improves generalization and give empirical evidence that multi task backprop generalizes better in real domains.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether a neural network can learn better by solving several related tasks together. Its starting idea is that good generalization depends on capturing regularities underlying a domain. Learning tasks jointly gives the network multiple sources of evidence about those regularities, rather than relying on the training signal from a single task.

The proposed approach uses backpropagation to train the related tasks at the same time. Each task provides an inductive bias for the others: it influences which patterns the learner is encouraged to represent. The paper extends the idea that domain information can enter learning through network outputs by making related prediction tasks a source of that guidance.

The authors identify five mechanisms through which multitask backpropagation improves generalization and provide empirical evidence from real domains. The stated finding is that joint learning can improve performance beyond the training examples. Relatedness is central to the argument because the tasks are intended to inform one another about useful structure in the domain.
summary.tldr: Training related tasks together lets them guide one another's representations and can improve neural network generalization.

title: Learning Many Related Tasks at the Same Time with Backpropagation

abstract: In supervised learning there is usually a clear distinction between inputs and outputs - inputs are what you will measure, outputs are what you will predict from those measurements. This paper shows that the distinction between inputs and outputs is not this simple. Some features are more useful as extra outputs than as inputs. By using a feature as an output we get more than just the case values but can. learn a mapping from the other inputs to that feature. For many features this mapping may be more useful than the feature value itself. We present two regression problems and one classification problem where performance improves if features that could have been used as inputs are used as extra outputs instead. This result is surprising since a feature used as an output is not used during testing.
originalAbstract: In supervised learning there is usually a clear distinction between inputs and outputs - inputs are what you will measure, outputs are what you will predict from those measurements. This paper shows that the distinction between inputs and outputs is not this simple. Some features are more useful as extra outputs than as inputs. By using a feature as an output we get more than just the case values but can. learn a mapping from the other inputs to that feature. For many features this mapping may be more useful than the feature value itself. We present two regression problems and one classification problem where performance improves if features that could have been used as inputs are used as extra outputs instead. This result is surprising since a feature used as an output is not used during testing.

paragraphs: The paper challenges the usual assumption that an available feature is most useful as an input. It shows that some features can help more when the learner is asked to predict them as additional outputs. This changes the feature’s role from information supplied to the model into a source of training guidance.

The reasoning is that an input supplies a feature’s value for each example, while an extra prediction task encourages learning a mapping from the other inputs to that feature. The authors argue that this learned relationship can be more useful than directly observing the feature value. The benefit therefore comes through what training teaches the model.

The paper presents two regression problems and one classification problem where moving features from inputs to extra outputs improves performance. Those features are not used during testing, making the result particularly informative: their contribution survives through the learning process. The findings show that deciding how to use available information can matter as much as deciding whether to include it at all.
summary.tldr: Some features improve learning more as additional prediction targets than as inputs, even though they are unused during testing.

title: Promoting Poor Features to Supervisors: Some Inputs Work Better as Outputs

abstract: We study a mistake-driven variant of an on-line Bayesian learn(cid:173) ing algorithm (similar to one studied by Cesa-Bianchi, Helmbold, and Panizza [CHP96]). This variant only updates its state (learns) on trials in which it makes a mistake. The algorithm makes binary classifications using a linear-threshold classifier and runs in time lin(cid:173) ear in the number of attributes seen by the learner. We have been able to show, theoretically and in simulations, that this algorithm performs well under assumptions quite different from those embod(cid:173) ied in the prior of the original Bayesian algorithm. It can handle situations that we do not know how to handle in linear time with Bayesian algorithms. We expect our techniques to be useful in deriving and analyzing other apobayesian algorithms.
originalAbstract: We study a mistake-driven variant of an on-line Bayesian learn(cid:173) ing algorithm (similar to one studied by Cesa-Bianchi, Helmbold, and Panizza [CHP96]). This variant only updates its state (learns) on trials in which it makes a mistake. The algorithm makes binary classifications using a linear-threshold classifier and runs in time lin(cid:173) ear in the number of attributes seen by the learner. We have been able to show, theoretically and in simulations, that this algorithm performs well under assumptions quite different from those embod(cid:173) ied in the prior of the original Bayesian algorithm. It can handle situations that we do not know how to handle in linear time with Bayesian algorithms. We expect our techniques to be useful in deriving and analyzing other apobayesian algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper studies an online classifier that learns only when it makes a mistake. On each trial it produces a binary decision using a linear threshold, and a correct prediction leaves its internal state unchanged. The algorithm is derived from a Bayesian learning procedure but changes when learning updates occur.

Its computational cost is linear in the number of attributes available to the learner. That property is important to the paper’s argument: the authors seek useful learning behavior without requiring a more expensive Bayesian computation. They examine the mistake-driven variant through both theoretical analysis and simulations, rather than relying only on its relationship to the original algorithm.

The results show good performance under assumptions substantially different from those encoded in the original Bayesian prior. The method also handles situations for which the authors do not know a linear-time Bayesian solution. The broader contribution is a demonstration that modifying a Bayesian-inspired update procedure can produce an efficient learner with useful behavior beyond the assumptions that originally motivated it.
summary.tldr: A mistake-driven Bayesian-inspired classifier learns efficiently and performs well beyond the assumptions of its original prior.

title: An Apobayesian Relative of Winnow

abstract: A non-linear modification to PI control is motivated by a model of a signal transduction pathway active in mammalian blood pressure regulation. This control algorithm, labeled PII (proportional with intermittent integral), is appropriate for plants requiring exact set-point matching and disturbance attenuation in the presence of infrequent step changes in load disturbances or set-point. The proportional aspect of the controller is independently designed to be a disturbance attenuator and set-point matching is achieved by intermittently invoking an integral controller. The mechanisms observed in the Angiotensin 11/ AT1 signaling pathway are used to control the switching of the integral control. Improved performance over PI control is shown on a model of cyc1opentenol production. A sign change in plant gain at the desirable operating point causes traditional PI control to result in an unstable system. Application of this new approach to this problem results in stable exact set-point matching for achievable set-points.
originalAbstract: A non-linear modification to PI control is motivated by a model of a signal transduction pathway active in mammalian blood pressure regulation. This control algorithm, labeled PII (proportional with intermittent integral), is appropriate for plants requiring exact set-point matching and disturbance attenuation in the presence of infrequent step changes in load disturbances or set-point. The proportional aspect of the controller is independently designed to be a disturbance attenuator and set-point matching is achieved by intermittently invoking an integral controller. The mechanisms observed in the Angiotensin 11/ AT1 signaling pathway are used to control the switching of the integral control. Improved performance over PI control is shown on a model of cyc1opentenol production. A sign change in plant gain at the desirable operating point causes traditional PI control to result in an unstable system. paragraphs: The paper proposes a nonlinear modification of proportional-integral control inspired by a signaling pathway involved in mammalian blood-pressure regulation. The method is called proportional with intermittent integral, or PII. It targets systems that require exact matching of a desired operating value while attenuating disturbances, with infrequent step changes in either load disturbances or the desired value.

The proportional controller is designed independently to attenuate disturbances. Integral control is then activated intermittently to achieve exact set-point matching. Mechanisms observed in the Angiotensin II/AT1 pathway motivate how the algorithm switches that integral action. This separates the two control roles while coordinating when the integral component operates.

The authors demonstrate improved performance over conventional PI control on a model of cyclopentenol production. At the desired operating point, a change in the sign of plant gain makes traditional PI control unstable. The proposed approach achieves stable, exact matching for achievable set-points in this example, supporting intermittent integral control for the particular control difficulty studied.
summary.tldr: A biologically inspired controller activates integral control intermittently, achieving stable set-point matching in a production model where traditional PI becomes unstable.

title: Non-Linear PI Control Inspired by Biological Control Systems

abstract: While classical experiments on spike-timing dependent plasticity analyzed synaptic changes as a function of the timing of pairs of pre- and postsynaptic spikes, more recent experiments also point to the effect of spike triplets. Here we develop a mathematical framework that allows us to characterize timing based learning rules. Moreover, we identify a candidate learning rule with five variables (and 5 free parameters) that captures a variety of experimental data, including the dependence of potentiation and depression upon pre- and postsynaptic firing frequencies. The relation to the Bienenstock-Cooper-Munro rule as well as to some timing-based rules is discussed.
originalAbstract: While classical experiments on spike-timing dependent plasticity analyzed synaptic changes as a function of the timing of pairs of pre- and postsynaptic spikes, more recent experiments also point to the effect of spike triplets. Here we develop a mathematical framework that allows us to characterize timing based learning rules. Moreover, we identify a candidate learning rule with five variables (and 5 free parameters) that captures a variety of experimental data, including the dependence of potentiation and depression upon pre- and postsynaptic firing frequencies. The relation to the Bienenstock-Cooper-Munro rule as well as to some timing-based rules is discussed.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to describe synaptic learning when the timing of a single pair of spikes is insufficient. Classical spike-timing-dependent plasticity experiments relate changes in connection strength to the relative timing of a presynaptic and a postsynaptic spike. More recent experiments also show effects involving three spikes, motivating a richer description.

The authors develop a mathematical framework for characterizing learning rules based on spike timing. Within that framework, they identify a candidate rule containing five variables and five adjustable parameters. The rule captures a range of experimental observations, including how synaptic strengthening and weakening depend on the firing frequencies of both participating neurons.

This matters because a timing-based account must explain more than isolated pair relationships if it is to describe those observations. The proposed rule provides a compact candidate that includes triplet and frequency effects. The paper also discusses its relationship to the Bienenstock-Cooper-Munro rule and other timing-based rules, connecting the candidate to existing descriptions of plasticity without claiming it is the uniquely correct biological mechanism.
summary.tldr: A compact candidate synaptic learning rule captures experimental spike-triplet and firing-frequency effects beyond classical pair-based timing rules.

title: Beyond Pair-Based STDP: a Phenomenological Rule for Spike Triplet and Frequency Effects

abstract: We consider regularized least-squares (RLS) with a Gaussian kernel. We prove that if we let the Gaussian bandwidth σ → ∞ while letting the regularization parameter λ → 0, the RLS solution tends to a polynomial whose order is controlled by the rielative rates of decay of 1 σ2 and λ: if λ = σ−(2k+1), then, as σ → ∞, the RLS solution tends to the kth order polynomial with minimal empirical error. We illustrate the result with an example.
originalAbstract: We consider regularized least-squares (RLS) with a Gaussian kernel. We prove that if we let the Gaussian bandwidth σ → ∞ while letting the regularization parameter λ → 0, the RLS solution tends to a polynomial whose order is controlled by the rielative rates of decay of 1 σ2 and λ: if λ = σ−(2k+1), then, as σ → ∞, the RLS solution tends to the kth order polynomial with minimal empirical error. We illustrate the result with an example.

paragraphs: The paper studies what happens to regularized least-squares fitting with a Gaussian kernel as two settings change together. The Gaussian bandwidth grows without bound, while the regularization parameter approaches zero. Rather than examining either setting in isolation, the analysis asks how their relative rates determine the fitted function's limiting form.

The authors prove that the solution approaches a polynomial whose order depends on those rates. In particular, when the regularization parameter equals the bandwidth raised to the power minus two k minus one, the solution approaches the kth-order polynomial with the smallest empirical error. Here, empirical error refers to error on the observed fitting data.

This result gives a precise connection between Gaussian kernel fitting and polynomial fitting under a specified limiting regime. The degree of the limiting polynomial is controlled through the coupling of bandwidth and regularization, rather than being stated independently of them. An example illustrates the theorem. The finding concerns this joint limit and the resulting fit to observed data.
summary.tldr: Gaussian regularized least squares approaches a minimum-empirical-error polynomial when bandwidth and regularization follow a specified joint limit.

title: Asymptotics of Gaussian Regularized Least Squares

abstract: We consider approximate value iteration with a parameterized approximator in which the state space is partitioned and the optimal cost-to-go function over each partition is approximated by a constant. We establish performance loss bounds for policies derived from approximations associated with fixed points. These bounds identify benefits to having projection weights equal to the invariant distribution of the resulting policy. Such projection weighting leads to the same fixed points as TD(0). Our analysis also leads to the first performance loss bound for approximate value iteration with an average cost objective.
originalAbstract: We consider approximate value iteration with a parameterized approximator in which the state space is partitioned and the optimal cost-to-go function over each partition is approximated by a constant. We establish performance loss bounds for policies derived from approximations associated with fixed points. These bounds identify benefits to having projection weights equal to the invariant distribution of the resulting policy. Such projection weighting leads to the same fixed points as TD(0). Our analysis also leads to the first performance loss bound for approximate value iteration with an average cost objective.

paragraphs: This paper studies policy quality when approximate value iteration represents costs using a partitioned state space. Within each partition, the optimal cost-to-go function is approximated by a constant. The analysis focuses on policies obtained from approximations at fixed points and derives bounds on how much performance those policies can lose.

The bounds reveal a benefit from choosing projection weights equal to the invariant state distribution of the policy that results. In other words, the weighting used to construct the approximation is linked to the states occupied under that policy. With this choice, the fixed points coincide with those of TD(0), connecting the weighting analysis to a temporal-difference method.

The analysis also supplies what the authors identify as the first performance-loss bound for approximate value iteration under an average-cost objective. The contribution explains why TD(0)-associated weighting can help policy quality in the specified approximation setting. The result is grounded in fixed-point performance bounds for partition-based approximators, giving the title's comparison a precise mathematical scope.
summary.tldr: For partition-based value approximation, performance bounds favor policy-distribution weighting that yields the same fixed points as TD(0).

title: TD(0) Leads to Better Policies than Approximate Value Iteration

abstract: We address the challenge of assessing conservation of gene expression in complex, non-homogeneous datasets. Recent studies have demonstrated the success of probabilistic models in studying the evolution of gene expression in simple eukaryotic organisms such as yeast, for which measurements are typically scalar and independent. Models capable of studying expression evolution in much more complex organisms such as vertebrates are particularly important given the medical and scientific interest in species such as human and mouse. We present a statistical model that makes a number of significant extensions to previous models to enable characterization of changes in expression among highly complex organisms. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on a microarray dataset containing diverse tissues from multiple vertebrate species. We anticipate that the model will be invaluable in the study of gene expression patterns in other diverse organisms as well, such as worms and insects.
originalAbstract: We address the challenge of assessing conservation of gene expression in complex, non-homogeneous datasets. Recent studies have demonstrated the success of probabilistic models in studying the evolution of gene expression in simple eukaryotic organisms such as yeast, for which measurements are typically scalar and independent. Models capable of studying expression evolution in much more complex organisms such as vertebrates are particularly important given the medical and scientific interest in species such as human and mouse. We present a statistical model that makes a number of significant extensions to previous models to enable characterization of changes in expression among highly complex organisms. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on a microarray dataset containing diverse tissues from multiple vertebrate species. We anticipate that the model will be invaluable in the study of gene expression patterns in other diverse organisms as well, such as worms and insects.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to assess whether gene expression is conserved across species when the measurements come from complex, heterogeneous datasets. Earlier probabilistic approaches had succeeded in simpler organisms such as yeast, where measurements were typically single values treated as independent. Diverse tissues from more complex organisms create a broader modeling challenge.

The authors introduce a statistical mixture model that extends previous expression-evolution models to handle this setting. Its purpose is to characterize changes in expression among complex organisms while accommodating the non-homogeneous nature of the data. The central contribution is therefore a modeling framework suited to comparisons involving richer biological measurements.

The method is demonstrated on microarray measurements covering multiple tissues and vertebrate species. This application supports its usefulness for studying expression evolution in the setting it was designed to address. Human and mouse help motivate the work because of their scientific and medical relevance. The authors also anticipate applications to organisms such as worms and insects, presenting that broader usefulness as a prospect rather than a demonstrated result.
summary.tldr: A mixture model extends gene-expression evolution analysis to heterogeneous measurements across tissues and vertebrate species.

title: A mixture model for the evolution of gene expression in non-homogeneous datasets

abstract: We present a multi-label multiple kernel learning (MKL) formulation, in which the data are embedded into a low-dimensional space directed by the instance-label correlations encoded into a hypergraph. We formulate the problem in the kernel-induced feature space and propose to learn the kernel matrix as a linear combination of a given collection of kernel matrices in the MKL framework. The proposed learning formulation leads to a non-smooth min-max problem, and it can be cast into a semi-infinite linear program (SILP). We further propose an approximate formulation with a guaranteed error bound which involves an unconstrained and convex optimization problem. In addition, we show that the objective function of the approximate formulation is continuously differentiable with Lipschitz gradient, and hence existing methods can be employed to compute the optimal solution efficiently. We apply the proposed formulation to the automated annotation of Drosophila gene expression pattern images, and promising results have been reported in comparison with representative algorithms.

paragraphs: When an example can have several labels, a useful representation should reflect the relationships between examples and those labels. This paper proposes a multiple-kernel learning formulation that embeds data in a low-dimensional space. A hypergraph encodes instance-label correlations and directs the construction of that representation.

The method works in a kernel-induced feature space and learns a kernel matrix as a linear combination of supplied kernel matrices. Its original optimization problem is a nonsmooth min-max problem that can be expressed as a semi-infinite linear program. The authors also develop an approximation with a guaranteed error bound, giving a mathematically controlled alternative to the original formulation.

The approximate problem is unconstrained and convex, with a continuously differentiable objective and a Lipschitz gradient. These properties allow existing optimization methods to compute its optimum efficiently. The authors apply the approach to automated annotation of Drosophila gene-expression images and report promising comparisons with representative algorithms. The contribution connects label-informed representation learning to an optimization formulation that is more manageable while retaining an explicit approximation guarantee.
summary.tldr: The method learns a label-informed combination of kernels and offers a smooth convex approximation with a guaranteed error bound.

title: Multi-label Multiple Kernel Learning

abstract: Many transductive inference algorithms assume that distributions over training and test estimates should be related, e.g. by providing a large margin of separation on both sets. We use this idea to design a transduction algorithm which can be used without modification for classification, regression, and structured estimation. At its heart we exploit the fact that for a good learner the distributions over the outputs on training and test sets should match. This is a classical two-sample problem which can be solved efficiently in its most general form by using distance measures in Hilbert Space. It turns out that a number of existing heuristics can be viewed as special cases of our approach.

paragraphs: Transductive inference uses the relationship between training and test data when producing estimates for the test set. This paper builds on the idea that a good learner should produce matching output distributions on those two sets. The relationship is imposed at the level of distributions over outputs, providing a common principle for several prediction tasks.

The authors formulate this comparison as a classical two-sample problem: assess how two collections differ in distribution. They use distance measures in Hilbert space to handle that comparison efficiently in a general form. Distribution matching becomes the central mechanism of the resulting transduction algorithm.

The same algorithm can be used without modification for classification, regression, and structured estimation. This breadth matters because the organizing principle does not depend on one particular kind of output. The authors also show that several existing heuristics are special cases of their approach. The contribution thus offers both a shared algorithmic framework and an interpretation of earlier methods through the assumption of matching output distributions.
summary.tldr: Matching training and test output distributions yields a transduction framework usable unchanged across classification, regression, and structured estimation.

title: Distribution Matching for Transduction

abstract: We consider the problem of finding the M assignments with maximum probability in a probabilistic graphical model. We show how this problem can be formulated as a linear program (LP) on a particular polytope. We prove that, for tree graphs (and junction trees in general), this polytope has a particularly simple form and differs from the marginal polytope in a single inequality constraint. We use this characterization to provide an approximation scheme for non-tree graphs, by using the set of spanning trees over such graphs. The method we present puts the M -best inference problem in the context of LP relaxations, which have recently received considerable attention and have proven useful in solving difficult inference problems. We show empirically that our method often finds the provably exact M best configurations for problems of high tree-width.

paragraphs: Inference in a probabilistic graphical model can require several likely configurations rather than just the single most probable one. This paper studies finding the M highest-probability assignments. It expresses that task as a linear program over a particular polytope, turning the search for ranked configurations into a constrained optimization problem.

For tree graphs and, more generally, junction trees, the authors prove that the relevant polytope has a particularly simple description. It differs from the marginal polytope by just one inequality. This characterization supplies a mathematical foundation for the method and identifies a close connection between M-best inference and an established representation used in graphical-model optimization.

For graphs that are not trees, the authors build an approximation scheme using spanning trees. This places the broader problem within the framework of linear-programming relaxations. Empirically, the method often returns configurations that can be proved to be the exact M best even for high-tree-width problems. That is an observed success with certifiable answers in those cases, rather than a guarantee of exact recovery for every non-tree graph.
summary.tldr: A linear-programming formulation enables M-best graphical-model inference and often yields provably exact answers in difficult empirical cases.

title: An LP View of the M-best MAP problem

abstract: We present a new learning strategy for classification problems in which train and/or test data suffer from missing features. In previous work, instances are represented as vectors from some feature space and one is forced to impute missing values or to consider an instance-specific subspace. In contrast, our method considers instances as sets of (feature,value) pairs which naturally handle the missing value case. Building onto this framework, we propose a classification strategy for sets. Our proposal maps (feature,value) pairs into an embedding space and then non-linearly combines the set of embedded vectors. The embedding and the combination parameters are learned jointly on the final classification objective. This simple strategy allows great flexibility in encoding prior knowledge about the features in the embedding step and yields advantageous results compared to alternative solutions over several datasets.

paragraphs: Classification data can have missing features during training, testing, or both. This paper changes how an example is represented: it becomes a set of observed feature-value pairs. Missing entries fit naturally into this representation because the example is described by the pairs that are available, rather than by a fully populated fixed-length vector.

The method maps each feature-value pair into an embedding space and then combines the embedded vectors nonlinearly to classify the set. Both the embedding parameters and the combination parameters are learned jointly for the final classification objective. This ties the representation of individual observations to the way their collective information is used for prediction.

The embedding step also offers flexibility for encoding prior knowledge about features. Across several datasets, the authors report advantageous results compared with alternative approaches. The contribution is therefore both representational and predictive: it supplies a way to express incomplete examples and shows that learning directly with this representation can be effective in the tested classification problems.
summary.tldr: Representing incomplete examples as sets of observed feature-value pairs enables jointly learned embeddings and classification with favorable reported results.

title: Feature Set Embedding for Incomplete Data

abstract: The max-norm was proposed as a convex matrix regularizer by Srebro et al (2004) and was shown to be empirically superior to the trace-norm for collaborative filtering problems. Although the max-norm can be computed in polynomial time, there are currently no practical algorithms for solving large-scale optimization problems that incorporate the max-norm. The present work uses a factorization technique of Burer and Monteiro (2003) to devise scalable first-order algorithms for convex programs involving the max-norm. These algorithms are applied to solve huge collaborative filtering, graph cut, and clustering problems. Empirically, the new methods outperform mature techniques from all three areas.

paragraphs: The max-norm is a convex matrix regularizer with earlier empirical evidence of advantages over the trace-norm in collaborative filtering. Its practical use faced an optimization barrier: polynomial-time computability did not provide an effective method for large problems involving the regularizer. This paper addresses that gap between theoretical tractability and usable computation.

The authors apply a matrix factorization technique to develop scalable first-order algorithms for convex programs involving the max-norm. The factorization is the means of making these optimization problems manageable at larger scales. The work therefore focuses on how to compute with an existing regularizer, rather than proposing the max-norm itself.

The algorithms are applied to very large collaborative filtering, graph cut, and clustering problems. Across all three areas, the authors report better empirical performance than mature techniques. Those results support the practical value of the optimization approach in several distinct applications. They also show how improving the solver can broaden access to a regularizer whose computational formulation had previously limited large-scale use.
summary.tldr: Factorization-based first-order algorithms make max-norm optimization practical at large scales and outperform evaluated methods in three application areas.

title: Practical Large-Scale Optimization for Max-norm Regularization

abstract: Given an ensemble of distinct, low-level segmentations of an image, our goal is to identify visually meaningful" segments in the ensemble. Knowledge about any specific objects and surfaces present in the image is not available. The selection of image regions occupied by objects is formalized as the maximum-weight independent set (MWIS) problem. MWIS is the heaviest subset of mutually non-adjacent nodes of an attributed graph. We construct such a graph from all segments in the ensemble. Then, MWIS selects maximally distinctive segments that together partition the image. A new MWIS algorithm is presented. The algorithm seeks a solution directly in the discrete domain, instead of relaxing MWIS to a continuous problem, as common in previous work. It iteratively finds a candidate discrete solution of the Taylor series expansion of the original MWIS objective function around the previous solution. The algorithm is shown to converge to a maximum. Our empirical evaluation on the benchmark Berkeley segmentation dataset shows that the new algorithm eliminates the need for hand-picking optimal input parameters of the state-of-the-art segmenters, and outperforms their best, manually optimized results."

paragraphs: Different low-level segmentations of one image provide competing candidate regions. This paper selects visually meaningful regions from that ensemble without knowing which specific objects or surfaces are present. It constructs a graph from the candidate segments and poses selection as a maximum-weight independent set problem.

The selected set contains mutually non-adjacent graph nodes with high combined weight. In the paper's construction, this identifies distinctive segments that together partition the image. The proposed solver works directly with discrete solutions, repeatedly using a Taylor expansion of the objective around the preceding solution. The authors show convergence to a maximum, without stating that this is necessarily the global maximum.

On the Berkeley segmentation benchmark, the method removes the need to hand-pick optimal input parameters for the evaluated state-of-the-art segmenters and exceeds their best manually optimized results. This demonstrates the value of selecting regions across an ensemble rather than relying on one parameter choice. The graph formulation links that selection task to a discrete optimization method with a stated convergence result.
summary.tldr: Discrete graph optimization selects image regions from multiple segmentations and beats the reported manually tuned results on the Berkeley benchmark.

title: Segmentation as Maximum-Weight Independent Set

abstract: We formulate clustering aggregation as a special instance of Maximum-Weight Independent Set (MWIS) problem. For a given dataset, an attributed graph is constructed from the union of the input clusterings generated by different underlying clustering algorithms with different parameters. The vertices, which represent the distinct clusters, are weighted by an internal index measuring both cohesion and separation. The edges connect the vertices whose corresponding clusters overlap. Intuitively, an optimal aggregated clustering can be obtained by selecting an optimal subset of non-overlapping clusters partitioning the dataset together. We formalize this intuition as the MWIS problem on the attributed graph, i.e., finding the heaviest subset of mutually non-adjacent vertices. This MWIS problem exhibits a special structure. Since the clusters of each input clustering form a partition of the dataset, the vertices corresponding to each clustering form a maximal independent set (MIS) in the attributed graph. We propose a variant of simulated annealing method that takes advantage of this special structure. Our algorithm starts from each MIS, which is close to a distinct local optimum of the MWIS problem, and utilizes a local search heuristic to explore its neighborhood in order to find the MWIS. Extensive experiments on many challenging datasets show that: 1. our approach to clustering aggregation automatically decides the optimal number of clusters; 2. it does not require any parameter tuning for the underlying clustering algorithms; 3. it can combine the advantages of different underlying clustering algorithms to achieve superior performance; 4. it is robust against moderate or even bad input clusterings.

paragraphs: Clustering aggregation combines several proposed groupings of the same dataset. This paper builds a graph whose vertices represent distinct clusters taken from those groupings. Each vertex receives a weight measuring how cohesive its cluster is and how well it separates from other data. An edge marks two clusters that overlap.

The aggregation problem becomes a maximum-weight independent-set problem: select a high-weight collection of vertices with no edges between them. This expresses the preference for strong clusters that do not overlap. Each original clustering already supplies a maximal independent set because its clusters partition the dataset, giving the search useful starting configurations.

The authors exploit this structure with a simulated-annealing variant that starts from each such configuration and searches nearby alternatives. Experiments report automatic selection of the cluster count, no need to tune the underlying clustering algorithms, and improved performance by combining their strengths. They also report robustness to mediocre or poor input clusterings. These are empirical findings about the aggregation method, rather than a claim that the search always finds the global optimum.
summary.tldr: Clustering aggregation is formulated as selecting high-quality, non-overlapping clusters through a structured maximum-weight independent-set search.

title: Clustering Aggregation as Maximum-Weight Independent Set

abstract: We present a novel non-parametric method for finding a subspace of stimulus features that contains all information about the response of a system. Our method generalizes similar approaches to this problem such as spike triggered average, spike triggered covariance, or maximally informative dimensions. Instead of maximizing the mutual information between features and responses directly, we use integral probability metrics in kernel Hilbert spaces to minimize the information between uninformative features and the combination of informative features and responses. Since estimators of these metrics access the data via kernels, are easy to compute, and exhibit good theoretical convergence properties, our method can easily be generalized to populations of neurons or spike patterns. By using a particular expansion of the mutual information, we can show that the informative features must contain all information if we can make the uninformative features independent of the rest.

Instead of maximizing the mutual information between features and responses directly, we use integral probability metrics in kernel Hilbert spaces to minimize the information between uninformative features and the combination of informative features and responses. Since estimators of these metrics access the data via kernels, are easy to compute, and exhibit good theoretical convergence properties, our method can easily be generalized to populations of neurons or spike patterns. By using a particular expansion of the mutual information, we can show that the informative features must contain all information if we can make the uninformative features independent of the rest.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to find a smaller set of stimulus features that retains all information about a system's response. This is useful when a stimulus has many dimensions but only a subspace matters for predicting the response. The proposed nonparametric method generalizes approaches including spike-triggered averages, spike-triggered covariance, and maximally informative dimensions.

Its strategy reverses the usual emphasis. Instead of directly maximizing mutual information between selected features and responses, it reduces dependence between the supposedly uninformative features and everything retained, including the response. The method measures this dependence using integral probability metrics in kernel Hilbert spaces, allowing the required estimates to be computed through kernels.

The authors state that these estimators are easy to calculate and have favorable theoretical convergence properties, supporting extensions to neural populations or spike patterns. They also prove a conditional completeness result: if the discarded features can be made independent of the remaining features and responses, the retained features contain all response information. That independence condition is sufficient for the guarantee, rather than something automatically achieved in every application.
summary.tldr: A kernel-based method seeks informative stimulus subspaces by making discarded features independent of the retained features and responses.

title: Least Informative Dimensions

abstract: Distance-based approaches to outlier detection are popular in data mining, as they do not require to model the underlying probability distribution, which is particularly challenging for high-dimensional data. We present an empirical comparison of various approaches to distance-based outlier detection across a large number of datasets. We report the surprising observation that a simple, sampling-based scheme outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in terms of both efficiency and effectiveness. To better understand this phenomenon, we provide a theoretical analysis why the sampling-based approach outperforms alternative methods based on k-nearest neighbor search.
originalAbstract: Distance-based approaches to outlier detection are popular in data mining, as they do not require to model the underlying probability distribution, which is particularly challenging for high-dimensional data. We present an empirical comparison of various approaches to distance-based outlier detection across a large number of datasets. To better understand this phenomenon, we provide a theoretical analysis why the sampling-based approach outperforms alternative methods based on k-nearest neighbor search.

paragraphs: Distance-based outlier detection identifies unusual observations through their distances to other data points. One attraction is that it does not require a model of the underlying probability distribution, which can be especially difficult to specify for high-dimensional data. This paper asks how different distance-based approaches compare in practice.

The authors conduct an empirical comparison across a large collection of datasets. Their central observation is that a simple sampling-based scheme beats the state-of-the-art techniques considered on both efficiency and effectiveness. The result matters because it challenges the expectation that a more elaborate search procedure will necessarily deliver the best combination of detection quality and computational cost.

The paper supplements this empirical finding with a theoretical analysis explaining why sampling can outperform alternatives based on k-nearest-neighbor search. That analysis aims to account for the observed advantage, rather than leaving it as an unexplained experimental result. Together, the comparison and theory make a case for sampling as a serious approach to distance-based detection, with the reported superiority grounded in the study's evaluated methods and datasets.
summary.tldr: A simple sampling scheme outperforms tested distance-based outlier detectors in speed and effectiveness, with theory explaining its advantage over nearest-neighbor approaches.

title: Rapid Distance-Based Outlier Detection via Sampling

abstract: It is well known that the optimal convergence rate for stochastic optimization of smooth functions is $[O(1/\sqrt{T})]$, which is same as stochastic optimization of Lipschitz continuous convex functions. This is in contrast to optimizing smooth functions using full gradients, which yields a convergence rate of $[O(1/T^2)]$. In this work, we consider a new setup for optimizing smooth functions, termed as {\bf Mixed Optimization}, which allows to access both a stochastic oracle and a full gradient oracle. Our goal is to significantly improve the convergence rate of stochastic optimization of smooth functions by having an additional small number of accesses to the full gradient oracle. We show that, with an $[O(\ln T)]$ calls to the full gradient oracle and an $O(T)$ calls to the stochastic oracle, the proposed mixed optimization algorithm is able to achieve an optimization error of $[O(1/T)]$.

paragraphs: Smoothness offers very different benefits depending on what information an optimizer can access. The abstract contrasts an optimal stochastic convergence rate of O(1/sqrt(T)) with an O(1/T²) rate using full gradients. This gap motivates a question: can occasional full-gradient information substantially improve an otherwise stochastic optimization procedure?

The paper introduces mixed optimization, a setup that provides both a stochastic oracle and a full-gradient oracle. The goal is to keep full-gradient queries infrequent while making extensive use of stochastic information. It therefore studies the value of combining two kinds of access, with separate accounting for how often each oracle is called.

The proposed algorithm achieves optimization error O(1/T) using O(T) stochastic calls and only O(ln T) full-gradient calls. Its error bound improves on the stochastic rate in the comparison, while the number of full-gradient queries grows only logarithmically. The result shows that relatively few precise gradient evaluations can meaningfully change the convergence guarantee in this mixed-access setting.
summary.tldr: Mixed optimization achieves O(1/T) error with O(T) stochastic oracle calls and only O(ln T) full-gradient calls.

title: Mixed Optimization for Smooth Functions

abstract: This paper presents a representation theory for permutation-valued functions, which in their general form can also be called listwise ranking functions. Pointwise ranking functions assign a score to each object independently, without taking into account the other objects under consideration; whereas listwise loss functions evaluate the set of scores assigned to all objects as a whole. In many supervised learning to rank tasks, it might be of interest to use listwise ranking functions instead; in particular, the Bayes Optimal ranking functions might themselves be listwise, especially if the loss function is listwise. A key caveat to using listwise ranking functions has been the lack of an appropriate representation theory for such functions. We show that a natural symmetricity assumption that we call exchangeability allows us to explicitly characterize the set of such exchangeable listwise ranking functions. Our analysis draws from the theories of tensor analysis, functional analysis and De Finetti theorems. We also present experiments using a novel reranking method motivated by our representation theory.

paragraphs: A ranking system can score each object independently, or it can choose an ordering using the whole collection of objects. The paper studies the second possibility: listwise ranking functions that return permutations. This distinction matters because a loss that evaluates an entire ordering may have a best possible ranking function that also depends on the collection as a whole.

The authors address a foundational obstacle to using such functions: how to represent their possible forms. They introduce a symmetry assumption called exchangeability and explicitly characterize the listwise ranking functions that satisfy it. The result provides a mathematical description of this class under the stated assumption, drawing on tensor analysis, functional analysis, and De Finetti theorems.

The paper also presents experiments with a new reranking method motivated by the theory. The theoretical contribution clarifies how collection-dependent rankings can be represented, while the method illustrates how that characterization can inform an algorithm. The motivation remains qualified: Bayes-optimal ranking functions may be listwise, especially with listwise losses, rather than necessarily having that form in every ranking task.
summary.tldr: Under an exchangeability assumption, the paper characterizes listwise ranking functions and uses the theory to motivate a reranking method.

title: A Representation Theory for Ranking Functions

abstract: Class ambiguity is typical in image classification problems with a large number of classes. When classes are difficult to discriminate, it makes sense to allow k guesses and evaluate classifiers based on the top-k error instead of the standard zero-one loss. We propose top-k multiclass SVM as a direct method to optimize for top-k performance. Our generalization of the well-known multiclass SVM is based on a tight convex upper bound of the top-k error. We propose a fast optimization scheme based on an efficient projection onto the top-k simplex, which is of its own interest. Experiments on five datasets show consistent improvements in top-k accuracy compared to various baselines.

paragraphs: When an image classification problem has many similar classes, requiring one correct guess can obscure whether a model has identified a useful shortlist. Top-k evaluation allows k guesses and checks whether the correct class appears among them. This paper develops a multiclass support vector machine specifically aimed at that evaluation criterion.

The proposed training objective uses a tight convex upper bound on top-k error. This gives the learning algorithm an optimizable surrogate tied directly to the desired shortlist performance. The authors also introduce a fast optimization method built around efficient projection onto the top-k simplex, a computational operation they identify as useful in its own right.

Experiments on five datasets show consistent improvements in top-k accuracy over the compared baselines. The findings support aligning the training objective with a task that allows multiple candidate labels. The paper contributes both the loss formulation and the optimization machinery needed to use it, with empirical evidence that this alignment improves the evaluated classifiers' ability to include the correct class in their guesses.
summary.tldr: A multiclass SVM trained with a convex surrogate for top-k error consistently improves top-k accuracy across five evaluated datasets.

title: Top-k Multiclass SVM

abstract: A version of the dueling bandit problem is addressed in which a Condorcet winner may not exist. Two algorithms are proposed that instead seek to minimize regret with respect to the Copeland winner, which, unlike the Condorcet winner, is guaranteed to exist. The first, Copeland Confidence Bound (CCB), is designed for small numbers of arms, while the second, Scalable Copeland Bandits (SCB), works better for large-scale problems. We provide theoretical results bounding the regret accumulated by CCB and SCB, both substantially improving existing results. Such existing results either offer bounds of the form O(K log T) but require restrictive assumptions, or offer bounds of the form O(K^2 log T) without requiring such assumptions. Our results offer the best of both worlds: O(K log T) bounds without restrictive assumptions.

We provide theoretical results bounding the regret accumulated by CCB and SCB, both substantially improving existing results. Such existing results either offer bounds of the form O(K log T) but require restrictive assumptions, or offer bounds of the form O(K^2 log T) without requiring such assumptions. Our results offer the best of both worlds: O(K log T) bounds without restrictive assumptions.

paragraphs: Dueling bandit problems involve learning from comparisons between alternatives. A difficulty arises when no single alternative beats every other one: a Condorcet winner may not exist. This paper instead measures performance relative to a Copeland winner, providing a target that is guaranteed to exist in the setting studied.

The authors propose two algorithms for different problem sizes. Copeland Confidence Bound is designed for relatively few alternatives, while Scalable Copeland Bandits is better suited to large collections. Both aim to limit cumulative regret relative to the Copeland benchmark, allowing the learning objective to remain meaningful even when pairwise preferences lack an overall Condorcet winner.

The theoretical contribution improves the dependence of regret bounds on the number of alternatives. Previous results either achieved O(K log T) with restrictive assumptions or O(K² log T) without them. The paper reports O(K log T) bounds without those restrictive assumptions, where K counts alternatives and T counts rounds. This combines a more broadly applicable winner criterion with improved scaling in the stated regret guarantees.
summary.tldr: Two dueling-bandit algorithms target Copeland winners and achieve O(K log T) regret bounds without requiring a Condorcet winner.

title: Copeland Dueling Bandits

abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have recently demonstrated the capability to synthesize compelling real-world images, such as room interiors, album covers, manga, faces, birds, and flowers. While existing models can synthesize images based on global constraints such as a class label or caption, they do not provide control over pose or object location. We propose a new model, the Generative Adversarial What-Where Network (GAWWN), that synthesizes images given instructions describing what content to draw in which location. We show high-quality 128 × 128 image synthesis on the Caltech-UCSD Birds dataset, conditioned on both informal text descriptions and also object location. Our system exposes control over both the bounding box around the bird and its constituent parts. By modeling the conditional distributions over part locations, our system also enables conditioning on arbitrary subsets of parts (e.g. only the beak and tail), yielding an efficient interface for picking part locations.

This paper introduces the Generative Adversarial What-Where Network, or GAWWN, to combine instructions about an image's content with instructions about where that content should appear.

The system exposes control over the bird's bounding box as well as the positions of its individual parts. This gives users ways to specify both the object's overall placement and more detailed spatial structure.

The model also learns conditional distributions over part locations, allowing users to specify arbitrary subsets of parts. For example, they can choose just the beak and tail positions rather than place every part individually. The contribution is therefore an image-generation model with a more selective spatial interface, demonstrated for birds, that connects descriptive content with user-specified layout.
summary.tldr: GAWWN generates bird images from text and spatial instructions, including bounding boxes and selected part locations.

title: Learning What and Where to Draw

abstract: In this paper, we analyze the numerics of common algorithms for training Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). Using the formalism of smooth two-player games we analyze the associated gradient vector field of GAN training objectives. Our findings suggest that the convergence of current algorithms suffers due to two factors: i) presence of eigenvalues of the Jacobian of the gradient vector field with zero real-part, and ii) eigenvalues with big imaginary part. Using these findings, we design a new algorithm that overcomes some of these limitations and has better convergence properties. Experimentally, we demonstrate its superiority on training common GAN architectures and show convergence on GAN architectures that are known to be notoriously hard to train.

paragraphs: GAN training involves two interacting players, so understanding its numerical behavior requires examining their joint updates. This paper models training as a smooth two-player game and studies the gradient vector field associated with the objective. The focus is on why commonly used training algorithms can have difficulty converging.

The analysis identifies two potentially troublesome features in the eigenvalues of the gradient field's Jacobian: zero real parts and large imaginary parts. These quantities describe aspects of the local update dynamics. The findings suggest that both features contribute to convergence problems, providing specific mathematical targets for changing the training algorithm.

Using this diagnosis, the authors design an algorithm with better convergence properties that addresses some of the identified limitations. Experiments show advantages on common GAN architectures and convergence on architectures described as especially difficult to train. The contribution joins an analysis of training dynamics with an algorithm motivated by that analysis, while the stated improvement concerns some numerical obstacles rather than a universal solution to GAN training.
summary.tldr: Analyzing GAN training as a two-player dynamical system reveals numerical obstacles and motivates an algorithm with improved convergence.

title: The Numerics of GANs

abstract: We study the online influence maximization problem in social networks under the independent cascade model. Specifically, we aim to learn the set of "best influencers" in a social network online while repeatedly interacting with it. We address the challenges of (i) combinatorial action space, since the number of feasible influencer sets grows exponentially with the maximum number of influencers, and (ii) limited feedback, since only the influenced portion of the network is observed. Under a stochastic semi-bandit feedback, we propose and analyze IMLinUCB, a computationally efficient UCB-based algorithm. Our bounds on the cumulative regret are polynomial in all quantities of interest, achieve near-optimal dependence on the number of interactions and reflect the topology of the network and the activation probabilities of its edges, thereby giving insights on the problem complexity. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first such results. Our experiments show that in several representative graph topologies, the regret of IMLinUCB scales as suggested by our upper bounds. IMLinUCB permits linear generalization and thus is both statistically and computationally suitable for large-scale problems. Our experiments also show that IMLinUCB with linear generalization can lead to low regret in real-world online influence maximization.
