paragraphs: This paper studies how to learn which people to select as influencers through repeated interaction with a social network. Influence follows the independent cascade model, and feedback reveals only the affected portion of the network. The learner therefore faces both incomplete observations and a rapidly growing number of possible influencer sets.

The proposed IMLinUCB algorithm uses upper confidence bounds under stochastic semi-bandit feedback. Its cumulative regret bounds are polynomial in the relevant quantities and have near-optimal dependence on the number of interactions. They also depend on network topology and edge activation probabilities, making the structure of the spreading process part of the performance analysis.

Experiments indicate that this extension can achieve low regret in real-world influence maximization. The contribution combines an efficient learning method with guarantees that reflect how influence actually propagates through the modeled network.
summary.tldr: IMLinUCB learns influencer sets from partial feedback with topology-sensitive regret guarantees and a scalable linear-generalization extension.

title: Online Influence Maximization under Independent Cascade Model with Semi-Bandit Feedback

abstract: The ability to transfer in reinforcement learning is key towards building an agent of general artificial intelligence. In this paper, we consider the problem of learning to simultaneously transfer across both environments and tasks, probably more importantly, by learning from only sparse (environment, task) pairs out of all the possible combinations. We propose a novel compositional neural network architecture which depicts a meta rule for composing policies from environment and task embeddings. Notably, one of the main challenges is to learn the embeddings jointly with the meta rule. We further propose new training methods to disentangle the embeddings, making them both distinctive signatures of the environments and tasks and effective building blocks for composing the policies. Experiments on GridWorld and THOR, of which the agent takes as input an egocentric view, show that our approach gives rise to high success rates on all the (environment, task) pairs after learning from only 40% of them.

paragraphs: An agent may need to perform different tasks in different environments without having trained on every possible combination. This paper studies simultaneous transfer across those two dimensions. Training covers only a sparse selection of environment-task pairs, so the agent must reuse what it has learned when facing other combinations.

The proposed neural architecture composes policies from separate environment and task embeddings. It learns both those representations and a shared rule for combining them into policies. The authors identify joint learning as a central challenge and introduce training methods to disentangle the embeddings. Each representation should distinguish its environment or task while also functioning as a useful component in policy construction.

Experiments use GridWorld and THOR, with the agent receiving an egocentric view. After training on only 40% of the environment-task combinations, the method achieves high success rates across all pairs. These findings support compositional policy learning in the evaluated settings: representations learned from a partial set of combinations can be recombined to support broader task and environment coverage.
summary.tldr: Policies composed from task and environment embeddings achieve high success across evaluated combinations after training on only 40% of them.

title: Synthesized Policies for Transfer and Adaptation across Tasks and Environments

abstract: We investigate the problem of learning a Lipschitz function from binary feedback. In this problem, a learner is trying to learn a Lipschitz function $f:[0,1]^d \rightarrow [0,1]$ over the course of $T$ rounds. On round $t$, an adversary provides the learner with an input $x_t$, the learner submits a guess $y_t$ for $f(x_t)$, and learns whether $y_t > f(x_t)$ or $y_t \leq f(x_t)$. The learner's goal is to minimize their total loss $\sum_t\ell(f(x_t), y_t)$ (for some loss function $\ell$). The problem is motivated by \textit{contextual dynamic pricing}, where a firm must sell a stream of differentiated products to a collection of buyers with non-linear valuations for the items and observes only whether the item was sold or not at the posted price. For the symmetric loss $\ell(f(x_t), y_t) = \vert f(x_t) - y_t \vert$, we provide an algorithm for this problem achieving total loss $O(\log T)$ when $d=1$ and $O(T^{(d-1)/d})$ when $d>1$, and show that both bounds are tight (up to a factor of $\sqrt{\log T}$). For the pricing loss function $\ell(f(x_t), y_t) = f(x_t) - y_t {\bf 1}\{y_t \leq f(x_t)\}$ we show a regret bound of $O(T^{d/(d+1)})$ and show that this bound is tight. We present improved bounds in the special case of a population of linear buyers.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning a function from feedback that says only whether a guess is too high. Inputs arrive over successive rounds and can be chosen adversarially. The function is assumed to be Lipschitz, meaning its values cannot change arbitrarily sharply between nearby inputs. This structure lets feedback about one input inform learning about related inputs.

The motivating application is pricing differentiated products. A seller posts a price and observes whether a buyer purchases, without seeing the buyer's exact valuation. The authors analyze both absolute prediction error and a pricing loss that accounts for revenue forgone through underpricing or failure to sell. These objectives distinguish accurate value estimation from effective selling.

For absolute error, the total-loss bounds are O(log T) in one dimension and O(T^((d-1)/d)) in higher dimensions, with tightness up to a sqrt(log T) factor. For pricing loss, the regret bound is O(T^(d/(d+1))) and is tight. Improved bounds also hold for a population of linear buyers, showing how additional valuation structure changes the learning guarantees.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes tight or nearly tight learning bounds for Lipschitz valuations observed only through above-or-below feedback, including contextual pricing.

title: Contextual Pricing for Lipschitz Buyers

abstract: High sensitivity of neural networks against malicious perturbations on inputs causes security concerns. To take a steady step towards robust classifiers, we aim to create neural network models provably defended from perturbations. Prior certification work requires strong assumptions on network structures and massive computational costs, and thus the range of their applications was limited. From the relationship between the Lipschitz constants and prediction margins, we present a computationally efficient calculation technique to lower-bound the size of adversarial perturbations that can deceive networks, and that is widely applicable to various complicated networks. Moreover, we propose an efficient training procedure that robustifies networks and significantly improves the provably guarded areas around data points. In experimental evaluations, our method showed its ability to provide a non-trivial guarantee and enhance robustness for even large networks.

paragraphs: The paper seeks classifiers with provable protection against small input perturbations. Its focus is certification: establishing a region around an input within which the network cannot be deceived by a perturbation. Earlier certification methods required restrictive network structures or substantial computation, limiting where such guarantees could be used.

The authors connect prediction margins with Lipschitz constants, which describe how strongly a network's outputs can change as its input changes. They use this relationship to compute a lower bound on the size of an adversarial perturbation capable of deceiving the network. The calculation is designed to be efficient and applicable to a broad range of complicated architectures.

They also propose a training procedure that increases the provably protected regions around data points. Experimental evaluations show non-trivial guarantees and enhanced robustness even for large networks. The protection is expressed through certified perturbation sizes around particular inputs, making the result a bounded guarantee whose practical strength can be improved during training.
summary.tldr: Lipschitz-margin calculations and training efficiently certify and enlarge regions of perturbation invariance, including for large networks in experiments.

title: Lipschitz-Margin Training: Scalable Certification of Perturbation Invariance for Deep Neural Networks

abstract: This paper proposes a stochastic variant of a classic algorithm---the cubic-regularized Newton method [Nesterov and Polyak]. The proposed algorithm efficiently escapes saddle points and finds approximate local minima for general smooth, nonconvex functions in only $\mathcal{\tilde{O}}(\epsilon^{-3.5})$ stochastic gradient and stochastic Hessian-vector product evaluations. The latter can be computed as efficiently as stochastic gradients. This improves upon the $\mathcal{\tilde{O}}(\epsilon^{-4})$ rate of stochastic gradient descent. Our rate matches the best-known result for finding local minima without requiring any delicate acceleration or variance-reduction techniques.

The latter can be computed as efficiently as stochastic gradients. This improves upon the $\mathcal{\tilde{O}}(\epsilon^{-4})$ rate of stochastic gradient descent. paragraphs: For smooth nonconvex objectives, reaching a point with little gradient does not by itself establish that the point is a local minimum; saddle points also matter. This paper proposes a stochastic version of the cubic-regularized Newton method designed to escape saddles efficiently and find approximate local minima.

The algorithm uses stochastic gradients and stochastic Hessian-vector products. A Hessian-vector product supplies curvature information along a direction, and the abstract states that these products can be computed as efficiently as stochastic gradients. This makes curvature information available through operations whose individual cost can remain comparable to the gradient computations already used in stochastic optimization.

The method requires Õ(ε^-3.5) evaluations of these quantities, improving on the stated Õ(ε^-4) rate for stochastic gradient descent. The notation suppresses logarithmic factors. Its rate matches the best-known local-minimum result cited in the abstract without delicate acceleration or variance-reduction techniques. The contribution is therefore a stronger evaluation-complexity guarantee for approximate local optimization, achieved through a stochastic curvature-based method.
summary.tldr: Stochastic cubic regularization finds approximate local minima with Õ(ε^-3.5) gradient and Hessian-vector evaluations, improving the stated SGD rate.

title: Stochastic Cubic Regularization for Fast Nonconvex Optimization

abstract: Key to structured prediction is exploiting the problem's structure to simplify the learning process. A major challenge arises when data exhibit a local structure (i.e., are made ``by parts'') that can be leveraged to better approximate the relation between (parts of) the input and (parts of) the output. Recent literature on signal processing, and in particular computer vision, shows that capturing these aspects is indeed essential to achieve state-of-the-art performance. However, in this context algorithms are typically derived on a case-by-case basis. In this work we propose the first theoretical framework to deal with part-based data from a general perspective and study a novel method within the setting of statistical learning theory. Our analysis is novel in that it explicitly quantifies the benefits of leveraging the part-based structure of a problem on the learning rates of the proposed estimator.

paragraphs: Structured prediction benefits from recognizing how a prediction problem is organized internally. The paper focuses on data composed of parts, where relationships between input parts and output parts can help approximate the overall mapping. Such local structure is important in areas including signal processing and computer vision, but algorithms often address it through problem-specific designs.

The authors propose a general theoretical framework for learning from part-based data and study a new method within statistical learning theory. The goal is to describe the role of local structure in terms that extend beyond an individual application. This makes the connection between the organization of the data and the learning procedure an explicit object of analysis.

The main theoretical contribution quantifies how using part-based structure benefits the proposed estimator’s learning rates. Learning rates describe how estimation improves as training information grows, so the analysis gives a precise way to discuss the value of locality. The paper’s significance lies in placing a widely useful design idea within a general framework that relates problem structure to learning behavior.
summary.tldr: A general framework for part-based structured prediction quantifies how exploiting local structure improves an estimator’s learning rates.

title: Localized Structured Prediction

abstract: We introduce graph normalizing flows: a new, reversible graph neural network model for prediction and generation. On supervised tasks, graph normalizing flows perform similarly to message passing neural networks, but at a significantly reduced memory footprint, allowing them to scale to larger graphs. In the unsupervised case, we combine graph normalizing flows with a novel graph auto-encoder to create a generative model of graph structures. Our model is permutation-invariant, generating entire graphs with a single feed-forward pass, and achieves competitive results with the state-of-the art auto-regressive models, while being better suited to parallel computing architectures.

In the unsupervised case, we combine graph normalizing flows with a novel graph auto-encoder to create a generative model of graph structures. Our model is permutation-invariant, generating entire graphs with a single feed-forward pass, and achieves competitive results with the state-of-the art auto-regressive models, while being better suited to parallel computing architectures.

paragraphs: Graph Normalizing Flows introduces a reversible graph neural network for both prediction and generation. The supervised part addresses a practical scaling problem: graph models must manage memory as graph size increases. The authors report predictive performance similar to message passing neural networks while using significantly less memory.

That smaller memory footprint allows the model to scale to larger graphs. For unsupervised learning, the authors combine the flow model with a new graph autoencoder to generate graph structures. The resulting generative model is permutation-invariant, so arbitrary ordering of graph elements does not define the modeled structure.

The model generates an entire graph in one feed-forward pass. This organization is better suited to parallel computing architectures than the autoregressive models used for comparison, while achieving competitive results. The paper thus connects two computational advantages to graph learning: reduced memory for supervised prediction and whole-graph generation that supports parallel execution. Its reported comparisons establish similar or competitive performance alongside these architectural benefits.
summary.tldr: Reversible graph networks reduce prediction memory requirements and support competitive, permutation-invariant graph generation in a single feed-forward pass.

title: Graph Normalizing Flows

abstract: The covariance matrix of a dataset is a fundamental statistic that can be used for calculating optimum regression weights as well as in many other learning and data analysis settings. For datasets containing private user information, we often want to estimate the covariance matrix in a way that preserves differential privacy. While there are known methods for privately computing the covariance matrix, they all have one of two major shortcomings. Some, like the Gaussian mechanism, only guarantee (epsilon, delta)-differential privacy, leaving a non-trivial probability of privacy failure. Others give strong epsilon-differential privacy guarantees, but are impractical, requiring complicated sampling schemes, and tend to perform poorly on real data. In this work we propose a new epsilon-differentially private algorithm for computing the covariance matrix of a dataset that addresses both of these limitations. We show that it has lower error than existing state-of-the-art approaches, both analytically and empirically. In addition, the algorithm is significantly less complicated than other methods and can be efficiently implemented with rejection sampling.

paragraphs: A covariance matrix summarizes how variables vary together and supports tasks such as calculating regression weights. When the underlying records contain private information, releasing this statistic requires privacy protection. This paper studies how to estimate covariance while obtaining a strong formal privacy guarantee and keeping the computation practical.

The authors identify two drawbacks in existing approaches. Some provide the relaxed guarantee of epsilon-delta differential privacy, while methods providing pure epsilon differential privacy can involve complicated sampling and perform poorly on real data. Their proposed algorithm targets both issues by providing epsilon differential privacy through a comparatively simple procedure that can be implemented efficiently with rejection sampling.

The paper reports lower estimation error than existing state-of-the-art methods, supported by both mathematical analysis and empirical evaluation. Its contribution therefore concerns privacy, accuracy, and implementation complexity together. For applications that need covariance estimates, the stated findings show that a stronger privacy guarantee can be paired with competitive computation and improved accuracy in the comparisons studied.
summary.tldr: A covariance estimation algorithm provides pure differential privacy with simpler sampling and lower theoretical and empirical error than existing approaches.

title: Differentially Private Covariance Estimation

abstract: In this work, we aim to leverage prior symbolic knowledge to improve the performance of deep models. We propose a graph embedding network that projects propositional formulae (and assignments) onto a manifold via an augmented Graph Convolutional Network (GCN). To generate semantically-faithful embeddings, we develop techniques to recognize node heterogeneity, and semantic regularization that incorporate structural constraints into the embedding. Experiments show that our approach improves the performance of models trained to perform entailment checking and visual relation prediction. Interestingly, we observe a connection between the tractability of the propositional theory representation and the ease of embedding. Future exploration of this connection may elucidate the relationship between knowledge compilation and vector representation learning.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how symbolic knowledge can help deep models. Its inputs include propositional formulas and assignments, which carry logical meaning as well as structure. The proposed graph embedding network maps these objects into a learned geometric representation using an augmented graph convolutional network, making symbolic information available in a form usable by neural models.

Preserving meaning during that mapping is a central concern. The method distinguishes different types of nodes and uses semantic regularization to incorporate structural constraints into the embeddings. These components aim to make the learned representations faithful to the symbolic objects, so their usefulness depends on more than simply turning a graph into a vector.

Experiments report improvements on entailment checking and visual relation prediction. The authors also observe a connection between how tractable a propositional theory's representation is and how easily it can be embedded. They present further study of that connection as a possible route to understanding the relationship between knowledge compilation and vector representation learning, rather than as an already established general result.
summary.tldr: A graph embedding network incorporates logical structure into neural representations and improves entailment checking and visual relation prediction.

title: Embedding Symbolic Knowledge into Deep Networks

abstract: We study first-order optimization algorithms obtained by discretizing ordinary differential equations (ODEs) corresponding to Nesterov’s accelerated gradient methods (NAGs) and Polyak’s heavy-ball method. We consider three discretization schemes: symplectic Euler (S), explicit Euler (E) and implicit Euler (I) schemes. We show that the optimization algorithm generated by applying the symplectic scheme to a high-resolution ODE proposed by Shi et al. [2018] achieves the accelerated rate for minimizing both strongly convex function and convex function. On the other hand, the resulting algorithm either fails to achieve acceleration or is impractical when the scheme is implicit, the ODE is low-resolution, or the scheme is explicit.

paragraphs: Optimization algorithms can be studied through differential equations that describe continuous motion toward a solution. Turning those equations into an executable algorithm requires choosing discrete update steps. This paper examines that conversion for equations associated with Nesterov's accelerated gradient methods and Polyak's heavy-ball method, asking which combinations preserve accelerated optimization.

The authors compare symplectic Euler, explicit Euler, and implicit Euler discretization. Their positive result pairs the symplectic scheme with a high-resolution differential equation. The resulting first-order algorithm achieves accelerated convergence for both convex and strongly convex objectives. Thus, the continuous model and the rule used to discretize it jointly determine the useful algorithmic behavior.

The alternatives examined do not provide the same practical outcome: using an implicit scheme, a low-resolution equation, or an explicit scheme leads to algorithms that either lack acceleration or are impractical. This finding makes discretization a substantive part of the acceleration story. A continuous description associated with fast optimization does not, by itself, settle how to obtain a practical accelerated discrete method.
summary.tldr: Symplectic discretization of a high-resolution differential equation produces accelerated algorithms for convex and strongly convex optimization.

title: Acceleration via Symplectic Discretization of High-Resolution Differential Equations

abstract: Sampling from log-concave distributions is a well researched problem that has many applications in statistics and machine learning. We study the distributions of the form $p^{*}\propto\exp(-f(x))$, where $f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ has an $L$-Lipschitz gradient and is $m$-strongly convex. In our paper, we propose a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm based on the underdamped Langevin diffusion (ULD). It can achieve $\epsilon\cdot D$ error (in 2-Wasserstein distance) in $\tilde{O}\left(\kappa^{7/6}/\epsilon^{1/3}+\kappa/\epsilon^{2/3}\right)$ steps, where $D\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\sqrt{\frac{d}{m}}$ is the effective diameter of the problem and $\kappa\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}\frac{L}{m}$ is the condition number. Our algorithm performs significantly faster than the previously best known algorithm for solving this problem, which requires $\tilde{O}\left(\kappa^{1.5}/\epsilon\right)$ steps \cite{chen2019optimal,dalalyan2018sampling}. Moreover, our algorithm can be easily parallelized to require only $O(\kappa\log\frac{1}{\epsilon})$ parallel steps. To solve the sampling problem, we propose a new framework to discretize stochastic differential equations. We apply this framework to discretize and simulate ULD, which converges to the target distribution $p^{*}$. The framework can be used to solve not only the log-concave sampling problem, but any problem that involves simulating (stochastic) differential equations.

title: The Randomized Midpoint Method for Log-Concave Sampling

abstract: We examine the problem of transferring a policy learned in a source environment to a target environment with different dynamics, particularly in the case where it is critical to reduce the amount of interaction with the target environment during learning. This problem is particularly important in sim-to-real transfer because simulators inevitably model real-world dynamics imperfectly. In this paper, we show that one existing solution to this transfer problem-- grounded action transformation --is closely related to the problem of imitation from observation (IfO): learning behaviors that mimic the observations of behavior demonstrations. After establishing this relationship, we hypothesize that recent state-of-the-art approaches from the IfO literature can be effectively repurposed for grounded transfer learning. To validate our hypothesis we derive a new algorithm -- generative adversarial reinforced action transformation (GARAT) -- based on adversarial imitation from observation techniques. We run experiments in several domains with mismatched dynamics, and find that agents trained with GARAT achieve higher returns in the target environment compared to existing black-box transfer methods.

paragraphs: A policy learned in one environment may perform poorly in another when the same actions produce different effects. This matters for transferring behavior from simulation to reality, where the simulator cannot perfectly reproduce physical dynamics. The paper studies this transfer problem with particular attention to situations where learning must limit interaction with the target environment.

The authors establish a close relationship between grounded action transformation, an existing transfer approach, and imitation from observation. In imitation from observation, the learner tries to reproduce observed behavior. This connection suggests that techniques developed for matching behavioral observations could also help adapt a policy across environments with different dynamics.

Building on that relationship, the paper introduces generative adversarial reinforced action transformation, or GARAT. The algorithm repurposes adversarial imitation-from-observation techniques for grounded transfer learning. Experiments across several domains with mismatched dynamics produce higher target-environment returns than the compared black-box transfer methods. The findings support the proposed connection as a useful source of transfer algorithms, with the reported advantage established in the tested domains.
summary.tldr: GARAT applies imitation-from-observation techniques to policy transfer and achieves higher returns in tested environments with mismatched dynamics.

title: An Imitation from Observation Approach to Transfer Learning with Dynamics Mismatch

abstract: Co-Salient Object Detection (CoSOD) aims at discovering salient objects that repeatedly appear in a given query group containing two or more relevant images. One challenging issue is how to effectively capture co-saliency cues by modeling and exploiting inter-image relationships. In this paper, we present an end-to-end collaborative aggregation-and-distribution network (CoADNet) to capture both salient and repetitive visual patterns from multiple images. First, we integrate saliency priors into the backbone features to suppress the redundant background information through an online intra-saliency guidance structure. After that, we design a two-stage aggregate-and-distribute architecture to explore group-wise semantic interactions and produce the co-saliency features. In the first stage, we propose a group-attentional semantic aggregation module that models inter-image relationships to generate the group-wise semantic representations. In the second stage, we propose a gated group distribution module that adaptively distributes the learned group semantics to different individuals in a dynamic gating mechanism. Finally, we develop a group consistency preserving decoder tailored for the CoSOD task, which maintains group constraints during feature decoding to predict more consistent full-resolution co-saliency maps. The proposed CoADNet is evaluated on four prevailing CoSOD benchmark datasets, which demonstrates the remarkable performance improvement over ten state-of-the-art competitors.

paragraphs: Co-salient object detection looks for visually prominent objects that recur across a group of related images. Success requires understanding both each image and the relationships among images. CoADNet addresses this with an end-to-end network that gathers shared information from the group and then returns relevant information to each individual image.

The network first uses saliency guidance to suppress redundant background information in its features. A group attention module then aggregates semantic information across images. Next, a gated distribution module adaptively sends the resulting group representation back to individual images. This lets shared evidence influence each image according to its particular content.

A final decoder preserves group consistency while producing full-resolution maps of the co-salient objects. The design thus carries relationships across images through both feature construction and output prediction. Evaluation on four benchmark datasets reports substantial improvements over ten state-of-the-art competitors. These findings support the value of combining shared group understanding with image-specific adaptation throughout the detection process.
summary.tldr: CoADNet improves co-salient object detection by aggregating information across related images and adaptively distributing it back to each image.

title: CoADNet: Collaborative Aggregation-and-Distribution Networks for Co-Salient Object Detection

abstract: The idea behind data augmentation techniques is based on the fact that slight changes in the percept do not change the brain cognition. In classification, neural networks use this fact by applying transformations to the inputs to learn to predict the same label. However, in deep subspace clustering (DSC), the ground-truth labels are not available, and as a result, one cannot easily use data augmentation techniques. We propose a technique to exploit the benefits of data augmentation in DSC algorithms. We learn representations that have consistent subspaces for slightly transformed inputs. In particular, we introduce a temporal ensembling component to the objective function of DSC algorithms to enable the DSC networks to maintain consistent subspaces for random transformations in the input data. In addition, we provide a simple yet effective unsupervised procedure to find efficient data augmentation policies. An augmentation policy is defined as an image processing transformation with a certain magnitude and probability of being applied to each image in each epoch. We search through the policies in a search space of the most common augmentation policies to find the best policy such that the DSC network yields the highest mean Silhouette coefficient in its clustering results on a target dataset. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on four standard subspace clustering datasets.

paragraphs: Data augmentation commonly teaches a classifier to assign the same label to slightly altered versions of an input. Deep subspace clustering cannot use that instruction directly because it lacks ground-truth labels. This paper instead asks the learned representation to preserve its subspace structure when inputs undergo small transformations, adapting the consistency idea to an unsupervised task.

The method adds a temporal ensembling component to the clustering objective. This encourages consistent subspaces across randomly transformed inputs, providing a training signal without labeled categories. The authors also propose an unsupervised procedure for choosing augmentation policies. Each policy specifies an image transformation, its strength, and the probability that it is applied during an epoch.

To select a policy, the procedure searches common augmentation choices and favors the one yielding the highest mean Silhouette coefficient on the target dataset. This uses the structure of the resulting clusters to guide augmentation selection. The authors report state-of-the-art performance on four standard subspace clustering datasets, supporting both the consistency objective and the practical value of selecting augmentations without labels.
summary.tldr: Subspace consistency and unsupervised augmentation selection bring the benefits of transformed training inputs to deep subspace clustering.

title: Deep Subspace Clustering with Data Augmentation

abstract: Global context is crucial for 3D point cloud scene understanding tasks. In this work, we extended the contextual encoding layer that was originally designed for 2D tasks to 3D Point Cloud scenarios. The encoding layer learns a set of code words in the feature space of the 3D point cloud to characterize the global semantic context, and then based on these code words, the method learns a global contextual descriptor to reweight the featuremaps accordingly. Moreover, compared to 2D scenarios, data sparsity becomes a major issue in 3D point cloud scenarios, and the performance of contextual encoding quickly saturates when the number of code words increases. To mitigate this problem, we further proposed a group contextual encoding method, which divides the channel into groups and then performs encoding on group-divided feature vectors. This method facilitates learning of global context in grouped subspace for 3D point clouds. We evaluate the effectiveness and generalizability of our method on three widely-studied 3D point cloud tasks. Experimental results have shown that the proposed method outperformed the VoteNet remarkably with 3 mAP on the benchmark of SUN-RGBD, with the metrics of mAP@ 0.25, and a much greater margin of 6.57 mAP on ScanNet with the metrics of mAP@ 0.5. Compared to the baseline of PointNet++, the proposed method leads to an accuracy of 86 %, outperforming the baseline by 1.5 %. Our proposed method have outperformed the non-grouping baseline methods across the board and establishes new state-of-the-art on these benchmarks.

This paper adapts a contextual encoding layer from two-dimensional tasks to point clouds. The layer learns representative code words in feature space and uses them to construct a global descriptor that reweights the network's feature maps.

Point-cloud sparsity creates a difficulty: adding more code words quickly stops improving ordinary contextual encoding. The proposed solution divides feature channels into groups and encodes each group's feature vectors separately. This lets the model learn global context within smaller feature subspaces, addressing the observed saturation through a change in how features are organized.

Experiments across three point-cloud tasks show improvements over non-grouped encoding. Relative to VoteNet, the method gains 3 mAP on SUN-RGBD at the 0.25 threshold and 6.57 mAP on ScanNet at the 0.5 threshold. It also reaches 86% accuracy, a reported 1.5% improvement over PointNet++. These findings support grouped context encoding as useful across the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Encoding global point-cloud context in groups of feature channels improves results across the paper's evaluated 3D tasks.

title: Group Contextual Encoding for 3D Point Clouds

abstract: Metropolis-Hastings (MH) is a commonly-used MCMC algorithm, but it can be intractable on large datasets due to requiring computations over the whole dataset. In this paper, we study \emph{minibatch MH} methods, which instead use subsamples to enable scaling. We observe that most existing minibatch MH methods are inexact (i.e. they may change the target distribution), and show that this inexactness can cause arbitrarily large errors in inference. We propose a new exact minibatch MH method, \emph{TunaMH}, which exposes a tunable trade-off between its minibatch size and its theoretically guaranteed convergence rate. We prove a lower bound on the batch size that any minibatch MH method \emph{must} use to retain exactness while guaranteeing fast convergence---the first such bound for minibatch MH---and show TunaMH is asymptotically optimal in terms of the batch size. Empirically, we show TunaMH outperforms other exact minibatch MH methods on robust linear regression, truncated Gaussian mixtures, and logistic regression.

paragraphs: Metropolis-Hastings can become expensive when its computations require the entire dataset. Minibatch methods reduce that workload by using subsets, but many existing approaches also change the distribution being sampled. The paper shows that this loss of exactness can produce arbitrarily large inference errors, making the computational shortcut potentially consequential.

The proposed method, TunaMH, preserves the target distribution while using minibatches. It exposes a tunable tradeoff between batch size and a theoretically guaranteed convergence rate. This makes the amount of data processed and the speed of convergence explicit parts of the same design, rather than treating smaller batches as an unconditional improvement.

The authors also prove a lower bound on the batch size required to combine exactness with guaranteed fast convergence. TunaMH meets this requirement asymptotically, establishing its batch-size optimality in that sense. Experiments on robust linear regression, truncated Gaussian mixtures, and logistic regression show that it outperforms other exact minibatch methods. Exactness here concerns preserving the target distribution; convergence rate remains a separate quantity controlled by the tradeoff.
summary.tldr: TunaMH preserves the target distribution while trading minibatch size against convergence rate, and achieves asymptotically optimal batch size under the stated requirements.

title: Asymptotically Optimal Exact Minibatch Metropolis-Hastings

abstract: Deep ensembles have recently gained popularity in the deep learning community for their conceptual simplicity and efficiency. However, maintaining functional diversity between ensemble members that are independently trained with gradient descent is challenging. This can lead to pathologies when adding more ensemble members, such as a saturation of the ensemble performance, which converges to the performance of a single model. Moreover, this does not only affect the quality of its predictions, but even more so the uncertainty estimates of the ensemble, and thus its performance on out-of-distribution data. We hypothesize that this limitation can be overcome by discouraging different ensemble members from collapsing to the same function. To this end, we introduce a kernelized repulsive term in the update rule of the deep ensembles. We show that this simple modification not only enforces and maintains diversity among the members but, even more importantly, transforms the maximum a posteriori inference into proper Bayesian inference. Namely, we show that the training dynamics of our proposed repulsive ensembles follow a Wasserstein gradient flow of the KL divergence with the true posterior. We study repulsive terms in weight and function space and empirically compare their performance to standard ensembles and Bayesian baselines on synthetic and real-world prediction tasks.

paragraphs: An ensemble benefits from having models that behave differently, but independently trained networks can converge to similar functions. Adding more members may then offer little improvement and can leave uncertainty estimates inadequate, especially for unfamiliar data. This paper investigates whether explicitly discouraging such functional collapse can improve the foundations of ensemble training.

The authors add a kernel-based repulsive term to the update rule, encouraging members to remain diverse. They study repulsion in both weight space and function space. The theoretical result connects the resulting training dynamics to a Wasserstein gradient flow of the Kullback–Leibler divergence relative to the true posterior.

This connection gives the modified dynamics a Bayesian interpretation beyond independent maximum a posteriori estimation. Diversity is therefore tied to an inference objective, rather than serving only as a practical preference among ensemble members. The paper also compares repulsive ensembles with standard ensembles and Bayesian baselines on synthetic and real-world prediction tasks, examining the behaviour of the proposed modification empirically.
summary.tldr: Kernel-based repulsion maintains ensemble diversity and connects ensemble training dynamics to Bayesian posterior inference.

title: Repulsive Deep Ensembles are Bayesian

abstract: Transformers, the de-facto standard for language modeling, have been recently applied for vision tasks. This paper introduces sparse queries for vision transformers to exploit the intrinsic spatial redundancy of natural images and save computational costs. Specifically, we propose a Dynamic Grained Encoder for vision transformers, which can adaptively assign a suitable number of queries to each spatial region. Thus it achieves a fine-grained representation in discriminative regions while keeping high efficiency. Besides, the dynamic grained encoder is compatible with most vision transformer frameworks. Without bells and whistles, our encoder allows the state-of-the-art vision transformers to reduce computational complexity by 40%-60% while maintaining comparable performance on image classification. Extensive experiments on object detection and segmentation further demonstrate the generalizability of our approach. Code is available at https://github.com/StevenGrove/vtpack.

paragraphs: Natural images contain spatial redundancy, so different regions need not receive the same amount of processing. This paper introduces a Dynamic Grained Encoder that adjusts how many queries a vision transformer assigns to each region. Its aim is to retain detailed representations where they help distinguish image content while reducing computational work elsewhere.

The mechanism uses sparse queries and adapts their allocation across space. Discriminative regions receive a finer representation, allowing the model to devote more of its representational effort to useful details. The encoder is designed to work with most vision transformer frameworks, making the proposed allocation strategy applicable across a broad family of models.

For image classification, the authors report reductions of 40%–60% in computational complexity while maintaining comparable performance with the evaluated state-of-the-art vision transformers. Additional detection and segmentation experiments support the approach's generalizability across vision tasks. These findings concern a more selective use of computation: the encoder changes spatial processing granularity while preserving useful information for the tested tasks.
summary.tldr: The Dynamic Grained Encoder allocates transformer queries by image region, reducing reported classification computation by 40%–60% with comparable performance.

title: Dynamic Grained Encoder for Vision Transformers

abstract: One of the challenges in online reinforcement learning (RL) is that the agent needs to trade off the exploration of the environment and the exploitation of the samples to optimize its behavior. Whether we optimize for regret, sample complexity, state-space coverage or model estimation, we need to strike a different exploration-exploitation trade-off. In this paper, we propose to tackle the exploration-exploitation problem following a decoupled approach composed of: 1) An "objective-specific" algorithm that (adaptively) prescribes how many samples to collect at which states, as if it has access to a generative model (i.e., a simulator of the environment); 2) An "objective-agnostic" sample collection exploration strategy responsible for generating the prescribed samples as fast as possible. Building on recent methods for exploration in the stochastic shortest path problem, we first provide an algorithm that, given as input the number of samples $b(s,a)$ needed in each state-action pair, requires $\widetilde{O}(B D + D^{3/2} S^2 A)$ time steps to collect the $B=\sum_{s,a} b(s,a)$ desired samples, in any unknown communicating MDP with $S$ states, $A$ actions and diameter $D$. Then we show how this general-purpose exploration algorithm can be paired with "objective-specific" strategies that prescribe the sample requirements to tackle a variety of settings — e.g., model estimation, sparse reward discovery, goal-free cost-free exploration in communicating MDPs — for which we obtain improved or novel sample complexity guarantees.

paragraphs: Different reinforcement learning objectives can require different kinds of exploration. Collecting data to estimate an environment is not the same task as finding rewarding behavior or covering its states. This paper separates decisions about which samples are needed from the practical problem of navigating the environment to obtain them.

The first component is specific to the learning objective: it requests numbers of samples at particular state-action pairs, behaving as though a simulator could supply them directly. The second component is a general collection strategy that fulfills those requests through actual interaction. Its design builds on exploration methods for stochastic shortest path problems.

For an unknown communicating Markov decision process, the paper bounds collection time using the total requested samples, the numbers of states and actions, and the environment's diameter. The bound is approximately BD plus D to the three-halves power times S squared A, ignoring logarithmic factors. Combining this collector with different request strategies yields improved or new sample guarantees for model estimation, sparse reward discovery, and exploration without predefined goals or costs.
summary.tldr: Separating sample requests from sample collection yields a reusable exploration strategy with provable efficiency across several reinforcement learning objectives.

title: A Provably Efficient Sample Collection Strategy for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: A seminal result in game theory is von Neumann's minmax theorem, which states that zero-sum games admit an essentially unique equilibrium solution. Classical learning results build on this theorem to show that online no-regret dynamics converge to an equilibrium in a time-average sense in zero-sum games. In the past several years, a key research direction has focused on characterizing the transient behavior of such dynamics. General results in this direction show that broad classes of online learning dynamics are cyclic, and formally Poincar\'{e} recurrent, in zero-sum games. We analyze the robustness of these online learning behaviors in the case of periodic zero-sum games with a time-invariant equilibrium. This model generalizes the usual repeated game formulation while also being a realistic and natural model of a repeated competition between players that depends on exogenous environmental variations such as time-of-day effects, week-to-week trends, and seasonality. Interestingly, time-average convergence may fail even in the simplest such settings, in spite of the equilibrium being fixed. In contrast, using novel analysis methods, we show that Poincar\'{e} recurrence provably generalizes despite the complex, non-autonomous nature of these dynamical systems.

Classical learning results build on this theorem to show that online no-regret dynamics converge to an equilibrium in a time-average sense in zero-sum games. In the past several years, a key research direction has focused on characterizing the transient behavior of such dynamics. General results in this direction show that broad classes of online learning dynamics are cyclic, and formally Poincar\'{e} recurrent, in zero-sum games. We analyze the robustness of these online learning behaviors in the case of periodic zero-sum games with a time-invariant equilibrium. This model generalizes the usual repeated game formulation while also being a realistic and natural model of a repeated competition between players that depends on exogenous environmental variations such as time-of-day effects, week-to-week trends, and seasonality. Interestingly, time-average convergence may fail even in the simplest such settings, in spite of the equilibrium being fixed. In contrast, using novel analysis methods, we show that Poincar\'{e} recurrence provably generalizes despite the complex, non-autonomous nature of these dynamical systems.

paragraphs: In fixed zero-sum games, classical results connect no-regret learning with convergence to equilibrium when behavior is averaged over time. The individual learning trajectories can still cycle. This paper asks which of these behaviors persist when the game itself changes periodically, while its equilibrium remains fixed throughout those changes.

Periodic games model repeated competition affected by external variation such as time of day or seasonality. The authors show that time-average convergence can fail even in simple instances of this setting. A fixed equilibrium therefore does not by itself preserve the familiar averaging result once the surrounding game changes over time.

The authors also prove that Poincaré recurrence generalizes to the periodic setting they analyze. Recurrence describes trajectories returning arbitrarily close to earlier states, so it captures a persistent form of cycling. Establishing this requires handling dynamics that explicitly depend on time. The results distinguish two behaviors often discussed together: equilibrium convergence through averaging can break down, while recurrent learning trajectories can remain.
summary.tldr: Periodic changes in zero-sum games can defeat time-average convergence even with a fixed equilibrium, while recurrence still generalizes.

title: Online Learning in Periodic Zero-Sum Games

abstract: We study a bandit version of phase retrieval where the learner chooses actions $(A_t)_{t=1}^n$ in the $d$-dimensional unit ball and the expected reward is $\langle A_t, \theta_\star \rangle^2$ with $\theta_\star \in \mathbb R^d$ an unknown parameter vector. We prove an upper bound on the minimax cumulative regret in this problem of $\smash{\tilde \Theta(d \sqrt{n})}$, which matches known lower bounds up to logarithmic factors and improves on the best known upper bound by a factor of $\smash{\sqrt{d}}$. We also show that the minimax simple regret is $\smash{\tilde \Theta(d / \sqrt{n})}$ and that this is only achievable by an adaptive algorithm. Our analysis shows that an apparently convincing heuristic for guessing lower bounds can be misleading and that uniform bounds on the information ratio for information-directed sampling (Russo and Van Roy, 2014) are not sufficient for optimal regret.

paragraphs: This paper studies a sequential decision problem in which an action is a vector inside a d-dimensional unit ball. Its expected reward is the squared inner product between that action and an unknown parameter vector. The learner therefore needs to discover rewarding directions while making decisions, with the squared reward obscuring the sign of the underlying alignment.

The authors establish a cumulative regret upper bound of order d times the square root of the number of rounds, ignoring logarithmic factors. Cumulative regret measures reward lost throughout learning relative to the best action. This bound matches known lower bounds up to logarithmic factors and improves the previous upper bound by a factor of the square root of d.

They also characterize simple regret, which concerns the quality of the final recommendation, as order d divided by the square root of the number of rounds, again up to logarithmic factors. Achieving this rate requires adaptivity. The analysis further shows that a plausible lower-bound heuristic can mislead and that uniform information-ratio bounds alone do not suffice for optimal regret.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes near-optimal regret rates for bandit phase retrieval and shows that optimal simple regret requires adaptive learning.

title: Bandit Phase Retrieval

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) often suffer from weak-generalization due to sparsely labeled data despite their promising results on various graph-based tasks. Data augmentation is a prevalent remedy to improve the generalization ability of models in many domains. However, due to the non-Euclidean nature of data space and the dependencies between samples, designing effective augmentation on graphs is challenging. In this paper, we propose a novel framework Metropolis-Hastings Data Augmentation (MH-Aug) that draws augmented graphs from an explicit target distribution for semi-supervised learning. MH-Aug produces a sequence of augmented graphs from the target distribution enables flexible control of the strength and diversity of augmentation. Since the direct sampling from the complex target distribution is challenging, we adopt the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm to obtain the augmented samples. We also propose a simple and effective semi-supervised learning strategy with generated samples from MH-Aug. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that MH-Aug can generate a sequence of samples according to the target distribution to significantly improve the performance of GNNs.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can generalize poorly when only a small portion of their data is labeled. Data augmentation offers a possible remedy, but graph structure and dependencies between samples complicate the design of useful transformations. This paper proposes an approach that specifies a target distribution over augmented graphs.

The framework, Metropolis-Hastings Data Augmentation or MH-Aug, generates a sequence of graphs according to that distribution. An explicit target gives control over both the strength and diversity of augmentation. Because directly sampling from the target can be difficult, the method uses the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm to obtain the augmented samples.

The authors also introduce a semi-supervised learning strategy that uses the generated graphs. Experiments show that MH-Aug can produce samples following the target distribution and significantly improve GNN performance. The contribution connects augmentation design to a sampling problem: the desired variation is expressed through a distribution, and a sampling method supplies graphs for training. This provides a structured way to control augmentation in the sparsely labeled setting studied.
summary.tldr: MH-Aug samples augmented graphs from an explicit target distribution to control augmentation and improve semi-supervised GNN performance.

title: Metropolis-Hastings Data Augmentation for Graph Neural Networks

abstract: We study the design of explicable reward functions for a reinforcement learning agent while guaranteeing that an optimal policy induced by the function belongs to a set of target policies. By being explicable, we seek to capture two properties: (a) informativeness so that the rewards speed up the agent's convergence, and (b) sparseness as a proxy for ease of interpretability of the rewards. The key challenge is that higher informativeness typically requires dense rewards for many learning tasks, and existing techniques do not allow one to balance these two properties appropriately. In this paper, we investigate the problem from the perspective of discrete optimization and introduce a novel framework, ExpRD, to design explicable reward functions. ExpRD builds upon an informativeness criterion that captures the (sub-)optimality of target policies at different time horizons in terms of actions taken from any given starting state. We provide a mathematical analysis of ExpRD, and show its connections to existing reward design techniques, including potential-based reward shaping. Experimental results on two navigation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of ExpRD in designing explicable reward functions.

paragraphs: A reward function should guide an agent toward desired behavior, but it can also shape how easily the agent learns and how understandable the rewards appear. This paper studies rewards with two properties: informativeness, intended to accelerate convergence, and sparseness, used as a proxy for interpretability. These goals can conflict because informative feedback often requires rewards at many points.

The proposed ExpRD framework treats reward design as a discrete optimization problem. It seeks a balance between those properties while guaranteeing that an optimal policy induced by the reward belongs to a specified target set. Its informativeness criterion evaluates how optimal or suboptimal target policies are across different time horizons and actions from each starting state.

The authors analyze the framework mathematically and relate it to existing techniques, including potential-based reward shaping. Experiments on two navigation tasks demonstrate its effectiveness at constructing explicable rewards. The contribution is a structured way to negotiate the trade-off between frequent learning guidance and sparse rewards while preserving the stated connection to target behavior.
summary.tldr: ExpRD balances informative and sparse rewards while ensuring that an induced optimal policy lies within a target policy set.

title: Explicable Reward Design for Reinforcement Learning Agents

abstract: Learning binary representations of instances and classes is a classical problem with several high potential applications. In modern settings, the compression of high-dimensional neural representations to low-dimensional binary codes is a challenging task and often require large bit-codes to be accurate. In this work, we propose a novel method for $\textbf{L}$earning $\textbf{L}$ow-dimensional binary $\textbf{C}$odes $(\textbf{LLC})$ for instances as well as classes. Our method does ${\textit{not}}$ require any side-information, like annotated attributes or label meta-data, and learns extremely low-dimensional binary codes ($\approx 20$ bits for ImageNet-1K). The learnt codes are super-efficient while still ensuring $\textit{nearly optimal}$ classification accuracy for ResNet50 on ImageNet-1K. We demonstrate that the learnt codes capture intrinsically important features in the data, by discovering an intuitive taxonomy over classes. We further quantitatively measure the quality of our codes by applying it to the efficient image retrieval as well as out-of-distribution (OOD) detection problems. For ImageNet-100 retrieval problem, our learnt binary codes outperform $16$ bit HashNet using only $10$ bits and also are as accurate as $10$ dimensional real representations. Finally, our learnt binary codes can perform OOD detection, out-of-the-box, as accurately as a baseline that needs $\approx3000$ samples to tune its threshold, while we require ${\textit{none}}$. Code is open-sourced at https://github.com/RAIVNLab/LLC.

paragraphs: Neural representations can contain many numerical values, making compact binary alternatives appealing. The challenge is preserving useful information when compressing them into very short bit sequences. LLC learns binary codes for both individual examples and classes without requiring extra information such as annotated attributes or label metadata.

For ImageNet-1K, the method learns codes of approximately 20 bits while retaining nearly optimal classification accuracy for ResNet50. The learned codes also reveal an intuitive taxonomy among classes. This suggests that their compactness does not simply discard all relationships between categories: the representations retain structure that is meaningful for organizing the data.

The authors test the same representations for retrieval and out-of-distribution detection. On ImageNet-100 retrieval, 10-bit codes outperform 16-bit HashNet codes and match the accuracy of 10-dimensional real-valued representations. For out-of-distribution detection, they match a baseline that requires approximately 3,000 samples for threshold tuning, without using any such tuning samples. These findings support the usefulness of the learned binary representation across several tasks, beyond its original classification role.
summary.tldr: LLC learns very short binary representations that retain strong classification, retrieval, and out-of-distribution detection performance without extra semantic metadata.

title: LLC: Accurate, Multi-purpose Learnt Low-dimensional Binary Codes

abstract: The ability to form complex plans based on raw visual input is a litmus test for current capabilities of artificial intelligence, as it requires a seamless combination of visual processing and abstract algorithmic execution, two traditionally separate areas of computer science. A recent surge of interest in this field brought advances that yield good performance in tasks ranging from arcade games to continuous control; these methods however do not come without significant issues, such as limited generalization capabilities and difficulties when dealing with combinatorially hard planning instances. Our contribution is two-fold: (i) we present a method that learns to represent its environment as a latent graph and leverages state reidentification to reduce the complexity of finding a good policy from exponential to linear (ii) we introduce a set of lightweight environments with an underlying discrete combinatorial structure in which planning is challenging even for humans. Moreover, we show that our methods achieves strong empirical generalization to variations in the environment, even across highly disadvantaged regimes, such as “one-shot” planning, or in an offline RL paradigm which only provides low-quality trajectories.

paragraphs: Planning directly from images requires a system to connect visual perception with reasoning about sequences of actions. The paper focuses on environments where the underlying search problem is combinatorially difficult. Such problems can challenge methods that perform well on other visual control tasks, particularly when those methods must generalize to unfamiliar variations.

The proposed method learns to represent the environment as a latent graph. A key ingredient is state reidentification: recognizing when observations correspond to a state already encountered. By using that recognition, the method reduces the stated complexity of finding a good policy from exponential to linear. The authors also introduce lightweight environments with discrete combinatorial structure and planning challenges difficult even for humans.

Experiments show strong generalization to variations in these environments. The reported settings include one-shot planning and offline reinforcement learning supplied only with low-quality trajectories. These results support the usefulness of learning a reusable graph of states for visual planning, including situations where opportunities to gather high-quality experience are restricted.
summary.tldr: Learning a latent state graph and recognizing repeated states reduces the stated planning complexity and supports strong empirical generalization from pixels.

title: Planning from Pixels in Environments with Combinatorially Hard Search Spaces

abstract: A recently proposed class of models attempts to learn latent dynamics from high-dimensional observations, like images, using priors informed by Hamiltonian mechanics. While these models have important potential applications in areas like robotics or autonomous driving, there is currently no good way to evaluate their performance: existing methods primarily rely on image reconstruction quality, which does not always reflect the quality of the learnt latent dynamics. In this work, we empirically highlight the problems with the existing measures and develop a set of new measures, including a binary indicator of whether the underlying Hamiltonian dynamics have been faithfully captured, which we call Symplecticity Metric or SyMetric. Our measures take advantage of the known properties of Hamiltonian dynamics and are more discriminative of the model's ability to capture the underlying dynamics than reconstruction error. Using SyMetric, we identify a set of architectural choices that significantly improve the performance of a previously proposed model for inferring latent dynamics from pixels, the Hamiltonian Generative Network (HGN). Unlike the original HGN, the new SyMetric is able to discover an interpretable phase space with physically meaningful latents on some datasets. Furthermore, it is stable for significantly longer rollouts on a diverse range of 13 datasets, producing rollouts of essentially infinite length both forward and backwards in time with no degradation in quality on a subset of the datasets.

This paper shows empirically that reconstruction quality does not always indicate whether the underlying dynamics were learned correctly. It focuses on models informed by Hamiltonian mechanics, where known physical structure can support a more direct evaluation.

The authors develop several measures, including SyMetric, a binary indicator intended to assess whether the underlying Hamiltonian dynamics have been faithfully captured. These qualified findings illustrate how a dynamics-focused metric can guide improvements in both interpretability and long-term prediction.
summary.tldr: SyMetric evaluates learned Hamiltonian structure more directly than image reconstruction and helps identify architectures with more interpretable and stable dynamics.

title: SyMetric: Measuring the Quality of Learnt Hamiltonian Dynamics Inferred from Vision

abstract: Our work reveals a structured shortcoming of the existing mainstream self-supervised learning methods. Whereas self-supervised learning frameworks usually take the prevailing perfect instance level invariance hypothesis for granted, we carefully investigate the pitfalls behind. Particularly, we argue that the existing augmentation pipeline for generating multiple positive views naturally introduces out-of-distribution (OOD) samples that undermine the learning of the downstream tasks. Generating diverse positive augmentations on the input does not always pay off in benefiting downstream tasks. To overcome this inherent deficiency, we introduce a lightweight latent variable model UOTA, targeting the view sampling issue for self-supervised learning. UOTA adaptively searches for the most important sampling region to produce views, and provides viable choice for outlier-robust self-supervised learning approaches. Our method directly generalizes to many mainstream self-supervised learning approaches, regardless of the loss's nature contrastive or not. We empirically show UOTA's advantage over the state-of-the-art self-supervised paradigms with evident margin, which well justifies the existence of the OOD sample issue embedded in the existing approaches. Especially, we theoretically prove that the merits of the proposal boil down to guaranteed estimator variance and bias reduction. Code is available: https://github.com/ssl-codelab/uota.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning often creates several transformed views of an example and trains the model to treat them as equivalent. This paper questions the assumption that every such view should preserve the same useful identity. The authors argue that augmentation can create out-of-distribution views that interfere with learning representations for downstream tasks.

They introduce UOTA, a lightweight latent-variable model that adjusts view sampling. It adaptively identifies the most important region from which to obtain views, addressing the influence of outliers within the augmentation process. The approach can be applied to multiple mainstream self-supervised methods, including those with contrastive losses and those using other objectives.

Experiments show improvements over state-of-the-art self-supervised approaches, providing evidence for the practical importance of the problematic views identified by the authors. The theoretical analysis also establishes reductions in estimator variance and bias. Together, these findings support making view selection adaptive instead of assuming that increasing augmentation diversity will always improve downstream learning.
summary.tldr: UOTA improves self-supervised learning by adapting view sampling to reduce harmful augmentation outliers, with theoretical bias and variance reductions.

title: Improving Self-supervised Learning with Automated Unsupervised Outlier Arbitration

abstract: Episodic control enables sample efficiency in reinforcement learning by recalling past experiences from an episodic memory. We propose a new model-based episodic memory of trajectories addressing current limitations of episodic control. Our memory estimates trajectory values, guiding the agent towards good policies. Built upon the memory, we construct a complementary learning model via a dynamic hybrid control unifying model-based, episodic and habitual learning into a single architecture. Experiments demonstrate that our model allows significantly faster and better learning than other strong reinforcement learning agents across a variety of environments including stochastic and non-Markovian settings.

paragraphs: Episodic control helps a reinforcement learning agent use past experiences when making new decisions. The paper develops a model-based episodic memory organized around trajectories, or sequences of experience. Its purpose is to improve how remembered experience guides learning, addressing limitations of existing episodic control methods.

The memory estimates trajectory values and uses those estimates to steer the agent toward good policies. Building on this memory, the authors introduce a complementary learning architecture with dynamic hybrid control. It brings model-based, episodic, and habitual learning into a single system. The central design contribution is this integration: trajectory memory becomes part of a control architecture that combines several forms of learning.

Experiments report significantly faster and better learning than other strong reinforcement learning agents across a variety of tested environments. Those environments include stochastic and non-Markovian settings, extending the empirical evaluation to both randomness and settings where the current state does not fully describe the relevant history. The results support the proposed combination as a way to improve learning efficiency and performance.
summary.tldr: A model-based memory of trajectories combines episodic, model-based, and habitual learning and improves learning in the evaluated environments.

title: Model-Based Episodic Memory Induces Dynamic Hybrid Controls

abstract: We present a new method to reconstruct 3D human body pose and shape by fusing visual features from multiview images captured by uncalibrated cameras. Existing multiview approaches often use spatial camera calibration (intrinsic and extrinsic parameters) to geometrically align and fuse visual features. Despite remarkable performances, the requirement of camera calibration restricted their applicability to real-world scenarios, e.g., reconstruction from social videos with wide-baseline cameras. We address this challenge by leveraging the commonly observed human body as a semantic calibration target, which eliminates the requirement of camera calibration. Specifically, we map per-pixel image features to a canonical body surface coordinate system agnostic to views and poses using dense keypoints (correspondences). This feature mapping allows us to semantically, instead of geometrically, align and fuse visual features from multiview images. We learn a self-attention mechanism to reason about the confidence of visual features across and within views. With fused visual features, a regressor is learned to predict the parameters of a body model. We demonstrate that our calibration-free multiview fusion method reliably reconstructs 3D body pose and shape, outperforming state-of-the-art single view methods with post-hoc multiview fusion, particularly in the presence of non-trivial occlusion, and showing comparable accuracy to multiview methods that require calibration.

paragraphs: Combining several camera views can help reconstruct a person’s three-dimensional pose and body shape, but many methods require known camera parameters. That requirement restricts their use with sources such as social videos. This paper aligns views using the shared human body itself, removing the need for spatial camera calibration.

The method uses dense body correspondences to map image features onto a common body-surface coordinate system that is independent of viewpoint and pose. Features from different images can then be combined according to which body locations they describe. A learned self-attention mechanism assesses confidence within and across views, and a regressor uses the fused features to predict body-model parameters.

The authors report reliable pose and shape reconstruction, outperforming single-view methods whose results are combined afterward. The advantage is especially apparent when substantial occlusion hides parts of the body. Accuracy is also comparable to multiview methods that require calibration. These findings support semantic correspondence as a useful basis for combining views when camera geometry is unavailable.
summary.tldr: Mapping image features onto a shared body surface enables multiview human reconstruction without camera calibration.

title: Multiview Human Body Reconstruction from Uncalibrated Cameras

abstract: We study the differentially private (DP) $k$-means and $k$-median clustering problems of $n$ points in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space in the massively parallel computation (MPC) model. We provide two near-optimal algorithms where the near-optimality is in three aspects: they both achieve (1). $O(1)$ parallel computation rounds, (2). near-linear in $n$ and polynomial in $k$ total computational work (i.e., near-linear running time when $n$ is a sufficient polynomial in $k$), (3). $O(1)$ relative approximation and $\text{poly}(k, d)$ additive error. Note that $\Omega(1)$ relative approximation is provably necessary even for any polynomial-time non-private algorithm, and $\Omega(k)$ additive error is a provable lower bound for any polynomial-time DP $k$-means/median algorithm. Our two algorithms provide a tradeoff between the relative approximation and the additive error: the first has $O(1)$ relative approximation and $\sim (k^{2.5} + k^{1.01} \sqrt{d})$ additive error, and the second one achieves $(1+\gamma)$ relative approximation to the optimal non-private algorithm for an arbitrary small constant $\gamma>0$ and with $\text{poly}(k, d)$ additive error for a larger polynomial dependence on $k$ and $d$. To achieve our result, we develop a general framework which partitions the data and reduces the DP clustering problem for the entire dataset to the DP clustering problem for each part. To control the blow-up of the additive error introduced by each part, we develop a novel charging argument which might be of independent interest.

To control the blow-up of the additive error introduced by each part, we develop a novel charging argument which might be of independent interest.

paragraphs: This paper studies differentially private k-means and k-median clustering in a massively parallel computation setting. The challenge is to obtain useful clusters while controlling privacy-related error, total computation, and the number of parallel rounds. The authors provide two algorithms with guarantees addressing all three concerns.

Both algorithms use a constant number of rounds and total work that is near-linear in the number of points and polynomial in the number of clusters. Their error guarantees combine a relative approximation with an additive term. The first offers a constant relative approximation with a smaller stated additive-error dependence. The second approaches the optimal non-private algorithm's relative performance within a factor of one plus an arbitrarily small constant, at the cost of larger polynomial additive error.

The shared framework partitions the data and reduces the full private clustering task to private clustering within each part. A new charging argument controls how additive errors accumulate across these parts. The results make explicit the tradeoff between relative solution quality and additive error while maintaining strong parallel-efficiency guarantees.
summary.tldr: Two private parallel clustering algorithms trade relative approximation against additive error while achieving constant rounds and efficient total work.

title: Near-Optimal Private and Scalable $k$-Clustering

abstract: Dataset distillation compresses large datasets into smaller synthetic coresets which retain performance with the aim of reducing the storage and computational burden of processing the entire dataset. Today's best performing algorithm, \textit{Kernel Inducing Points} (KIP), which makes use of the correspondence between infinite-width neural networks and kernel-ridge regression, is prohibitively slow due to the exact computation of the neural tangent kernel matrix, scaling $O(|S|^2)$, with $|S|$ being the coreset size. To improve this, we propose a novel algorithm that uses a random feature approximation (RFA) of the Neural Network Gaussian Process (NNGP) kernel which reduces the kernel matrix computation to $O(|S|)$. Our algorithm provides at least a 100-fold speedup over KIP and can run on a single GPU. Our new method, termed an RFA Distillation (RFAD), performs competitively with KIP and other dataset condensation algorithms in accuracy over a range of large-scale datasets, both in kernel regression and finite-width network training. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on tasks involving model interpretability and privacy preservation.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation creates a small synthetic training set intended to preserve the usefulness of a much larger dataset. This can reduce storage and the computation needed for subsequent learning. The paper targets a bottleneck in Kernel Inducing Points, or KIP, which uses the relationship between infinite-width neural networks and kernel ridge regression.

The proposed RFA Distillation method, called RFAD, instead uses random features to approximate a Neural Network Gaussian Process kernel. This reduces the stated kernel matrix computation scaling to linear in coreset size, making the construction of distilled datasets substantially less expensive.
