They also demonstrate applications involving interpretability and privacy preservation. These findings support a practical speed advantage without claiming that RFAD always produces the most accurate distilled dataset.
summary.tldr: RFAD uses random feature kernel approximation to accelerate dataset distillation while retaining competitive accuracy.

title: Efficient Dataset Distillation using Random Feature Approximation

abstract: Mapping between discrete and continuous distributions is a difficult task and many have had to resort to heuristical approaches. We propose a tessellation-based approach that directly learns quantization boundaries in a continuous space, complete with exact likelihood evaluations. This is done through constructing normalizing flows on convex polytopes parameterized using a simple homeomorphism with an efficient log determinant Jacobian. We explore this approach in two application settings, mapping from discrete to continuous and vice versa. Firstly, a Voronoi dequantization allows automatically learning quantization boundaries in a multidimensional space. The location of boundaries and distances between regions can encode useful structural relations between the quantized discrete values. Secondly, a Voronoi mixture model has near-constant computation cost for likelihood evaluation regardless of the number of mixture components. Empirically, we show improvements over existing methods across a range of structured data modalities.

paragraphs: Connecting discrete values with continuous distributions often requires choosing how continuous space is divided into discrete regions. This paper learns those boundaries directly through a geometric partition, or tessellation. The method retains exact likelihood evaluation, so the learned mapping comes with a way to compute probabilities.

The construction places normalizing flows on convex polytopes using a continuous, invertible mapping with an efficiently computed log-determinant Jacobian. In the discrete-to-continuous direction, Voronoi dequantization learns multidimensional region boundaries. The positions of those boundaries and the distances between regions can represent useful structural relationships among discrete values.

In the other direction, the authors introduce a Voronoi mixture model whose likelihood-evaluation cost is nearly constant as the number of mixture components grows. Experiments report improvements over existing methods across several structured data modalities. The contribution combines learnable geometry with tractable probability calculations: the partition itself becomes part of the model, and the same construction supports both dequantization and efficient mixture modeling.
summary.tldr: Learned geometric partitions connect discrete and continuous distributions while supporting exact likelihoods and efficient mixture evaluation.

title: Semi-Discrete Normalizing Flows through Differentiable Tessellation

abstract: Co-speech gesture is crucial for human-machine interaction and digital entertainment. While previous works mostly map speech audio to human skeletons (e.g., 2D keypoints), directly generating speakers' gestures in the image domain remains unsolved. In this work, we formally define and study this challenging problem of audio-driven co-speech gesture video generation, i.e., using a unified framework to generate speaker image sequence driven by speech audio. Our key insight is that the co-speech gestures can be decomposed into common motion patterns and subtle rhythmic dynamics. To this end, we propose a novel framework, Audio-driveN Gesture vIdeo gEneration (ANGIE), to effectively capture the reusable co-speech gesture patterns as well as fine-grained rhythmic movements. To achieve high-fidelity image sequence generation, we leverage an unsupervised motion representation instead of a structural human body prior (e.g., 2D skeletons). Specifically, 1) we propose a vector quantized motion extractor (VQ-Motion Extractor) to summarize common co-speech gesture patterns from implicit motion representation to codebooks. 2) Moreover, a co-speech gesture GPT with motion refinement (Co-Speech GPT) is devised to complement the subtle prosodic motion details. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework renders realistic and vivid co-speech gesture video. Demo video and more resources can be found in: https://alvinliu0.github.io/projects/ANGIE

paragraphs: Generating gestures from speech often means predicting a skeleton or a set of body keypoints. This paper studies generating a sequence of speaker images directly from speech audio. It learns an unsupervised motion representation instead of imposing a structural body representation such as a two-dimensional skeleton. A vector-quantized motion extractor gathers common gesture patterns into codebooks, giving the system a collection of reusable motion elements.

A second component, Co-Speech GPT with motion refinement, supplies subtle movement details connected to speech prosody. This division lets the framework represent both recurring gesture structure and fine rhythmic variation. The authors report that extensive experiments produce realistic, vivid gesture videos. The stated finding supports combining these two levels of motion within a unified image-generation framework.
summary.tldr: ANGIE generates gesture videos from speech by combining reusable motion patterns with fine rhythmic movement.

title: Audio-Driven Co-Speech Gesture Video Generation

abstract: The availability of compute and data to train larger and larger language models increases the demand for robust methods of benchmarking the true progress of LM training. Recent years witnessed significant progress in standardized benchmarking for English. Benchmarks such as GLUE, SuperGLUE, or KILT have become a de facto standard tools to compare large language models. Following the trend to replicate GLUE for other languages, the KLEJ benchmark\ (klej is the word for glue in Polish) has been released for Polish. In this paper, we evaluate the progress in benchmarking for low-resourced languages. We note that only a handful of languages have such comprehensive benchmarks. We also note the gap in the number of tasks being evaluated by benchmarks for resource-rich English/Chinese and the rest of the world.In this paper, we introduce LEPISZCZE (lepiszcze is the Polish word for glew, the Middle English predecessor of glue), a new, comprehensive benchmark for Polish NLP with a large variety of tasks and high-quality operationalization of the benchmark.We design LEPISZCZE with flexibility in mind. Including new models, datasets, and tasks is as simple as possible while still offering data versioning and model tracking. In the first run of the benchmark, we test 13 experiments (task and dataset pairs) based on the five most recent LMs for Polish. We use five datasets from the Polish benchmark and add eight novel datasets. As the paper's main contribution, apart from LEPISZCZE, we provide insights and experiences learned while creating the benchmark for Polish as the blueprint to design similar benchmarks for other low-resourced languages.

This paper examines an imbalance in benchmarking: languages such as English and Chinese have more comprehensive task coverage than many others. It introduces LEPISZCZE as a broader benchmark for Polish natural-language processing.

The initial evaluation contains 13 task-and-dataset pairs using five Polish language models described as the most recent at the time.

summary.tldr: LEPISZCZE broadens Polish NLP evaluation and provides benchmark-design lessons for other low-resource languages.

title: This is the way: designing and compiling LEPISZCZE, a comprehensive NLP benchmark for Polish

abstract: Among United Nations' 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), we highlight SDG 8 on Decent Work and Economic Growth. Specifically, we consider how to achieve subgoal 8.8, "protect labour rights and promote safe working environments for all workers [...]", in light of poor health, safety and environment (HSE) conditions being a widespread problem at workplaces. In EU alone, it is estimated that more than 4000 deaths occur each year due to poor working conditions. To handle the problem and achieve SDG 8, governmental agencies conduct labour inspections and it is therefore essential that these are carried out efficiently. Current research suggests that machine learning (ML) can be used to improve labour inspections, for instance by selecting organisations for inspections more effectively. However, the research in this area is very limited, in part due to a lack of publicly available data. Consequently, we introduce a new dataset called the Labour Inspection Checklists Dataset (LICD), which we have made publicly available. LICD consists of 63634 instances where each instance is an inspection conducted by the Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority. LICD has 577 features and labels. The dataset provides several ML research opportunities; we discuss two demonstration experiments. One experiment deals with the problem of selecting a relevant checklist for inspecting a given target organisation. The other experiment concerns the problem of predicting HSE violations, given a specific checklist and a target organisation. Our experimental results, while promising, suggest that achieving good ML classification performance is difficult for both problems. This motivates future research to improve ML performance, inspire other data analysis efforts, and ultimately achieve SDG 8.

Limited access to public data has restricted research in this area.

The Labour Inspection Checklists Dataset, or LICD, contains 63,634 inspection records from the Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority, with 577 features and labels. The second is predicting health, safety, and environment violations for an organisation when a particular checklist is used.

The demonstration experiments produce promising results, but also show that strong classification performance is difficult on both tasks. The contribution is therefore a research resource and a set of concrete prediction problems, rather than evidence that automated inspection decisions are already solved. By making inspection records available, the work supports further modelling and analysis connected to the goal of safe working environments.
summary.tldr: LICD provides public Norwegian labour inspection data and two challenging prediction tasks to support research on safer workplaces.

title: A Dataset for Efforts Towards Achieving the Sustainable Development Goal of Safe Working Environments

abstract: In cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, centralized training and decentralized execution (CTDE) has achieved remarkable success. Individual Global Max (IGM) decomposition, which is an important element of CTDE, measures the consistency between local and joint policies. The majority of IGM-based research focuses on how to establish this consistent relationship, but little attention has been paid to examining IGM's potential flaws. In this work, we reveal that the IGM condition is a lossy decomposition, and the error of lossy decomposition will accumulated in hypernetwork-based methods. To address the above issue, we propose to adopt an imitation learning strategy to separate the lossy decomposition from Bellman iterations, thereby avoiding error accumulation. The proposed strategy is theoretically proved and empirically verified on the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge benchmark problem with zero sight view. The results also confirm that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art IGM-based approaches.

paragraphs: Cooperative multi-agent learning often trains agents centrally but requires them to act separately. Individual Global Max decomposition helps connect these stages by aligning local decisions with the joint policy. This paper examines a potential weakness in that connection: the decomposition loses information, and the resulting error accumulates in methods based on hypernetworks.

The proposed remedy uses imitation learning to separate the lossy decomposition from Bellman iterations, the repeated value-learning updates. This separation is intended to keep decomposition error from repeatedly feeding into those updates. The method addresses how centralized learning is translated into decentralized behavior, rather than focusing only on satisfying the consistency condition between local and joint policies.

The authors provide theoretical support for the strategy and evaluate it on the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge under a zero-sight-view setting. They report that it outperforms state-of-the-art IGM-based methods in that evaluation. The contribution highlights that consistency of decisions does not by itself eliminate information loss, and that isolating the decomposition step can avoid the identified accumulation of error.
summary.tldr: Separating lossy policy decomposition from Bellman updates through imitation learning avoids identified error accumulation in cooperative multi-agent learning.

title: Rethinking Individual Global Max in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Analysis of neural network optimization in the mean-field regime is important as the setting allows for feature learning. Existing theory has been developed mainly for neural networks in finite dimensions, i.e., each neuron has a finite-dimensional parameter. However, the setting of infinite-dimensional input naturally arises in machine learning problems such as nonparametric functional data analysis and graph classification. In this paper, we develop a new mean-field analysis of two-layer neural network in an infinite-dimensional parameter space. We first give a generalization error bound, which shows that the regularized empirical risk minimizer properly generalizes when the data size is sufficiently large, despite the neurons being infinite-dimensional. Next, we present two gradient-based optimization algorithms for infinite-dimensional mean-field networks, by extending the recently developed particle optimization framework to the infinite-dimensional setting. We show that the proposed algorithms converge to the (regularized) global optimal solution, and moreover, their rates of convergence are of polynomial order in the online setting and exponential order in the finite sample setting, respectively. To our knowledge this is the first quantitative global optimization guarantee of neural network on infinite-dimensional input and in the presence of feature learning.

paragraphs: Some learning problems naturally involve inputs beyond fixed-length vectors, including functional data analysis and graph classification. This paper extends mean-field analysis of two-layer neural networks to an infinite-dimensional parameter space. The setting matters because it supports feature learning while moving beyond theories developed mainly for neurons with finitely many parameters.

The authors first derive a generalization error bound for a regularized empirical risk minimizer. With sufficiently much data, that minimizer generalizes despite the infinite-dimensional neurons. They then extend a particle optimization framework to construct two gradient-based algorithms for training these networks, linking the statistical question of generalization with the computational question of finding a solution.

Both algorithms are shown to converge to a regularized global optimum. Their convergence rates are polynomial in the online setting and exponential in the finite-sample setting, respectively. The authors identify this as, to their knowledge, the first quantitative global optimization guarantee combining infinite-dimensional inputs with feature learning. The guarantees concern the specified mean-field, regularized framework.
summary.tldr: The paper proves generalization and quantitative global optimization guarantees for regularized, two-layer mean-field networks with infinite-dimensional parameters.

title: Two-layer neural network on infinite dimensional data: global optimization guarantee in the mean-field regime

abstract: Simulated humanoids are an appealing research domain due to their physical capabilities. Nonetheless, they are also challenging to control, as a policy must drive an unstable, discontinuous, and high-dimensional physical system. One widely studied approach is to utilize motion capture (MoCap) data to teach the humanoid agent low-level skills (e.g., standing, walking, and running) that can then be re-used to synthesize high-level behaviors. However, even with MoCap data, controlling simulated humanoids remains very hard, as MoCap data offers only kinematic information. Finding physical control inputs to realize the demonstrated motions requires computationally intensive methods like reinforcement learning. Thus, despite the publicly available MoCap data, its utility has been limited to institutions with large-scale compute. In this work, we dramatically lower the barrier for productive research on this topic by training and releasing high-quality agents that can track over three hours of MoCap data for a simulated humanoid in the dm_control physics-based environment. We release MoCapAct (Motion Capture with Actions), a dataset of these expert agents and their rollouts, which contain proprioceptive observations and actions. We demonstrate the utility of MoCapAct by using it to train a single hierarchical policy capable of tracking the entire MoCap dataset within dm_control and show the learned low-level component can be re-used to efficiently learn downstream high-level tasks. Finally, we use MoCapAct to train an autoregressive GPT model and show that it can control a simulated humanoid to perform natural motion completion given a motion prompt.Videos of the results and links to the code and dataset are available at https://microsoft.github.io/MoCapAct.

paragraphs: Motion capture shows how a body moves, but it does not directly supply the physical control actions needed to make a simulated humanoid reproduce that movement. Learning those actions can require substantial reinforcement-learning computation. MoCapAct addresses this barrier by releasing trained expert agents together with recordings of their behavior.

The experts track more than three hours of motion-capture data in the dm_control physics environment. Their rollouts include observations of the humanoid’s own physical state and the actions it takes. This makes the dataset useful for learning control from demonstrated actions, extending the utility of motion data that otherwise provides only kinematic information.

The authors demonstrate a single hierarchical policy that tracks the full motion dataset and show that its low-level component can be reused to learn downstream tasks efficiently. They also train an autoregressive GPT model that produces natural motion completion in simulation from a motion prompt. These demonstrations illustrate several ways the released control experience can lower the computational barrier to research on simulated humanoids.
summary.tldr: MoCapAct adds trained controllers and action-labeled rollouts to motion capture, making simulated humanoid-control research more accessible.

title: MoCapAct: A Multi-Task Dataset for Simulated Humanoid Control

abstract: Error correction code is a major part of the physical communication layer, ensuring the reliable transfer of data over noisy channels.Recently, neural decoders were shown to outperform classical decoding techniques.However, the existing neural approaches present strong overfitting, due to the exponential training complexity, or a restrictive inductive bias, due to reliance on Belief Propagation.Recently, Transformers have become methods of choice in many applications, thanks to their ability to represent complex interactions between elements.In this work, we propose to extend for the first time the Transformer architecture to the soft decoding of linear codes at arbitrary block lengths.We encode each channel's output dimension to a high dimension for a better representation of the bits' information to be processed separately.The element-wise processing allows the analysis of channel output reliability, while the algebraic code and the interaction between the bits are inserted into the model via an adapted masked self-attention module.The proposed approach demonstrates the power and flexibility of Transformers and outperforms existing state-of-the-art neural decoders by large margins, at a fraction of their time complexity.

paragraphs: Error-correction decoding recovers transmitted information after a communication channel introduces noise. Neural decoders have shown strong results, but the paper identifies two difficulties in existing approaches: overfitting associated with exponential training complexity and restrictive assumptions inherited from belief propagation. It proposes a transformer architecture for soft decoding of linear codes at arbitrary block lengths.

Each dimension of the channel output is embedded into a higher-dimensional representation, allowing the model to process information about individual bits separately. This element-wise processing supports assessment of the reliability of received information. An adapted masked self-attention module incorporates the algebraic structure of the code and interactions between bits.

The design gives separate roles to local reliability information and code-dependent relationships, while using attention to combine them during decoding. The authors report large improvements over existing state-of-the-art neural decoders at a fraction of their time complexity. These findings support transformers as a flexible architecture for this decoding problem, with the reported gains covering both decoding performance and computational demands.
summary.tldr: A transformer decoder combines bit-reliability representations with code-aware masked attention and reports substantial gains over existing neural decoders.

title: Error Correction Code Transformer

abstract: Meta-Bayesian optimisation (meta-BO) aims to improve the sample efficiency of Bayesian optimisation by leveraging data from related tasks. While previous methods successfully meta-learn either a surrogate model or an acquisition function independently, joint training of both components remains an open challenge. This paper proposes the first end-to-end differentiable meta-BO framework that generalises neural processes to learn acquisition functions via transformer architectures. We enable this end-to-end framework with reinforcement learning (RL) to tackle the lack of labelled acquisition data. Early on, we notice that training transformer-based neural processes from scratch with RL is challenging due to insufficient supervision, especially when rewards are sparse. We formalise this claim with a combinatorial analysis showing that the widely used notion of regret as a reward signal exhibits a logarithmic sparsity pattern in trajectory lengths. To tackle this problem, we augment the RL objective with an auxiliary task that guides part of the architecture to learn a valid probabilistic model as an inductive bias. We demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art regret results against various baselines in experiments on standard hyperparameter optimisation tasks and also outperforms others in the real-world problems of mixed-integer programming tuning, antibody design, and logic synthesis for electronic design automation.

While previous methods successfully meta-learn either a surrogate model or an acquisition function independently, joint training of both components remains an open challenge. This paper proposes the first end-to-end differentiable meta-BO framework that generalises neural processes to learn acquisition functions via transformer architectures. We enable this end-to-end framework with reinforcement learning (RL) to tackle the lack of labelled acquisition data. Early on, we notice that training transformer-based neural processes from scratch with RL is challenging due to insufficient supervision, especially when rewards are sparse. We formalise this claim with a combinatorial analysis showing that the widely used notion of regret as a reward signal exhibits a logarithmic sparsity pattern in trajectory lengths. To tackle this problem, we augment the RL objective with an auxiliary task that guides part of the architecture to learn a valid probabilistic model as an inductive bias. We demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art regret results against various baselines in experiments on standard hyperparameter optimisation tasks and also outperforms others in the real-world problems of mixed-integer programming tuning, antibody design, and logic synthesis for electronic design automation.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimisation seeks good choices with few evaluations, and meta-learning can improve this process using experience from related tasks. Two central components are a surrogate model of the objective and an acquisition function that chooses what to evaluate next. This paper develops an end-to-end differentiable framework that learns these components together using transformer-based neural processes.

Because suitable acquisition decisions lack direct training labels, the authors use reinforcement learning. However, training the transformer architecture from scratch this way provides insufficient supervision. Their combinatorial analysis shows that a commonly used regret-based reward has a logarithmic sparsity pattern as trajectories grow. They address this by adding an auxiliary objective that teaches part of the architecture to form a valid probabilistic model.

This additional learning signal guides joint training rather than leaving the entire system dependent on sparse rewards. Experiments report state-of-the-art regret on standard hyperparameter optimisation tasks and improvements over other methods in mixed-integer programming tuning, antibody design, and logic synthesis. The results support combining probabilistic modeling supervision with learned evaluation decisions.
summary.tldr: A transformer framework jointly learns Bayesian optimisation components, using auxiliary probabilistic modeling to strengthen sparse reinforcement-learning supervision.

title: End-to-End Meta-Bayesian Optimisation with Transformer Neural Processes

abstract: Semantic segmentation has witnessed tremendous progress due to the proposal of various advanced network architectures. However, they are extremely hungry for delicate annotations to train, and the acquisition is laborious and unaffordable. Therefore, we present FreeMask in this work, which resorts to synthetic images from generative models to ease the burden of both data collection and annotation procedures. Concretely, we first synthesize abundant training images conditioned on the semantic masks provided by realistic datasets. This yields extra well-aligned image-mask training pairs for semantic segmentation models. We surprisingly observe that, solely trained with synthetic images, we already achieve comparable performance with real ones (e.g., 48.3 vs. 48.5 mIoU on ADE20K, and 49.3 vs. 50.5 on COCO-Stuff). Then, we investigate the role of synthetic images by joint training with real images, or pre-training for real images. Meantime, we design a robust filtering principle to suppress incorrectly synthesized regions. In addition, we propose to inequally treat different semantic masks to prioritize those harder ones and sample more corresponding synthetic images for them. As a result, either jointly trained or pre-trained with our filtered and re-sampled synthesized images, segmentation models can be greatly enhanced, e.g., from 48.7 to 52.0 on ADE20K.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation requires detailed annotations assigning semantic categories throughout an image, making training data expensive to collect. FreeMask expands available training data by generating images conditioned on semantic masks from real datasets. Each existing mask can therefore support additional synthetic images paired with aligned annotations, reducing the need to collect and annotate every new example.

The paper finds that models trained only on synthetic images can approach the performance of models trained on real images. Reported mIoU scores are 48.3 versus 48.5 on ADE20K and 49.3 versus 50.5 on COCO-Stuff. These comparisons show that the generated image-mask pairs can provide useful segmentation supervision in the evaluated settings.

The authors also combine synthetic and real data through joint training or pretraining. They filter incorrectly generated regions and produce more images for harder semantic masks, improving how the synthetic data are used. With filtering and resampling, they report an ADE20K improvement from 48.7 to 52.0. The approach thus combines data generation with attention to generation quality and training difficulty.
summary.tldr: FreeMask generates images from existing semantic masks, then filters and resamples them to improve segmentation training.

title: FreeMask: Synthetic Images with Dense Annotations Make Stronger Segmentation Models

abstract: We introduce Functional Diffusion Processes (FDPs), which generalize score-based diffusion models to infinite-dimensional function spaces. FDPs require a new mathematical framework to describe the forward and backward dynamics, and several extensions to derive practical training objectives. These include infinite-dimensional versions of Girsanov theorem, in order to be able to compute an ELBO, and of the sampling theorem, in order to guarantee that functional evaluations in a countable set of points are equivalent to infinite-dimensional functions. We use FDPs to build a new breed of generative models in function spaces, which do not require specialized network architectures, and that can work with any kind of continuous data.Our results on real data show that FDPs achieve high-quality image generation, using a simple MLP architecture with orders of magnitude fewer parameters than existing diffusion models.

paragraphs: Functional Diffusion Processes extend score-based diffusion modeling to spaces of functions with infinitely many dimensions. The central change is to formulate generation around continuous functions. This requires describing how those functions evolve during both the forward diffusion process and the backward process used for generation.

The paper develops mathematical tools that make this formulation usable for training. An infinite-dimensional version of Girsanov's theorem supports computation of an evidence lower bound, a training-related quantity. An extension of the sampling theorem establishes the equivalence between functions and their evaluations at a countable set of points within the framework. These steps connect the infinite-dimensional description to quantities a practical model can handle.

The resulting generative models do not require specialized neural architectures and are designed to handle continuous data. In experiments on real data, the authors report high-quality image generation using a simple multilayer perceptron with orders of magnitude fewer parameters than existing diffusion models. This demonstrates that the function-space formulation can support compact image generators.
summary.tldr: Functional Diffusion Processes extend diffusion to infinite-dimensional function spaces and demonstrate high-quality image generation with compact, simple networks.

title: Continuous-Time Functional Diffusion Processes

abstract: Recently, researchers have found that representations learned by large-scale pre-trained language models are useful in various downstream tasks. However, there is little theoretical understanding of how pre-training performance is related to downstream task performance. In this paper, we analyze how this performance transfer depends on the properties of the downstream task and the structure of the representations. We consider a log-linear model where a word can be predicted from its context through a network having softmax as its last layer. We show that even if the downstream task is highly structured and depends on a simple function of the hidden representation, there are still cases when a low pre-training loss cannot guarantee good performance on the downstream task. On the other hand, we propose and empirically validate the existence of an ``anchor vector'' in the representation space, and show that this assumption, together with properties of the downstream task, guarantees performance transfer.

paragraphs: A language model can perform well during pretraining and still leave an important question unanswered: when does that success translate into useful performance on another task? This paper investigates the connection theoretically, focusing on how transfer depends jointly on the structure of learned representations and the properties of the downstream task.

The analysis considers a log-linear model that predicts a word from its context through a network ending in a softmax layer. Within this setting, the authors show that low pretraining loss alone does not always guarantee good downstream performance. This can remain true even when the downstream task is highly structured and depends on a simple function of the hidden representation.

The positive result introduces an anchor vector in representation space. The authors provide empirical support for its existence and show that assuming such a vector, together with suitable downstream task properties, guarantees performance transfer. This identifies additional structure that can make pretraining success informative, while preserving the distinction between low loss by itself and a conditional transfer guarantee.
summary.tldr: Low pretraining loss alone need not ensure task transfer, but an anchor-vector assumption combined with task properties provides a guarantee.

title: Connecting Pre-trained Language Model and Downstream Task via Properties of Representation

abstract: The relevance of optimal transport methods to machine learning has long been hindered by two salient limitations.First, the $O(n^3)$ computational cost of standard sample-based solvers (when used on batches of $n$ samples) is prohibitive.Second, the mass conservation constraint makes OT solvers too rigid in practice: because they must match \textit{all} points from both measures, their output can be heavily influenced by outliers.A flurry of recent works in OT has addressed these computational and modelling limitations, but has resulted in two separate strains of methods:While the computational outlook was much improved by entropic regularization, more recent $O(n)$ linear-time \textit{low-rank} solvers hold the promise to scale up OT further.On the other hand, modelling rigidities have been eased owing to unbalanced variants of OT, that rely on penalization terms to promote, rather than impose, mass conservation.The goal of this paper is to merge these two strains, to achieve the promise of \textit{both} versatile/scalable unbalanced/low-rank OT solvers. We propose custom algorithms to implement these extensions for the linear OT problem and its Fused-Gromov-Wasserstein generalization, and demonstrate their practical relevance to challenging spatial transcriptomics matching problems.

We propose custom algorithms to implement these extensions for the linear OT problem and its Fused-Gromov-Wasserstein generalization, and demonstrate their practical relevance to challenging spatial transcriptomics matching problems.

paragraphs: Optimal transport matches two collections of mass, but conventional solvers face both computational and modeling difficulties. Standard sample-based methods can cost cubic time in the number of samples. Requiring all mass to be matched can also make the result sensitive to outliers, because every point must participate in the matching.

Two research directions address these issues separately. Low-rank solvers offer the prospect of linear-time computation, while unbalanced transport relaxes exact mass conservation through penalties. This paper brings the two ideas together, aiming for solvers that combine scalable representations with flexibility about how much mass is matched.

The authors develop custom algorithms for both the linear optimal transport problem and its Fused-Gromov-Wasserstein generalization. They demonstrate practical relevance on challenging spatial transcriptomics matching problems. The contribution is the integration of two complementary improvements: reducing the cost of representing and computing a match while easing the requirement to force every part of both inputs into that match.
summary.tldr: New transport algorithms combine low-rank computation with relaxed mass conservation and demonstrate usefulness for spatial transcriptomics matching.

title: Unbalanced Low-rank Optimal Transport Solvers

abstract: In this paper, we present conditions for identifying the generator of a linear stochastic differential equation (SDE) from the distribution of its solution process with a given fixed initial state. These identifiability conditions are crucial in causal inference using linear SDEs as they enable the identification of the post-intervention distributions from its observational distribution. Specifically, we derive a sufficient and necessary condition for identifying the generator of linear SDEs with additive noise, as well as a sufficient condition for identifying the generator of linear SDEs with multiplicative noise. We show that the conditions derived for both types of SDEs are generic. Moreover, we offer geometric interpretations of the derived identifiability conditions to enhance their understanding. To validate our theoretical results, we perform a series of simulations, which support and substantiate the established findings.

Specifically, we derive a sufficient and necessary condition for identifying the generator of linear SDEs with additive noise, as well as a sufficient condition for identifying the generator of linear SDEs with multiplicative noise. We show that the conditions derived for both types of SDEs are generic. Moreover, we offer geometric interpretations of the derived identifiability conditions to enhance their understanding. To validate our theoretical results, we perform a series of simulations, which support and substantiate the established findings.

paragraphs: A linear stochastic differential equation describes dynamics with both structured evolution and randomness. This paper asks when the distribution of the resulting process, starting from one fixed initial state, determines its generator. Identifiability matters because observational behavior must contain enough information to distinguish the underlying dynamics before those dynamics can support intervention predictions.

The authors derive different results for two forms of noise. For additive noise, they give a condition that is both necessary and sufficient for identifying the generator. For multiplicative noise, they establish a sufficient condition. The latter guarantees identification when it holds, but does not establish that identification is impossible whenever it fails.

The conditions for both settings are shown to be generic, and geometric interpretations help explain their meaning. Simulations support the theoretical findings. The causal relevance is that these identification conditions enable post-intervention distributions to be determined from the observational distribution within the linear-SDE setting. The paper therefore connects a precise mathematical identification question to the possibility of reasoning about changes to a stochastic system.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes generator-identification conditions for linear SDEs, with a full characterization for additive noise and a sufficient condition for multiplicative noise.

title: Generator Identification for Linear SDEs with Additive and Multiplicative Noise

abstract: We present the first nontrivial procedure for configuring heuristic algorithms to maximize the utility provided to their end users while also offering theoretical guarantees about performance. Existing procedures seek configurations that minimize expected runtime. However, very recent theoretical work argues that expected runtime minimization fails to capture algorithm designers' preferences. Here we show that the utilitarian objective also confers significant algorithmic benefits. Intuitively, this is because mean runtime is dominated by extremely long runs even when they are incredibly rare; indeed, even when an algorithm never gives rise to such long runs, configuration procedures that provably minimize mean runtime must perform a huge number of experiments to demonstrate this fact. In contrast, utility is bounded and monotonically decreasing in runtime, allowing for meaningful empirical bounds on a configuration's performance. This paper builds on this idea to describe effective and theoretically sound configuration procedures. We prove upper bounds on the runtime of these procedures that are similar to theoretical lower bounds, while also demonstrating their performance empirically.

paragraphs: Algorithm configuration selects settings for a heuristic algorithm. Existing procedures commonly aim to minimize expected runtime, but this paper instead targets the utility delivered to users. The authors argue that this objective better captures relevant preferences and also makes it easier to develop configuration procedures with meaningful theoretical performance guarantees.

The difficulty with mean runtime is its sensitivity to extremely rare, extremely long runs. Even if a configuration never produces such runs, proving that through experiments can require substantial effort. The paper works with utility that is bounded and decreases as runtime increases. Boundedness makes empirical performance bounds possible without the same sensitivity to arbitrarily large runtime contributions.

Building on this distinction, the authors develop configuration procedures with theoretical guarantees and prove runtime upper bounds similar to theoretical lower bounds. They also demonstrate the procedures empirically. The contribution shows how changing the objective can affect both what counts as a good configuration and how efficiently a reliable configuration choice can be established.
summary.tldr: Optimizing bounded user utility enables theoretically grounded algorithm configuration without mean runtime’s extreme sensitivity to rare long executions.

title: Utilitarian Algorithm Configuration

abstract: Value decomposition methods have gained popularity in the field of cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning. However, almost all existing methods follow the principle of Individual Global Max (IGM) or its variants, which limits their problem-solving capabilities. To address this, we propose a dual self-awareness value decomposition framework, inspired by the notion of dual self-awareness in psychology, that entirely rejects the IGM premise. Each agent consists of an ego policy for action selection and an alter ego value function to solve the credit assignment problem. The value function factorization can ignore the IGM assumption by utilizing an explicit search procedure. On the basis of the above, we also suggest a novel anti-ego exploration mechanism to avoid the algorithm becoming stuck in a local optimum. As the first fully IGM-free value decomposition method, our proposed framework achieves desirable performance in various cooperative tasks.

paragraphs: In cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, a team learns to act together while assigning credit to individual agents. Value decomposition separates the team’s value into agent-level components. Most existing approaches rely on Individual Global Max, or related conditions, which constrain how individual action preferences connect to the team’s preferred joint action.

This paper proposes a framework that removes that premise. Each agent has an ego policy responsible for selecting actions and an alter ego value function responsible for credit assignment. An explicit search procedure allows the value factorization to operate without the IGM assumption. Separating these responsibilities creates a different route to coordinating action selection and evaluating contributions.

The framework also introduces anti-ego exploration, intended to keep learning from becoming trapped in a local optimum. The authors describe their method as the first fully IGM-free value decomposition approach and report desirable performance across several cooperative tasks. The stated finding supports the feasibility of value decomposition without its usual structural restriction; the exploration mechanism is a proposed aid against local traps, rather than a stated guarantee of finding a global optimum.
summary.tldr: The framework separates action selection from credit assignment and uses explicit search to enable cooperative value decomposition without IGM.

title: Dual Self-Awareness Value Decomposition Framework without Individual Global Max for Cooperative MARL

abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiT) excel at image and video generation but face computational challenges due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention operators. We propose DiTFastAttn, a post-training compression method to alleviate the computational bottleneck of DiT.We identify three key redundancies in the attention computation during DiT inference: (1) spatial redundancy, where many attention heads focus on local information; (2) temporal redundancy, with high similarity between the attention outputs of neighboring steps; (3) conditional redundancy, where conditional and unconditional inferences exhibit significant similarity. We propose three techniques to reduce these redundancies: (1) $\textit{Window Attention with Residual Sharing}$ to reduce spatial redundancy; (2) $\textit{Attention Sharing across Timesteps}$ to exploit the similarity between steps; (3) $\textit{Attention Sharing across CFG}$ to skip redundant computations during conditional generation.

paragraphs: DiTFastAttn tackles the computational cost of attention in diffusion transformers used for image and video generation. Self-attention has quadratic complexity, making it a bottleneck as the amount of visual information grows. The proposed method compresses attention after training by targeting repeated or unnecessarily broad computation during inference.

The authors identify three sources of redundancy. Spatially, many attention heads concentrate on nearby information. Across neighboring diffusion steps, attention outputs can be highly similar. Conditional and unconditional inference also produce similar results in parts of their attention computation. These observations motivate different forms of sharing rather than treating every attention calculation as independent.

Window Attention with Residual Sharing addresses spatial redundancy, Attention Sharing across Timesteps reuses information between generation steps, and Attention Sharing across CFG targets repeated work during conditional generation. Together, the techniques provide a structured approach to reducing attention computation across space, time, and conditioning. The contribution described in the abstract is this post-training compression design, grounded in the three observed similarities.
summary.tldr: DiTFastAttn compresses diffusion-transformer attention by sharing computation across spatial regions, neighboring steps, and conditional generation paths.

title: DiTFastAttn: Attention Compression for Diffusion Transformer Models

abstract: Tandem mass spectrometry has played a pivotal role in advancing proteomics, enabling the high-throughput analysis of protein composition in biological tissues. Despite the development of several deep learning methods for predicting amino acid sequences (peptides) responsible for generating the observed mass spectra, training data biases hinder further advancements of \emph{de novo} peptide sequencing. Firstly, prior methods struggle to identify amino acids with Post-Translational Modifications (PTMs) due to their lower frequency in training data compared to canonical amino acids, further resulting in unsatisfactory peptide sequencing performance. Secondly, various noise and missing peaks in mass spectra reduce the reliability of training data (Peptide-Spectrum Matches, PSMs). To address these challenges, we propose AdaNovo, a novel and domain knowledge-inspired framework that calculates Conditional Mutual Information (CMI) between the mass spectra and amino acids or peptides, using CMI for robust training against above biases. Extensive experiments indicate that AdaNovo outperforms previous competitors on the widely-used 9-species benchmark, meanwhile yielding 3.6\% - 9.4\% improvements in PTMs identification. The supplements contain the code.

paragraphs: AdaNovo addresses a problem in identifying peptides from tandem mass spectra: the training examples can systematically favor some amino acids and provide unreliable evidence for others. Modified amino acids appear less frequently than ordinary ones, making them harder for existing models to identify. Noise and missing peaks also weaken the reliability of the associations between spectra and peptide sequences.

The proposed framework uses conditional mutual information between a spectrum and an amino acid or peptide to guide robust training. This information-based quantity concerns how much one variable tells us about another after accounting for conditioning information. AdaNovo brings that perspective into peptide sequencing, using domain knowledge to address both underrepresented modifications and unreliable training matches.

Experiments report better performance than previous competitors on the nine-species benchmark, alongside improvements of 3.6%–9.4% in identifying post-translational modifications. These findings connect improved sequencing with better handling of a biologically meaningful source of training imbalance. They support the framework’s effectiveness on the reported evaluations without implying that all kinds of mass-spectrum noise or data bias have been eliminated.
summary.tldr: AdaNovo uses conditional mutual information to improve peptide sequencing under training biases involving rare modifications and unreliable spectra.

title: AdaNovo: Towards Robust \emph{De Novo} Peptide Sequencing in Proteomics against Data Biases

abstract: Epitope identification is vital for antibody design yet challenging due to the inherent variability in antibodies. While many deep learning methods have been developed for general protein binding site prediction tasks, whether they work for epitope prediction remains an understudied research question. The challenge is also heightened by the lack of a consistent evaluation pipeline with sufficient dataset size and epitope diversity. We introduce a filtered antibody-antigen complex structure dataset, AsEP (Antibody-specific Epitope Prediction). AsEP is the largest of its kind and provides clustered epitope groups, allowing the community to develop and test novel epitope prediction methods and evaluate their generalisability. AsEP comes with an easy-to-use interface in Python and pre-built graph representations of each antibody-antigen complex while also supporting customizable embedding methods. Using this new dataset, we benchmark several representative general protein-binding site prediction methods and find that their performances fall short of expectations for epitope prediction. To address this, we propose a novel method, WALLE, which leverages both unstructured modeling from protein language models and structural modeling from graph neural networks. WALLE demonstrate up to 3-10X performance improvement over the baseline methods. Our empirical findings suggest that epitope prediction benefits from combining sequential features provided by language models with geometrical information from graph representations. This provides a guideline for future epitope prediction method design. In addition, we reformulate the task as bipartite link prediction, allowing convenient model performance attribution and interpretability. We open source our data and code at https://github.com/biochunan/AsEP-dataset.

paragraphs: Epitope prediction identifies the region of an antigen associated with binding by a particular antibody. Antibody variability makes this more demanding than simply finding general protein binding sites. The paper introduces AsEP, a filtered collection of antibody-antigen structures described as the largest dataset of its kind, with clustered epitope groups for evaluating generalization.

summary.tldr: AsEP benchmarks antibody-specific epitope prediction, and WALLE improves results by combining protein sequence representations with structural graphs.

title: AsEP: Benchmarking Deep Learning Methods for Antibody-specific Epitope Prediction

abstract: The nadir objective vector plays a key role in solving multi-objective optimization problems (MOPs), where it is often used to normalize the objective space and guide the search. The current methods for estimating the nadir objective vector perform effectively only on specific MOPs. This paper reveals the limitations of these methods: exact methods can only work on discrete MOPs, while heuristic methods cannot deal with the MOP with a complicated feasible objective region. To fill this gap, we propose a general and rigorous method, namely boundary decomposition for nadir objective vector estimation (BDNE). BDNE scalarizes the MOP into a set of boundary subproblems. By utilizing bilevel optimization, boundary subproblems are optimized and adjusted alternately, thereby refining their optimal solutions to align with the nadir objective vector. We prove that the bilevel optimization identifies the nadir objective vector under mild conditions. We compare BDNE with existing methods on various black-box MOPs. The results conform to the theoretical analysis and show the significant potential of BDNE for real-world application.

paragraphs: Multi-objective optimization searches for solutions that balance competing goals. The nadir objective vector helps put these goals on comparable scales and guide that search. Estimating it reliably is therefore useful beyond obtaining a descriptive statistic: the estimate can influence how an optimization method explores possible solutions.

The paper identifies shortcomings in existing approaches. The exact methods it discusses work only for discrete problems, while heuristic methods struggle when the feasible objective region has a complicated shape. Its proposed method, boundary decomposition for nadir objective vector estimation, converts the original problem into a collection of boundary subproblems.

A bilevel optimization procedure alternates between solving these subproblems and adjusting them. This progressively aligns their optimal solutions with the desired nadir vector. The authors prove identification under mild conditions, rather than claiming an unconditional guarantee. Comparisons on several black-box multi-objective problems agree with the theoretical analysis and suggest potential for practical applications involving difficult objective regions.
summary.tldr: BDNE estimates nadir objective vectors through boundary subproblems and bilevel optimization, with identification guarantees under mild conditions.

title: Boundary Decomposition for Nadir Objective Vector Estimation

abstract: The need for large text corpora has increased with the advent of pretrained language models and, in particular, the discovery of scaling laws for these models. Most available corpora have sufficient data only for languages with large dominant communities. However, there is no corpus available that (i) covers a wide range of minority languages; (ii) is generated by an open-source reproducible pipeline; and (iii) is rigorously cleaned from noise, making it trustworthy to use. We present GlotCC, a clean, document-level, 2TB general domain corpus derived from CommonCrawl, covering more than 1000 languages. We make GlotCC and the system used to generate it— including the pipeline, language identification model, and filters—available to the research community.Corpus v. 1.0 https://huggingface.co/datasets/cis-lmu/GlotCC-v1Pipeline v. 3.0 https://github.com/cisnlp/GlotCC

paragraphs: Language models require substantial amounts of text, but available corpora tend to provide sufficient coverage mainly for languages with large, dominant communities. This paper addresses a resource gap for minority languages. It focuses on combining broad language coverage, reproducible collection, and rigorous cleaning in a single openly available corpus.

The resulting resource, GlotCC, contains 2 TB of general-domain text derived from CommonCrawl and covers more than 1,000 languages. It is organized at the document level. The authors present it as a cleaned corpus, addressing the noise that can make large web-derived collections difficult to trust for research use.

The release includes both the text collection and the system that produced it: the processing pipeline, language-identification model, and filters. Providing these components makes the construction process available for inspection and reproduction, alongside the finished data. The contribution is therefore broader than assembling multilingual text. It supplies an open method for producing a corpus with wide language coverage and makes minority-language data more accessible to the research community.
summary.tldr: GlotCC releases a cleaned 2 TB web-text corpus covering over 1,000 languages together with its reproducible processing pipeline.

title: GlotCC: An Open Broad-Coverage CommonCrawl Corpus and Pipeline for Minority Languages

abstract: In this paper, we show that applying adaptive methods directly to distributed minimax problems can result in non-convergence due to inconsistency in locally computed adaptive stepsizes. To address this challenge, we propose D-AdaST, a Distributed Adaptive minimax method with Stepsize Tracking. The key strategy is to employ an adaptive stepsize tracking protocol involving the transmission of two extra (scalar) variables. This protocol ensures the consistency among stepsizes of nodes, eliminating the steady-state error due to the lack of coordination of stepsizes among nodes that commonly exists in vanilla distributed adaptive methods, and thus guarantees exact convergence. For nonconvex-strongly-concave distributed minimax problems, we characterize the specific transient times that ensure time-scale separation of stepsizes and quasi-independence of networks, leading to a near-optimal convergence rate of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}} \left( \epsilon ^{-\left( 4+\delta \right)} \right)$ for any small $\delta > 0$, matching that of the centralized counterpart. To our best knowledge, D-AdaST is the *first* distributed adaptive method achieving near-optimal convergence without knowing any problem-dependent parameters for nonconvex minimax problems. Extensive experiments are conducted to validate our theoretical results.

paragraphs: Distributed minimax optimization involves several computing nodes working together on a problem with competing minimization and maximization objectives. Adaptive methods adjust their update sizes during learning, but separate nodes can make inconsistent adjustments. The paper shows that directly applying these methods can prevent convergence: local adaptation can leave a persistent error when update sizes are not coordinated.

The proposed method, D-AdaST, adds a protocol that tracks adaptive step sizes across nodes. It communicates two additional scalar variables to keep those step sizes consistent. This coordination removes the steady error attributed to mismatched step sizes and supports exact convergence, while retaining adaptation without requiring knowledge of problem-dependent parameters.

For problems that are nonconvex in the minimizing variables and strongly concave in the maximizing variables, the analysis identifies transient periods needed for the convergence result. After accounting for these periods, the method achieves a near-optimal rate matching its centralized counterpart, with accuracy dependence arbitrarily close to an inverse fourth power, up to logarithmic factors. Experiments support the theoretical findings.
summary.tldr: D-AdaST coordinates adaptive step sizes across computing nodes to achieve near-optimal convergence for nonconvex, strongly concave distributed minimax problems.

title: Achieving Near-Optimal Convergence for Distributed Minimax Optimization with Adaptive Stepsizes

abstract: We propose a novel text-to-video (T2V) generation benchmark, *ChronoMagic-Bench*, to evaluate the temporal and metamorphic knowledge skills in time-lapse video generation of the T2V models (e.g. Sora and Lumiere). Compared to existing benchmarks that focus on visual quality and text relevance of generated videos, *ChronoMagic-Bench* focuses on the models’ ability to generate time-lapse videos with significant metamorphic amplitude and temporal coherence. The benchmark probes T2V models for their physics, biology, and chemistry capabilities, in a free-form text control. For these purposes, *ChronoMagic-Bench* introduces **1,649** prompts and real-world videos as references, categorized into four major types of time-lapse videos: biological, human creation, meteorological, and physical phenomena, which are further divided into 75 subcategories. This categorization ensures a comprehensive evaluation of the models’ capacity to handle diverse and complex transformations. To accurately align human preference on the benchmark, we introduce two new automatic metrics, MTScore and CHScore, to evaluate the videos' metamorphic attributes and temporal coherence. MTScore measures the metamorphic amplitude, reflecting the degree of change over time, while CHScore assesses the temporal coherence, ensuring the generated videos maintain logical progression and continuity. Based on the *ChronoMagic-Bench*, we conduct comprehensive manual evaluations of eighteen representative T2V models, revealing their strengths and weaknesses across different categories of prompts, providing a thorough evaluation framework that addresses current gaps in video generation research. More encouragingly, we create a large-scale *ChronoMagic-Pro* dataset, containing **460k** high-quality pairs of 720p time-lapse videos and detailed captions. Each caption ensures high physical content and large metamorphic amplitude, which have a far-reaching impact on the video generation community. The source data and code are publicly available on [https://pku-yuangroup.github.io/ChronoMagic-Bench](https://pku-yuangroup.github.io/ChronoMagic-Bench).

Its focus is whether generated changes exhibit temporal continuity and knowledge relevant to physical, biological, and chemical processes.

The benchmark contains 1,649 prompts with real-world reference videos. They cover biological phenomena, human creation, meteorological phenomena, and physical phenomena, divided into 75 subcategories. The authors also introduce two automatic measures intended to align with human preferences. MTScore evaluates the amount of transformation over time, while CHScore evaluates temporal coherence, including logical progression and continuity.

The paper reports manual evaluations of eighteen representative video-generation models, identifying strengths and weaknesses across prompt categories. It also introduces ChronoMagic-Pro, a dataset of 460,000 pairs of 720p time-lapse videos and detailed captions. Together, the benchmark, measures, and larger dataset provide resources for examining and developing a specific capability: generating substantial, coherent transformations rather than merely producing individually plausible video frames.
summary.tldr: ChronoMagic-Bench evaluates how well text-to-video models generate substantial transformations that remain coherent over time.

title: ChronoMagic-Bench: A Benchmark for Metamorphic Evaluation of Text-to-Time-lapse Video Generation

abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained models for downstream tasks is a widely adopted technique known for its adaptability and reliability across various domains. Despite its conceptual simplicity, fine-tuning entails several troublesome engineering choices, such as selecting hyperparameters and determining checkpoints from an optimization trajectory. To tackle the difficulty of choosing the best model, one effective solution is model fusion, which combines multiple models in a parameter space. However, we observe a large discrepancy between loss and metric landscapes during the fine-tuning of pre-trained language models. Building on this observation, we introduce a novel model fusion technique that optimizes both the desired metric and loss through multi-objective Bayesian optimization. In addition, to effectively select hyperparameters, we establish a two-stage procedure by integrating Bayesian optimization processes into our framework. Experiments across various downstream tasks show considerable performance improvements using our Bayesian optimization-guided method.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a language model involves decisions about hyperparameters and which checkpoint to retain. Model fusion offers another option by combining multiple models in parameter space. But choosing a good combination requires deciding what to optimize, and the paper observes a substantial mismatch between the training loss landscape and the landscape of the desired evaluation metric.

The proposed method uses multi-objective Bayesian optimization to guide model fusion while considering both loss and the target metric. This directly addresses the possibility that a combination favored by one objective may not be favored by the other. The authors also introduce a two-stage procedure that incorporates Bayesian optimization into hyperparameter selection.

Experiments across multiple downstream tasks report considerable performance improvements from the resulting framework. The contribution is an approach to selecting and combining fine-tuned models that explicitly recognizes the difference between a training objective and the outcome users evaluate. By coordinating fusion and hyperparameter selection, the method addresses two engineering choices that otherwise complicate finding an effective final model.
summary.tldr: The paper uses multi-objective Bayesian optimization to fuse fine-tuned language models while jointly considering loss, target metrics, and hyperparameter selection.

title: Model Fusion through Bayesian Optimization in Language Model Fine-Tuning

abstract: In this work, we introduce Pixelsmith, a zero-shot text-to-image generative framework to sample images at higher resolutions with a single GPU. We are the first to show that it is possible to scale the output of a pre-trained diffusion model by a factor of 1000, opening the road to gigapixel image generation at no extra cost. Our cascading method uses the image generated at the lowest resolution as baseline to sample at higher resolutions. For the guidance, we introduce the Slider, a mechanism that fuses the overall structure contained in the first-generated image with enhanced fine details. At each inference step, we denoise patches rather than the entire latent space, minimizing memory demands so that a single GPU can handle the process, regardless of the image's resolution. Our experimental results show that this method not only achieves higher quality and diversity compared to existing techniques but also reduces sampling time and ablation artifacts.

paragraphs: Generating very large images puts pressure on GPU memory because the model must process a large spatial representation. Pixelsmith addresses this problem with a zero-shot framework that extends a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model to higher resolutions. The authors demonstrate output scaling by a factor of 1,000, pointing toward gigapixel generation.

The method works in stages, using a low-resolution generated image as the starting guide for larger images. A mechanism called the Slider combines the overall structure of that first image with finer detail. During each inference step, the framework denoises patches instead of the complete latent representation, reducing the memory demands of processing the image.

This patch-based design is presented as enabling a single GPU to handle the process regardless of image resolution. Experiments report better image quality and diversity than existing techniques, together with shorter sampling times and fewer artifacts. The approach connects global guidance with local computation: the initial image supplies overall organization while patch processing makes higher-resolution generation more manageable.
summary.tldr: Pixelsmith combines cascading guidance and patchwise denoising to scale pretrained image generation to much higher resolutions on one GPU.

title: Is One GPU Enough? Pushing Image Generation at Higher-Resolutions with Foundation Models.

abstract: One of the fundamental challenges for offline reinforcement learning (RL) is ensuring robustness to data distribution. Whether the data originates from a near-optimal policy or not, we anticipate that an algorithm should demonstrate its ability to learn an effective control policy that seamlessly aligns with the inherent distribution of offline data. Unfortunately, behavior regularization, a simple yet effective offline RL algorithm, tends to struggle in this regard. In this paper, we propose a new algorithm that substantially enhances behavior-regularization based on conservative policy iteration. Our key observation is that by iteratively refining the reference policy used for behavior regularization, conservative policy update guarantees gradually improvement, while also implicitly avoiding querying out-of-sample actions to prevent catastrophic learning failures. We prove that in the tabular setting this algorithm is capable of learning the optimal policy covered by the offline dataset, commonly referred to as the in-sample optimal policy. We then explore several implementation details of the algorithm when function approximations are applied. The resulting algorithm is easy to implement, requiring only a few lines of code modification to existing methods. Experimental results on the D4RL benchmark indicate that our method outperforms previous state-of-the-art baselines in most tasks, clearly demonstrate its superiority over behavior regularization.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn a useful control policy from a fixed dataset, whose behavior may be strong or poor. Behavior regularization helps control this learning process by keeping updates related to a reference policy. The paper addresses the difficulty of making this approach work reliably across different offline data distributions.

The proposed algorithm repeatedly refines the reference policy rather than leaving it fixed. Its conservative policy updates provide gradual improvement while implicitly avoiding queries about actions outside the data. This combination is intended to prevent catastrophic learning failures while letting the policy improve beyond the behavior initially used as its reference.

The theoretical guarantee is specific to the tabular setting: the algorithm can learn the best policy supported by the offline dataset, called the in-sample optimal policy. The authors also investigate implementation choices with function approximation, producing an algorithm that needs only a few lines of changes to existing methods. On D4RL, it outperforms previous state-of-the-art baselines on most tasks. The results support iterative reference refinement, while the formal optimum remains tied to dataset coverage and the tabular setting.
summary.tldr: Repeatedly refining behavior regularization’s reference policy improves offline learning and provably reaches the dataset-supported optimum in the tabular setting.

title: Iteratively Refined Behavior Regularization for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The standard approach for Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) is to convert them to a fully observed belief-state MDP. However, the belief state depends on the system model and is therefore not viable in reinforcement learning (RL) settings. A widely used alternative is to use an agent state, which is a model-free, recursively updateable function of the observation history. Examples include frame stacking and recurrent neural networks. Since the agent state is model-free, it is used to adapt standard RL algorithms to POMDPs. However, standard RL algorithms like Q-learning learn a stationary policy. Our main thesis that we illustrate via examples is that because the agent state does not satisfy the Markov property, non-stationary agent-state based policies can outperform stationary ones. To leverage this feature, we propose PASQL (periodic agent-state based Q-learning), which is a variant of agent-state-based Q-learning that learns periodic policies. By combining ideas from periodic Markov chains and stochastic approximation, we rigorously establish that PASQL converges to a cyclic limit and characterize the approximation error of the converged periodic policy. Finally, we present a numerical experiment to highlight the salient features of PASQL and demonstrate the benefit of learning periodic policies over stationary policies.

paragraphs: In partially observed reinforcement learning, an agent often summarizes its observation history using stacked frames or a recurrent network. Such an agent state can be updated without knowing the environment model. However, it need not preserve the Markov property: the summary may omit history relevant to predicting what happens next.

Standard Q-learning learns a stationary policy, meaning that its decision rule for an agent state stays the same over time. The authors use examples to show that, when the state summary lacks the Markov property, allowing the decision rule to vary with time can improve performance. They propose PASQL, a Q-learning variant that learns policies whose decision rules repeat periodically.

Using periodic Markov chains and stochastic approximation, the paper proves convergence to a cyclic limit and characterizes the resulting policy’s approximation error. A numerical experiment demonstrates benefits of periodic policies over stationary ones. The central insight is that a repeating schedule of decision rules can be useful when an agent’s internal state is an imperfect summary of its history.
summary.tldr: PASQL learns periodic policies that can outperform stationary policies when an agent’s history summary does not satisfy the Markov property.

title: Periodic agent-state based Q-learning for POMDPs

abstract: We study causal representation learning, the task of recovering high-level latent variables and their causal relationships in the form of a causal graph from low-level observed data (such as text and images), assuming access to observations generated from multiple environments. Prior results on the identifiability of causal representations typically assume access to single-node interventions which is rather unrealistic in practice, since the latent variables are unknown in the first place. In this work, we consider the task of learning causal representation learning with data collected from general environments. We show that even when the causal model and the mixing function are both linear, there exists a surrounded-node ambiguity (SNA) [Varici et al. 2023] which is basically unavoidable in our setting. On the other hand, in the same linear case, we show that identification up to SNA is possible under mild conditions, and propose an algorithm, LiNGCReL which provably achieves such identifiability guarantee. We conduct extensive experiments on synthetic data and demonstrate the effectiveness of LiNGCReL in the finite-sample regime.

paragraphs: Causal representation learning seeks hidden high-level variables and their causal relationships from observed data. Many identifiability results assume access to interventions on individual hidden variables. That is a demanding assumption when those variables are themselves unknown. This paper instead studies observations gathered from general environments.

The analysis focuses on the case where both the causal model and the mapping from latent variables to observations are linear. Even in that setting, the authors identify a largely unavoidable obstacle called surrounded-node ambiguity. This establishes a boundary on what can be uniquely recovered from the available environments, rather than promising complete identification.

Within the same linear setting, the authors show that recovery up to this ambiguity is possible under mild conditions. Their algorithm, LiNGCReL, provably achieves that guarantee. Extensive synthetic-data experiments also demonstrate its effectiveness with finite samples. The contribution combines a statement of intrinsic ambiguity with a constructive method that reaches the corresponding level of identifiability.
summary.tldr: LiNGCReL provably recovers linear causal representations up to an intrinsic ambiguity under mild conditions across general environments.

title: Learning Linear Causal Representations from General Environments: Identifiability and Intrinsic Ambiguity

abstract: In offline reinforcement learning, a policy is learned using a static dataset in the absence of costly feedback from the environment. In contrast to the online setting, only using static datasets poses additional challenges, such as policies generating out-of-distribution samples. Model-based offline reinforcement learning methods try to overcome these by learning a model of the underlying dynamics of the environment and using it to guide policy search. It is beneficial but, with limited datasets, errors in the model and the issue of value overestimation among out-of-distribution states can worsen performance. Current model-based methods apply some notion of conservatism to the Bellman update, often implemented using uncertainty estimation derived from model ensembles. In this paper, we propose Constrained Latent Action Policies (C-LAP) which learns a generative model of the joint distribution of observations and actions. We cast policy learning as a constrained objective to always stay within the support of the latent action distribution, and use the generative capabilities of the model to impose an implicit constraint on the generated actions. Thereby eliminating the need to use additional uncertainty penalties on the Bellman update and significantly decreasing the number of gradient steps required to learn a policy. We empirically evaluate C-LAP on the D4RL and V-D4RL benchmark, and show that C-LAP is competitive to state-of-the-art methods, especially outperforming on datasets with visual observations.
