paragraphs: This paper develops a theoretical approach to diffusion training when a few classes dominate the data and many others have few examples. Its objective combines the usual diffusion loss with a mutual-learning term intended to support balanced performance across labels. The goal includes underrepresented classes rather than focusing only on aggregate performance.

The authors formulate training as a multiplayer game and use Nash equilibrium as the solution concept. They derive a finite-iteration convergence result for individual gradient descent. Specifically, the Nash gap is bounded by an expression of order 1/√T_train + β, where T_train counts training iterations and β controls regularization. The bound therefore reflects both training progress and the chosen regularization strength.

Under the paper's model, the authors also establish training and sampling hyperparameters yielding a worst-case sampling-error bound of order ε + 1 across all class labels, for any positive ε. This stated bound retains a constant term. The contribution is a mathematical framework connecting imbalanced diffusion training, game-based optimization, and class-wide sampling guarantees.
summary.tldr: A game-theoretic diffusion objective provides convergence and class-wide sampling-error guarantees for long-tailed learning under the proposed model.

title: Principled Long-Tailed Generative Modeling via Diffusion Models

abstract: Agents based on large language models (LLMs) for machine learning engineering (MLE) can automatically implement ML models via code generation. However, existing approaches to build such agents often rely heavily on inherent LLM knowledge and employ coarse exploration strategies that modify the entire code structure at once. This limits their ability to select effective task-specific models and perform deep exploration within specific components, such as experimenting extensively with feature engineering options. To overcome these, we propose MLE-STAR, a novel approach to build MLE agents. MLE-STAR first leverages external knowledge by using a search engine to retrieve effective models from the web, forming an initial solution, then iteratively refines it by exploring various strategies targeting specific ML components. This exploration is guided by ablation studies analyzing the impact of individual code blocks. Furthermore, we introduce a novel ensembling method using an effective strategy suggested by MLE-STAR. Our experimental results show that MLE-STAR achieves medals in 64% of the Kaggle competitions on the MLE-bench, significantly outperforming the best alternative.

The agent then improves selected parts of the solution through repeated, targeted exploration. This supports deeper investigation of specific components, such as feature engineering, instead of making every iteration a complete redesign. The authors also introduce an ensembling method based on a strategy suggested by MLE-STAR.

The result supports a workflow that combines external model discovery with evidence-guided local refinement. Its central contribution is organizing automated machine learning engineering around informed starting points and focused experimentation.
summary.tldr: MLE-STAR combines web-based model discovery with ablation-guided component refinement, earning medals in 64% of MLE-bench competitions.

title: MLE-STAR: Machine Learning Engineering Agent via Search and Targeted Refinement

abstract: Generating natural-sounding, multi-speaker dialogue is crucial for applications such as podcast creation, virtual agents, and multimedia content generation. However, existing systems struggle to maintain speaker consistency, model overlapping speech, and synthesize coherent conversations efficiently. In this paper, we introduce CoVoMix2, a fully non-autoregressive framework for zero-shot multi-talker dialogue generation. CoVoMix2 directly predicts mel-spectrograms from multi-stream transcriptions using a flow-matching-based generative model, eliminating the reliance on intermediate token representations. To better capture realistic conversational dynamics, we propose transcription-level speaker disentanglement, sentence-level alignment, and prompt-level random masking strategies. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming strong baselines like MoonCast and Sesame in speech quality, speaker consistency, and inference speed. Notably, CoVoMix2 operates without requiring transcriptions for the prompt and supports controllable dialogue generation, including overlapping speech and precise timing control, demonstrating strong generalizability to real-world speech generation scenarios. Audio samples are available at https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/project/covomix/covomix2.

paragraphs: Generating a conversation requires more than producing clear speech for each sentence. A system must preserve distinct speakers, handle overlaps, and place utterances at appropriate times. CoVoMix2 addresses these requirements with a fully non-autoregressive framework for zero-shot dialogue generation involving multiple speakers.

The model uses flow matching to predict mel-spectrograms directly from multiple transcription streams, bypassing intermediate token representations. Its training approach includes separating speakers at the transcription level, aligning information at the sentence level, and randomly masking information at the prompt level. These strategies are intended to help the model capture conversational structure while maintaining coherent speaker identities.

The authors report better speech quality, speaker consistency, and inference speed than strong baselines including MoonCast and Sesame. CoVoMix2 does not require a transcript of the prompt, although transcriptions still specify the dialogue to generate. It also supports overlapping speech and precise timing control. These capabilities make the reported advance relevant to controllable conversation synthesis as well as natural-sounding output.
summary.tldr: CoVoMix2 directly generates multi-speaker speech with flow matching, improving reported quality, speaker consistency, and speed while supporting overlap and timing control.

title: CoVoMix2: Advancing Zero-Shot Dialogue Generation with Fully Non-Autoregressive Flow Matching

abstract: State Space models (SSMs) like PointMamba provide efficient feature extraction for point cloud self-supervised learning with linear complexity, surpassing Transformers in computational efficiency. However, existing PointMamba-based methods rely on complex token ordering and random masking, disrupting spatial continuity and local semantic correlations. We propose \textbf{ZigzagPointMamba} to address these challenges. The key to our approach is a simple zigzag scan path that globally sequences point cloud tokens, enhancing spatial continuity by preserving the proximity of spatially adjacent point tokens. Yet, random masking impairs local semantic modeling in self-supervised learning. To overcome this, we introduce a Semantic-Siamese Masking Strategy (SMS), which masks semantically similar tokens to facilitate reconstruction by integrating local features of original and similar tokens, thus overcoming dependence on isolated local features and enabling robust global semantic modeling. Our pre-training ZigzagPointMamba weights significantly boost downstream tasks, achieving a 1.59\% mIoU gain on ShapeNetPart for part segmentation, a 0.4\% higher accuracy on ModelNet40 for classification, and 0.19\%, 1.22\%, and 0.72\% higher accuracies respectively for the classification tasks on the OBJ-BG, OBJ-ONLY, and PB-T50-RS subsets of ScanObjectNN. Code is available at https://github.com/Rabbitttttt218/ZigzagPointMamba.

paragraphs: State-space models offer computationally efficient feature extraction for point clouds, but converting spatial data into token sequences can disrupt neighborhood relationships. Random masking during self-supervised training can also weaken local semantic connections. ZigzagPointMamba addresses both the ordering of point-cloud tokens and the way tokens are masked for learning.

A zigzag scan orders tokens globally while preserving proximity between spatially adjacent tokens, improving spatial continuity. The Semantic-Siamese Masking Strategy masks semantically similar tokens and supports reconstruction by integrating local features from original and similar tokens. This is intended to reduce dependence on isolated local features and strengthen global semantic modeling.

The pretrained model improves downstream part segmentation and classification. The authors report a 1.59% mIoU gain on ShapeNetPart, 0.4% higher ModelNet40 accuracy, and accuracy gains of 0.19%, 1.22%, and 0.72% on three ScanObjectNN subsets. These results support considering spatial ordering and semantic masking together when learning point-cloud representations, with benefits demonstrated across the evaluated segmentation and classification tasks.
summary.tldr: ZigzagPointMamba combines spatially coherent token ordering with semantic masking to improve learned point-cloud representations.

title: ZigzagPointMamba: Spatial-Semantic Mamba for Point Cloud Understanding

abstract: The concept of causal abstraction got recently popularised to demystify the opaque decision-making processes of machine learning models; in short, a neural network can be abstracted as a higher-level algorithm if there exists a function which allows us to map between them. Notably, most interpretability papers implement these maps as linear functions, motivated by the linear representation hypothesis: the idea that features are encoded linearly in a model's representations. However, this linearity constraint is not required by the definition of causal abstraction. In this work, we critically examine the concept of causal abstraction by considering arbitrarily powerful alignment maps. In particular, we prove that under reasonable assumptions, any neural network can be mapped to any algorithm, rendering this unrestricted notion of causal abstraction trivial and uninformative. We complement these theoretical findings with empirical evidence, demonstrating that it is possible to perfectly map models to algorithms even when these models are incapable of solving the actual task; e.g., on an experiment using randomly initialised language models, our alignment maps reach 100\% interchange-intervention accuracy on the indirect object identification task. This raises the non-linear representation dilemma: if we lift the linearity constraint imposed to alignment maps in causal abstraction analyses, we are left with no principled way to balance the inherent trade-off between these maps' complexity and accuracy. Together, these results suggest an answer to our title's question: causal abstraction is not enough for mechanistic interpretability, as it becomes vacuous without assumptions about how models encode information. Studying the connection between this information-encoding assumption and causal abstraction should lead to exciting future work.

Many interpretability studies restrict that map to be linear, motivated by the idea that models encode features linearly. The definition of causal abstraction itself does not require this restriction, so the paper asks what happens when alignment maps become arbitrarily powerful.

Under reasonable assumptions, the authors prove that any neural network can then be mapped to any algorithm. Such unrestricted alignment becomes uninformative about the network's actual mechanism. Their experiments illustrate the problem: alignment maps achieve 100% interchange-intervention accuracy on indirect object identification using randomly initialized language models, even though the models cannot solve the underlying task.

The resulting dilemma concerns how to balance the complexity of an alignment map against its accuracy. A perfect match can reflect the power of the map rather than informative structure in the model. The paper therefore argues that causal abstraction requires assumptions about how information is encoded to support mechanistic interpretation; removing constraints does not automatically produce a more faithful explanation.
summary.tldr: Arbitrarily powerful alignment maps can make causal abstraction uninformative, so mechanistic interpretation needs assumptions about how models encode information.

title: The Non-Linear Representation Dilemma: Is Causal Abstraction Enough for Mechanistic Interpretability?

abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) often rely on rate coding, where high-precision inference depends on long time-steps, leading to significant latency and energy cost—especially for ANN-to-SNN conversions. To address this, we propose Adaptive Fission, a post-training encoding technique that selectively splits high-sensitivity neurons into groups with varying scales and weights. This enables neuron-specific, on-demand precision and threshold allocation while introducing minimal spatial overhead. As a generalized form of population coding, it seamlessly applies to a wide range of pretrained SNN architectures without requiring additional training or fine-tuning. Experiments on neuromorphic hardware demonstrate up to 80\% reductions in latency and power consumption without degrading accuracy.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks often represent information through firing rates. Obtaining precise outputs with this coding scheme can require many time steps, increasing latency and energy costs. The problem is especially relevant when conventional artificial neural networks are converted into spiking networks. Adaptive Fission addresses the encoding of an already trained network to reduce this dependence on long computation periods.

The method selectively splits highly sensitive neurons into groups with different scales and weights. These groups provide neuron-specific precision and threshold allocation, concentrating additional representational capacity where it is needed. The authors describe this as a generalized form of population coding, with minimal additional spatial overhead.

Because the modification happens after training, it applies to a range of pretrained spiking architectures without further training or fine-tuning. Experiments on neuromorphic hardware report reductions of up to 80% in latency and power consumption without an accuracy decrease. The findings show that selectively changing how neurons encode information can substantially improve the measured efficiency of pretrained spiking models.
summary.tldr: Adaptive Fission selectively splits sensitive spiking neurons after training, achieving up to 80% reductions in latency and power consumption without degrading accuracy.

title: Adaptive Fission: Post-training Encoding for Low-latency Spike Neural Networks

abstract: We sharply characterize the optimal first-order query complexity of agnostic active learning for all concept classes, and propose a new general active learning algorithm which achieves it. Remarkably, the optimal query complexity admits a leading term which is always strictly smaller than the sample complexity of passive supervised learning (by a factor proportional to the best-in-class error rate). This was not previously known to be possible in the agnostic setting. For comparison, in all previous general analyses, the leading term exhibits an additional factor, such as the disagreement coefficient or related complexity measure, and therefore only provides improvements over passive learning in restricted cases. The present work completely removes such factors from the leading term, implying that $\textit{every}$ concept class benefits from active learning in the non-realizable case. The results established in this work resolve an important long-standing open question central to the past two decades of research on the theory of agnostic active learning.

paragraphs: Active learning lets a learner choose which examples to have labeled, while passive learning receives labeled examples without that choice. This paper asks whether selective querying helps in the agnostic setting, where even the best predictor in the chosen class can make errors. It gives a sharp characterization of optimal first-order label-query complexity for every concept class.

The authors also propose a general algorithm that achieves this characterization. Its leading query-complexity term is strictly smaller than the sample complexity of passive supervised learning, with the improvement tied to the best achievable error within the class. Earlier general analyses included an extra factor, such as a disagreement coefficient, that restricted when they could establish an advantage.

Removing that factor from the leading term establishes a benefit for every concept class in the non-realizable case. The significance is specifically about the dominant theoretical cost of acquiring labels; the abstract does not equate it with a universal reduction in runtime or every finite-sample cost. Within that scope, the result resolves a longstanding question about the reach of agnostic active learning.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes optimal agnostic active-learning query complexity and proves a strictly better leading term than passive learning for every concept class in the non-realizable case.

title: Agnostic Active Learning Is Always Better Than Passive Learning

abstract: This paper presents a multimodal framework that attempts to unify visual understanding and generation within a shared discrete semantic representation. At its core is the Text-Aligned Tokenizer (TA-Tok), which converts images into discrete tokens using a text-aligned codebook projected from a large language model's (LLM) vocabulary. By integrating vision and text into a unified space with an expanded vocabulary, our multimodal LLM, **Tar**, enables cross-modal input and output through a shared interface, without the need for modality-specific designs. Additionally, we propose scale-adaptive encoding and decoding to balance efficiency and visual detail, along with a generative de-tokenizer to produce high-fidelity visual outputs. To address diverse decoding needs, we utilize two complementary de-tokenizers: a fast autoregressive model and a diffusion-based model. To enhance modality fusion, we investigate advanced pre-training tasks, demonstrating improvements in both visual understanding and generation. Experiments across benchmarks show that **Tar** matches or surpasses existing multimodal LLM methods, achieving faster convergence and greater training efficiency. All code, models, and data will be made publicly available.

paragraphs: This paper attempts to bring visual understanding and image generation into one discrete semantic representation. Its Text-Aligned Tokenizer converts images into tokens using a codebook projected from a language model’s vocabulary. This makes the visual representation explicitly connected to the model’s textual vocabulary, supporting a shared space for processing both kinds of information.

The resulting multimodal model, Tar, uses an expanded vocabulary and a shared interface for cross-modal inputs and outputs. Scale-adaptive encoding and decoding balance computational efficiency with visual detail. To convert token representations back into images, the framework provides two complementary de-tokenizers: a fast autoregressive model and a diffusion-based model intended to support diverse decoding needs.

The authors also investigate pretraining tasks that strengthen the integration of modalities, reporting improvements in both understanding and generation. Across benchmarks, Tar matches or exceeds existing multimodal methods while converging faster and using training more efficiently. The findings support text-aligned visual tokens as a useful foundation for a model that both interprets and produces visual content.
summary.tldr: Tar uses text-aligned image tokens to unify visual understanding and generation, reporting competitive performance and improved training efficiency.

title: Vision as a Dialect: Unifying Visual Understanding and Generation via Text-Aligned Representations

abstract: The rapid spread of multimodal misinformation on social media has raised growing concerns, while research on video misinformation detection remains limited due to the lack of large-scale, diverse datasets. Existing methods often overfit to rigid templates and lack deep reasoning over deceptive content. To address these challenges, we introduce FakeVV, a large-scale benchmark comprising over 100,000 video-text pairs with fine-grained, interpretable annotations. In addition, we further propose Fact-R1, a novel framework that integrates deep reasoning with collaborative rule-based reinforcement learning. Fact-R1 is trained through a three-stage process: (1) misinformation long-Chain-of-Thought (CoT) instruction tuning, (2) preference alignment via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and (3) Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using a novel verifiable reward function. This enables Fact-R1 to exhibit emergent reasoning behaviors comparable to those observed in advanced text-based reinforcement learning systems, but in the more complex multimodal misinformation setting. Our work establishes a new paradigm for misinformation detection, bridging large-scale video understanding, reasoning-guided alignment, and interpretable verification.

paragraphs: Detecting misleading videos requires interpreting both visual material and associated text. The paper identifies two obstacles: a shortage of large, diverse datasets and methods that rely too heavily on fixed templates instead of reasoning about deceptive content. It addresses both with a new benchmark and a dedicated training framework.

The benchmark, FakeVV, contains more than 100,000 video-text pairs with detailed annotations intended to support interpretable analysis. The proposed model framework, Fact-R1, follows three training stages. It first learns from misinformation instructions containing extended reasoning, then undergoes Direct Preference Optimization, and finally uses Group Relative Policy Optimization with a newly designed verifiable reward function.

This sequence connects examples of reasoning, preference alignment, and reinforcement learning guided by checkable rewards. The authors report emergent reasoning behaviors comparable to those seen in advanced text-based reinforcement learning systems, now in a multimodal misinformation setting. The stated contribution is a combined basis for studying detection and explanation: richer video-text evidence, reasoning-oriented training, and verification are developed together.
summary.tldr: Fact-R1 combines a large annotated video-text benchmark with staged reasoning and reinforcement learning for explainable misinformation detection.

title: Fact-R1: Towards Explainable Video Misinformation Detection with Deep Reasoning

abstract: Anomaly detection is a crucial task in data mining, focusing on identifying data points that deviate significantly from the main patterns in the data. This paper introduces Anomaly Detection by an Ensemble of Random Pairs of Hyperspheres (ADERH), a new isolation-based technique leveraging two key observations: (i) anomalies are comparatively rare, and (ii) they typically deviate more strongly from general patterns than normal data points. Drawing on a delta-separation argument, ADERH constructs an ensemble of multi-scale hyperspheres built upon randomly paired data points to identify anomalies. To address inevitable overlaps between anomalous and normal regions in the feature space, ADERH integrates two complementary concepts: Pitch, which highlights points near hypersphere boundaries, and NDensity, which down-weights hyperspheres centered on sparse (and often anomalous) regions. By averaging these local, density-adjusted ``isolation'' indicators across many random subsets, ADERH yields robust anomaly scores that clearly separate normal from abnormal samples. Extensive experiments on diverse real-world datasets show that ADERH consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods while maintaining linear runtime scalability and stable performance across varying hyperparameter settings.

paragraphs: ADERH detects unusual data points using two observations: anomalies are relatively rare, and they usually differ more strongly from the main data patterns than ordinary points do. Its approach is based on isolation, using geometric neighborhoods to help distinguish points that behave differently from the surrounding data.

The method builds many hyperspheres, the higher-dimensional counterparts of spheres, from randomly paired data points and at multiple scales. Because normal and anomalous regions can overlap, it adjusts its local indicators in two complementary ways. Pitch emphasizes points near sphere boundaries, while NDensity reduces the weight of spheres centered in sparse regions that may themselves be anomalous. It averages these adjusted indicators across random subsets to produce anomaly scores.

Experiments on diverse real-world datasets report consistently better performance than the compared state-of-the-art methods, alongside linear runtime scaling and stable behavior across different hyperparameter settings. The contribution combines randomized geometric coverage with density-sensitive scoring, addressing the problem that a single local boundary or sparse neighborhood can give a misleading impression of abnormality.
summary.tldr: ADERH combines random hypersphere neighborhoods and density-adjusted isolation scores to detect anomalies efficiently.

title: Anomaly Detection by an Ensemble of Random Pairs of Hyperspheres

abstract: Among explainability techniques, SHAP stands out as one of the most popular, but often overlooks the causal structure of the problem. In response, do-SHAP employs interventional queries, but its reliance on estimands hinders its practical application. To address this problem, we propose the use of estimand-agnostic approaches, which allow for the estimation of any identifiable query from a single model, making do-SHAP feasible on complex graphs. We also develop a novel algorithm to significantly accelerate its computation at a negligible cost, as well as a method to explain inaccessible Data Generating Processes. We demonstrate the estimation and computational performance of our approach, and validate it on two real-world datasets, highlighting its potential in obtaining reliable explanations.

paragraphs: SHAP explanations are widely used, but they can overlook the causal relationships underlying a problem. do-SHAP addresses this by using intervention-based queries. Its practical difficulty is a reliance on estimands, which complicates application when the causal graph and the required queries become complex.

This paper proposes using estimand-agnostic causal inference to estimate any identifiable query from a single model. That shared model makes do-SHAP feasible on complex graphs. Identifiability remains an explicit condition: the proposal supports queries whose causal effects can be identified, rather than claiming that a single model resolves every causal question.

The authors also introduce an algorithm that substantially accelerates computation at negligible cost and a method for explaining inaccessible data-generating processes. They demonstrate estimation and computational performance and validate the approach on two real-world datasets. The contribution addresses several practical obstacles together, linking a reusable causal inference model with faster explanation computation. The reported results highlight the potential for more reliable explanations that incorporate causal structure.
summary.tldr: A shared causal inference model and faster computation make intervention-based do-SHAP explanations more practical for complex graphs.

title: Practical do-Shapley Explanations with Estimand-Agnostic Causal Inference

abstract: Radar-based indoor 3D human pose estimation typically relied on fine-grained 3D keypoint labels, which are costly to obtain especially in complex indoor settings involving clutter, occlusions, or multiple people. In this paper, we propose \textbf{RAPTR} (RAdar Pose esTimation using tRansformer) under weak supervision, using only 3D BBox and 2D keypoint labels which are considerably easier and more scalable to collect. Our RAPTR is characterized by a two-stage pose decoder architecture with a pseudo-3D deformable attention to enhance (pose/joint) queries with multi-view radar features: a pose decoder estimates initial 3D poses with a 3D template loss designed to utilize the 3D BBox labels and mitigate depth ambiguities; and a joint decoder refines the initial poses with 2D keypoint labels and a 3D gravity loss. Evaluated on two indoor radar datasets, RAPTR outperforms existing methods, reducing joint position error by $34.3$\% on HIBER and $76.9$\% on MMVR. Our implementation is available at \url{https://github.com/merlresearch/radar-pose-transformer}.

paragraphs: Estimating a person’s three-dimensional pose from indoor radar typically requires detailed 3D joint annotations during training. Those labels are costly to collect, especially with clutter, occlusion, or multiple people. RAPTR instead learns with 3D bounding boxes and 2D keypoints, which the authors describe as easier to obtain at scale.

Its transformer-based architecture uses two decoding stages and a pseudo-3D deformable attention mechanism to incorporate radar features from multiple views. The second stage refines individual joints using the 2D keypoint labels together with a 3D gravity loss.

The contribution is a way to learn accurate 3D pose estimates while requiring less detailed annotation.
summary.tldr: RAPTR learns radar-based 3D human poses from bounding boxes and 2D keypoints, reporting lower joint errors without detailed 3D keypoint labels.

title: RAPTR: Radar-based 3D Pose Estimation using Transformer

abstract: Forward inference techniques such as sequential Monte Carlo and particle Markov chain Monte Carlo for probabilistic programming can be implemented in any programming language by creative use of standardized operating system functionality including processes, forking, mutexes, and shared memory. Exploiting this we have defined, developed, and tested a probabilistic programming language intermediate representation language we call probabilistic C, which itself can be compiled to machine code by standard compilers and linked to operating system libraries yielding an efficient, scalable, portable probabilistic programming compilation target. This opens up a new hardware and systems research path for optimizing probabilistic programming systems.

paragraphs: Probabilistic programming needs machinery for carrying out inference as a program executes. This paper addresses that systems problem by introducing probabilistic C, an intermediate representation that other probabilistic programming languages can target. The goal is to make inference compatible with established compilation and operating system infrastructure.

The approach uses standard facilities such as processes, process forking, mutexes, and shared memory to implement forward inference techniques. The abstract specifically identifies sequential Monte Carlo and particle Markov chain Monte Carlo. These facilities provide the execution and coordination mechanisms needed to support inference, allowing the implementation to draw on capabilities already available in ordinary programming environments.

The authors developed and tested probabilistic C, which can be compiled into machine code using standard compilers and linked with operating system libraries. They describe the resulting target as efficient, scalable, and portable. Its broader significance is architectural: probabilistic language implementations can share a compilation destination, while hardware and systems research can investigate ways to optimize the execution infrastructure beneath them.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic C provides a tested compilation target that implements probabilistic inference using standard compilers and operating system facilities.

title: A Compilation Target for Probabilistic Programming Languages

abstract: Factorized information criterion (FIC) is a recently developed approximation technique for the marginal log-likelihood, which provides an automatic model selection framework for a few latent variable models (LVMs) with tractable inference algorithms. This paper reconsiders FIC and fills theoretical gaps of previous FIC studies. First, we reveal the core idea of FIC that allows generalization for a broader class of LVMs, including continuous LVMs, in contrast to previous FICs, which are applicable only to binary LVMs. Second, we investigate the model selection mechanism of the generalized FIC. Our analysis provides a formal justification of FIC as a model selection criterion for LVMs and also a systematic procedure for pruning redundant latent variables that have been removed heuristically in previous studies. Third, we provide an interpretation of FIC as a variational free energy and uncover previously-unknown their relationship. A demonstrative study on Bayesian principal component analysis is provided and numerical experiments support our theoretical results.

paragraphs: The factorized information criterion, or FIC, approximates marginal log-likelihood to support automatic selection among latent-variable models. Earlier versions applied to a limited set of models and left theoretical questions unresolved. This paper revisits the underlying idea to clarify why the criterion works and broaden where it can be used.

The authors generalize FIC beyond binary latent variables to a wider class that includes continuous latent-variable models. They also analyze how the criterion selects models. That analysis supplies a formal justification for model selection and a systematic procedure for pruning redundant latent variables, replacing removals that earlier work had handled heuristically.

A further contribution interprets FIC as a variational free energy, revealing a previously unrecognized relationship between the two formulations. This places the approximation and its model-selection behavior within a broader inference perspective. A demonstration using Bayesian principal component analysis and numerical experiments supports the theoretical results. The paper therefore combines wider applicability with a more principled explanation of how unnecessary latent structure can be removed.
summary.tldr: The paper generalizes FIC to broader latent-variable models and formally explains its model-selection, pruning, and variational interpretation.

title: Rebuilding Factorized Information Criterion: Asymptotically Accurate Marginal Likelihood

abstract: The goal of the paper is to design sequential strategies which lead to efficient optimization of an unknown function under the only assumption that it has a finite Lipschitz constant. We first identify sufficient conditions for the consistency of generic sequential algorithms and formulate the expected minimax rate for their performance. We introduce and analyze a first algorithm called LIPO which assumes the Lipschitz constant to be known. Consistency, minimax rates for LIPO are proved, as well as fast rates under an additional Hölder like condition. An adaptive version of LIPO is also introduced for the more realistic setup where Lipschitz constant is unknown and has to be estimated along with the optimization. Similar theoretical guarantees are shown to hold for the adaptive LIPO algorithm and a numerical assessment is provided at the end of the paper to illustrate the potential of this strategy with respect to state-of-the-art methods over typical benchmark problems for global optimization.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential optimization of an unknown function under the assumption that it has a finite Lipschitz constant. That constant bounds how quickly function values can change with distance. The goal is to choose successive evaluations efficiently while requiring only this regularity assumption for the basic problem.

The authors identify sufficient conditions for consistency of generic sequential methods and formulate an expected minimax performance rate. They introduce LIPO for the case where the Lipschitz constant is known, proving consistency and minimax rates. Faster rates require an additional Hölder-like condition, so those stronger results rely on more structure than the basic Lipschitz assumption.

An adaptive version estimates the Lipschitz constant while optimizing, addressing the setting where the bound is initially unknown. Similar theoretical guarantees are established for this version. Numerical comparisons on standard global-optimization benchmarks illustrate the strategy’s potential relative to existing methods. The contribution combines formal performance analysis with an adaptive procedure that removes the need to supply the constant in advance.
summary.tldr: LIPO and its adaptive variant provide theoretically analyzed strategies for optimizing unknown Lipschitz functions through sequential evaluations.

title: Global optimization of Lipschitz functions

abstract: We study the problem on how to learn the pure Nash Equilibrium of a two-player zero-sum static game with random payoffs under unknown distributions via efficient payoff queries. We introduce a multi-armed bandit model to this problem due to its ability to find the best arm efficiently among random arms and propose two algorithms for this problem—LUCB-G based on the confidence bounds and a racing algorithm based on successive action elimination. We provide an analysis on the sample complexity lower bound when the Nash Equilibrium exists.

We provide an analysis on the sample complexity lower bound when the Nash Equilibrium exists.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to identify a pure Nash equilibrium in a two-player zero-sum static game when payoffs are random and their distributions are unknown. The learner obtains information by querying payoffs. The central challenge is to use those queries efficiently while distinguishing useful evidence from randomness in the observed outcomes.

The authors frame the task through a multi-armed bandit model, drawing on its ability to identify good choices from noisy observations. They propose two algorithms. LUCB-G uses confidence bounds to reason about uncertain payoffs, while a racing algorithm progressively eliminates actions. These provide different ways to narrow the search as payoff information accumulates.

The paper also analyzes a lower bound on sample complexity when a Nash equilibrium exists. This gives a theoretical perspective on the amount of information the identification problem requires. The existence qualification matters because the target is a pure equilibrium. Together, the algorithms and lower-bound analysis connect equilibrium identification with the efficient allocation of queries under payoff uncertainty.
summary.tldr: Two bandit-based algorithms seek pure Nash equilibria from noisy payoff queries, alongside a sample-complexity lower bound when an equilibrium exists.

title: Identify the Nash Equilibrium in Static Games with Random Payoffs

abstract: We propose and analyze a novel adaptive step size variant of the Davis-Yin three operator splitting, a method that can solve optimization problems composed of a sum of a smooth term for which we have access to its gradient and an arbitrary number of potentially non-smooth terms for which we have access to their proximal operator. The proposed method leverages local information of the objective function, allowing for larger step sizes while preserving the convergence properties of the original method. It only requires two extra function evaluations per iteration and does not depend on any step size hyperparameter besides an initial estimate. We provide a convergence rate analysis of this method, showing sublinear convergence rate for general convex functions and linear convergence under stronger assumptions, matching the best known rates of its non adaptive variant. Finally, an empirical comparison with related methods on 6 different problems illustrates the computational advantage of the adaptive step size strategy.

The proposed method leverages local information of the objective function, allowing for larger step sizes while preserving the convergence properties of the original method. It only requires two extra function evaluations per iteration and does not depend on any step size hyperparameter besides an initial estimate. We provide a convergence rate analysis of this method, showing sublinear convergence rate for general convex functions and linear convergence under stronger assumptions, matching the best known rates of its non adaptive variant. Finally, an empirical comparison with related methods on 6 different problems illustrates the computational advantage of the adaptive step size strategy.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization problems built from several terms that require different computational tools. One term is smooth and provides a gradient, while other terms may be nonsmooth but provide proximal operators. Three operator splitting combines these tools to solve the overall problem. The authors introduce a version that adapts its step size using local information about the objective.

The practical motivation is to take larger steps when the objective permits them while retaining the original method’s convergence properties. The adaptation requires two additional function evaluations per iteration and only an initial step size estimate, without further step size hyperparameters. This gives the algorithm a way to respond to the problem during optimization.

The analysis establishes sublinear convergence for general convex objectives and linear convergence under stronger assumptions. These rates match the best known rates for the nonadaptive version. Comparisons across six problems illustrate a computational advantage, supporting adaptation as a practical improvement without claiming a universally faster convergence rate.
summary.tldr: Adaptive step sizes make three operator splitting more computationally effective in experiments while preserving established convergence rates.

title: Adaptive Three Operator Splitting

abstract: We consider the fully decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) problem, where the agents are connected via a time-varying and possibly sparse communication network. Specifically, we assume that the reward functions of the agents might correspond to different tasks, and are only known to the corresponding agent. Moreover, each agent makes individual decisions based on both the information observed locally and the messages received from its neighbors over the network. To maximize the globally averaged return over the network, we propose two fully decentralized actor-critic algorithms, which are applicable to large-scale MARL problems in an online fashion. Convergence guarantees are provided when the value functions are approximated within the class of linear functions. Our work appears to be the first theoretical study of fully decentralized MARL algorithms for networked agents that use function approximation.

Specifically, we assume that the reward functions of the agents might correspond to different tasks, and are only known to the corresponding agent. Moreover, each agent makes individual decisions based on both the information observed locally and the messages received from its neighbors over the network. To maximize the globally averaged return over the network, we propose two fully decentralized actor-critic algorithms, which are applicable to large-scale MARL problems in an online fashion. paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning by agents connected through a communication network that may be sparse and may change over time. Each agent has its own reward function, potentially corresponding to a different task, and that reward function is known only to that agent. Decisions depend on local observations and messages from neighboring agents.

Despite these local information boundaries, the collective objective is to maximize the average return across the network. The authors propose two fully decentralized actor-critic algorithms for this purpose. Their approach is designed for online use in large-scale multi-agent problems, allowing agents to learn through local computation and communication.

The paper provides convergence guarantees when value functions are represented using linear function approximation. That qualification is central to the stated theory. The authors describe the work as apparently the first theoretical study of fully decentralized, networked multi-agent reinforcement learning with function approximation. Its contribution is to connect a shared learning objective with decentralized decisions and a mathematically analyzed approximation setting.
summary.tldr: Two decentralized actor-critic algorithms optimize network-wide average return, with convergence guarantees for linear value-function approximation.

title: Fully Decentralized Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Networked Agents

abstract: In this paper, we investigate the problem of overfitting in deep reinforcement learning. Among the most common benchmarks in RL, it is customary to use the same environments for both training and testing. This practice offers relatively little insight into an agent’s ability to generalize. We address this issue by using procedurally generated environments to construct distinct training and test sets. Most notably, we introduce a new environment called CoinRun, designed as a benchmark for generalization in RL. Using CoinRun, we find that agents overfit to surprisingly large training sets. We then show that deeper convolutional architectures improve generalization, as do methods traditionally found in supervised learning, including L2 regularization, dropout, data augmentation and batch normalization.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we investigate the problem of overfitting in deep reinforcement learning. Among the most common benchmarks in RL, it is customary to use the same environments for both training and testing. This practice offers relatively little insight into an agent’s ability to generalize. We address this issue by using procedurally generated environments to construct distinct training and test sets. Most notably, we introduce a new environment called CoinRun, designed as a benchmark for generalization in RL. Using CoinRun, we find that agents overfit to surprisingly large training sets. We then show that deeper convolutional architectures improve generalization, as do methods traditionally found in supervised learning, including L2 regularization, dropout, data augmentation and batch normalization.

paragraphs: An agent can perform well in environments it has practiced without handling unfamiliar environments equally well. This paper examines that distinction in deep reinforcement learning. It argues that using the same environments for training and testing, as common benchmarks often do, reveals relatively little about generalization.

The authors use procedural generation to create separate training and test environments and introduce CoinRun as a benchmark for this purpose. Separating the two sets makes it possible to assess performance beyond the environments encountered during learning. In CoinRun, the authors find that agents can overfit even when the training set is surprisingly large.

The study also identifies changes that improve generalization in its experiments. Deeper convolutional architectures help, as do L2 regularization, dropout, data augmentation, and batch normalization, all familiar from supervised learning. The findings make generalization a measurable concern within reinforcement-learning evaluation and show that both architectural choices and training techniques can improve performance on held-out environments.
summary.tldr: CoinRun exposes reinforcement-learning overfitting on large training sets and shows that deeper networks and familiar regularization methods improve generalization.

title: Quantifying Generalization in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Model selection is an essential task for many applications in scientific discovery. The most common approaches rely on univariate linear measures of association between each feature and the outcome. Such classical selection procedures fail to take into account nonlinear effects and interactions between features. Kernel-based selection procedures have been proposed as a solution. However, current strategies for kernel selection fail to measure the significance of a joint model constructed through the combination of the basis kernels. In the present work, we exploit recent advances in post-selection inference to propose a valid statistical test for the association of a joint model of the selected kernels with the outcome. The kernels are selected via a step-wise procedure which we model as a succession of quadratic constraints in the outcome variable.

The most common approaches rely on univariate linear measures of association between each feature and the outcome. Such classical selection procedures fail to take into account nonlinear effects and interactions between features. Kernel-based selection procedures have been proposed as a solution. However, current strategies for kernel selection fail to measure the significance of a joint model constructed through the combination of the basis kernels. In the present work, we exploit recent advances in post-selection inference to propose a valid statistical test for the association of a joint model of the selected kernels with the outcome. The kernels are selected via a step-wise procedure which we model as a succession of quadratic constraints in the outcome variable.

paragraphs: Scientific model selection often starts by measuring the association between each individual feature and an outcome. Linear, one-feature-at-a-time measures can miss nonlinear relationships and interactions among features. Kernel-based methods offer a way to represent richer relationships, but selecting useful kernels leaves another question: whether the model formed by combining the selected kernels has a statistically significant association with the outcome.

kernelPSI addresses that joint-model question using post-selection inference. The statistical test accounts for the fact that the kernels have already been chosen through a selection procedure. The target is the association between the outcome and the combined selected model, rather than merely a collection of separate assessments of individual kernels.

The authors use a stepwise kernel-selection procedure and express its successive choices as quadratic constraints on the outcome variable. This mathematical description lets the selection process enter the inference framework. The resulting contribution is a valid statistical test for the selected joint model. It connects flexible nonlinear selection with a significance assessment that explicitly incorporates how that model was obtained.
summary.tldr: kernelPSI tests the outcome association of a combined kernel model while accounting for the procedure that selected its kernels.

title: kernelPSI: a Post-Selection Inference Framework for Nonlinear Variable Selection

abstract: Great computational effort is invested in generating equilibrium states for molecular systems using, for example, Markov chain Monte Carlo. We present a probabilistic model that generates statistically independent samples for molecules from their graph representations. Our model learns a low-dimensional manifold that preserves the geometry of local atomic neighborhoods through a principled learning representation that is based on Euclidean distance geometry. In a new benchmark for molecular conformation generation, we show experimentally that our generative model achieves state-of-the-art accuracy. Finally, we show how to use our model as a proposal distribution in an importance sampling scheme to compute molecular properties.

In a new benchmark for molecular conformation generation, we show experimentally that our generative model achieves state-of-the-art accuracy. Finally, we show how to use our model as a proposal distribution in an importance sampling scheme to compute molecular properties.

paragraphs: Generating molecular configurations can require substantial computation, especially when using methods such as Markov chain Monte Carlo to explore equilibrium states. This paper proposes a probabilistic model that takes a molecule’s graph representation and generates statistically independent samples. The task is to connect the molecule’s structural description with the spatial arrangements that its atoms can take.

The model learns a low-dimensional space that preserves the geometry of local atomic neighborhoods. Its representation is based on Euclidean distance geometry, so distances provide the organizing principle for learning molecular structure. This matters because a compact representation must still retain the local spatial relationships needed to produce useful molecular configurations.

In a new benchmark for molecular conformation generation, the authors report state-of-the-art accuracy. They also show how the model can serve as a proposal distribution for importance sampling when computing molecular properties. That application connects configuration generation to downstream estimation: generated samples become inputs to a sampling scheme for calculating quantities of scientific interest.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic model generates independent molecular configurations from graphs and supports importance sampling for molecular property calculations.

title: A Generative Model for Molecular Distance Geometry

abstract: The healthcare industry generates troves of unlabelled physiological data. This data can be exploited via contrastive learning, a self-supervised pre-training method that encourages representations of instances to be similar to one another. We propose a family of contrastive learning methods, CLOCS, that encourages representations across space, time, \textit{and} patients to be similar to one another. We show that CLOCS consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art methods, BYOL and SimCLR, when performing a linear evaluation of, and fine-tuning on, downstream tasks. We also show that CLOCS achieves strong generalization performance with only 25% of labelled training data. Furthermore, our training procedure naturally generates patient-specific representations that can be used to quantify patient-similarity.

paragraphs: Healthcare produces large amounts of physiological data without labels. CLOCS explores how cardiac signals can provide useful training information before labels are available. It uses contrastive learning, which trains representations by encouraging selected instances to have similar internal descriptions. The goal is to make unlabeled recordings contribute to models that will later perform supervised tasks.

The proposed family of methods organizes this similarity learning across spatial, temporal, and patient dimensions. That choice makes the structure of cardiac data central to pretraining. The authors assess the resulting representations through both linear evaluation and fine-tuning on downstream tasks, testing their usefulness in two different ways of adapting pretrained features.

Across the reported evaluations, CLOCS consistently outperforms BYOL and SimCLR. It also shows strong generalization with only 25% of the labeled training data. In addition, its training procedure produces patient-specific representations that can quantify similarity between patients. The findings therefore concern both reduced dependence on labels and the creation of representations that describe relationships among patients.
summary.tldr: CLOCS learns cardiac-signal representations from unlabeled data, outperforming BYOL and SimCLR in reported downstream evaluations and supporting patient-similarity measurement.

title: CLOCS: Contrastive Learning of Cardiac Signals Across Space, Time, and Patients

abstract: This work studies the classical spectral clustering algorithm which embeds the vertices of some graph G=(V_G, E_G) into R^k using k eigenvectors of some matrix of G, and applies k-means to partition V_G into k clusters. Our first result is a tighter analysis on the performance of spectral clustering, and explains why it works under some much weaker condition than the ones studied in the literature. For the second result, we show that, by applying fewer than k eigenvectors to construct the embedding, spectral clustering is able to produce better output for many practical instances; this result is the first of its kind in spectral clustering. Besides its conceptual and theoretical significance, the practical impact of our work is demonstrated by the empirical analysis on both synthetic and real-world data sets, in which spectral clustering produces comparable or better results with fewer than k eigenvectors.

Our first result is a tighter analysis on the performance of spectral clustering, and explains why it works under some much weaker condition than the ones studied in the literature. For the second result, we show that, by applying fewer than k eigenvectors to construct the embedding, spectral clustering is able to produce better output for many practical instances; this result is the first of its kind in spectral clustering. Besides its conceptual and theoretical significance, the practical impact of our work is demonstrated by the empirical analysis on both synthetic and real-world data sets, in which spectral clustering produces comparable or better results with fewer than k eigenvectors.

paragraphs: Spectral clustering groups graph vertices by first representing them as points and then applying k-means. In the classical setup studied here, finding k clusters involves constructing coordinates from k eigenvectors of a matrix associated with the graph. The paper reexamines both the conditions under which this procedure works and the number of eigenvectors it needs.

Its first contribution is a tighter performance analysis that supports spectral clustering under a substantially weaker condition than earlier analyses considered. This expands the theoretical explanation of when the classical algorithm succeeds. Its second contribution shows that using fewer than k eigenvectors can produce better clustering for many practical instances, even though the desired number of clusters remains k.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the practical relevance of using fewer eigenvectors: the resulting clusterings are comparable to or better than those from the conventional choice. The findings therefore distinguish the number of groups being sought from the dimension of the representation used to find them. They support a smaller embedding in many instances, without asserting that it is always the better choice.
summary.tldr: A tighter analysis supports spectral clustering under weaker conditions and shows that fewer eigenvectors can yield better clustering in many practical instances.

title: A Tighter Analysis of Spectral Clustering, and Beyond

abstract: In many real-world multi-agent systems, the sparsity of team rewards often makes it difficult for an algorithm to successfully learn a cooperative team policy. At present, the common way for solving this problem is to design some dense individual rewards for the agents to guide the cooperation. However, most existing works utilize individual rewards in ways that do not always promote teamwork and sometimes are even counterproductive. In this paper, we propose Individual Reward Assisted Team Policy Learning (IRAT), which learns two policies for each agent from the dense individual reward and the sparse team reward with discrepancy constraints for updating the two policies mutually. Experimental results in different scenarios, such as the Multi-Agent Particle Environment and the Google Research Football Environment, show that IRAT significantly outperforms the baseline methods and can greatly promote team policy learning without deviating from the original team objective, even when the individual rewards are misleading or conflict with the team rewards.
originalAbstract: In many real-world multi-agent systems, the sparsity of team rewards often makes it difficult for an algorithm to successfully learn a cooperative team policy. At present, the common way for solving this problem is to design some dense individual rewards for the agents to guide the cooperation. However, most existing works utilize individual rewards in ways that do not always promote teamwork and sometimes are even counterproductive. In this paper, we propose Individual Reward Assisted Team Policy Learning (IRAT), which learns two policies for each agent from the dense individual reward and the sparse team reward with discrepancy constraints for updating the two policies mutually. Experimental results in different scenarios, such as the Multi-Agent Particle Environment and the Google Research Football Environment, show that IRAT significantly outperforms the baseline methods and can greatly promote team policy learning without deviating from the original team objective, even when the individual rewards are misleading or conflict with the team rewards.

paragraphs: Cooperative agents often receive team rewards too infrequently to learn useful behavior easily. Designers can provide more frequent rewards for individual agents, but these rewards may encourage actions that do not help the team. The challenge is to obtain a useful learning signal from individual rewards while preserving the original cooperative objective.

Individual Reward Assisted Team Policy Learning, or IRAT, gives each agent two policies. One learns from dense individual rewards, while the other learns from sparse team rewards. Constraints on the discrepancy between the policies allow them to influence each other's updates. This design keeps the two reward signals associated with separate policies while providing a controlled mechanism for sharing what they learn.

Experiments in scenarios including the Multi-Agent Particle Environment and Google Research Football show significant improvements over the evaluated baselines. The authors report that IRAT promotes team-policy learning without drifting from the team objective, including cases where individual rewards mislead agents or conflict with team rewards. The results support using individual feedback as assistance for cooperation rather than assuming individual incentives already align with collective success.
summary.tldr: IRAT couples individual-reward and team-reward policies to improve cooperative learning even when individual incentives conflict with team goals.

title: Individual Reward Assisted Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Although machine learning (ML) algorithms are widely used to make decisions about individuals in various domains, concerns have arisen that (1) these algorithms are vulnerable to strategic manipulation and "gaming the algorithm"; and (2) ML decisions may exhibit bias against certain social groups. Existing works have largely examined these as two separate issues, e.g., by focusing on building ML algorithms robust to strategic manipulation, or on training a fair ML algorithm. In this study, we set out to understand the impact they each have on the other, and examine how to characterize fair policies in the presence of strategic behavior. The strategic interaction between a decision maker and individuals (as decision takers) is modeled as a two-stage (Stackelberg) game; when designing an algorithm, the former anticipates the latter may manipulate their features in order to receive more favorable decisions. We analytically characterize the equilibrium strategies of both, and examine how the algorithms and their resulting fairness properties are affected when the decision maker is strategic (anticipates manipulation), as well as the impact of fairness interventions on equilibrium strategies. In particular, we identify conditions under which anticipation of strategic behavior may mitigate/exacerbate unfairness, and conditions under which fairness interventions can serve as (dis)incentives for strategic manipulation.
originalAbstract: Although machine learning (ML) algorithms are widely used to make decisions about individuals in various domains, concerns have arisen that (1) these algorithms are vulnerable to strategic manipulation and "gaming the algorithm"; and (2) ML decisions may exhibit bias against certain social groups. Existing works have largely examined these as two separate issues, e.g., by focusing on building ML algorithms robust to strategic manipulation, or on training a fair ML algorithm. In this study, we set out to understand the impact they each have on the other, and examine how to characterize fair policies in the presence of strategic behavior. The strategic interaction between a decision maker and individuals (as decision takers) is modeled as a two-stage (Stackelberg) game; when designing an algorithm, the former anticipates the latter may manipulate their features in order to receive more favorable decisions. We analytically characterize the equilibrium strategies of both, and examine how the algorithms and their resulting fairness properties are affected when the decision maker is strategic (anticipates manipulation), as well as the impact of fairness interventions on equilibrium strategies. In particular, we identify conditions under which anticipation of strategic behavior may mitigate/exacerbate unfairness, and conditions under which fairness interventions can serve as (dis)incentives for strategic manipulation.

paragraphs: A decision rule can affect both how fairly people are treated and how they change their reported features to obtain favorable outcomes. This paper studies these issues together. Its central question is how fairness policies and strategic manipulation influence one another when the people being evaluated respond to the algorithm.

The authors model the interaction as a two-stage Stackelberg game. The decision maker designs a rule while anticipating that individuals may manipulate their features. They analytically characterize equilibrium strategies for both sides, then examine how anticipating manipulation changes the resulting algorithm and its fairness properties. Fairness interventions are also analyzed through their effects on those equilibrium strategies.

The findings identify conditions under which anticipating strategic behavior can either reduce or worsen unfairness. They likewise identify conditions under which fairness interventions can encourage or discourage manipulation. The contribution is therefore conditional guidance about interacting incentives, rather than a claim that strategic awareness or fairness constraints always move outcomes in a beneficial direction.
summary.tldr: A game-theoretic analysis identifies when fairness interventions encourage or discourage manipulation and when anticipating manipulation improves or worsens fairness.

title: Fairness Interventions as (Dis)Incentives for Strategic Manipulation

abstract: Training data is always finite, making it unclear how to generalise to unseen situations. But, animals do generalise, wielding Occam’s razor to select a parsimonious explanation of their observations. How they do this is called their inductive bias, and it is implicitly built into the operation of animals’ neural circuits. This relationship between an observed circuit and its inductive bias is a useful explanatory window for neuroscience, allowing design choices to be understood normatively. However, it is generally very difficult to map circuit structure to inductive bias. Here, we present a neural network tool to bridge this gap. The tool meta-learns the inductive bias by learning functions that a neural circuit finds easy to generalise, since easy-to-generalise functions are exactly those the circuit chooses to explain incomplete data. In systems with analytically known inductive bias, i.e. linear and kernel regression, our tool recovers it. Generally, we show it can flexibly extract inductive biases from supervised learners, including spiking neural networks, and show how it could be applied to real animals. Finally, we use our tool to interpret recent connectomic data illustrating our intended use: understanding the role of circuit features through the resulting inductive bias.

This paper treats that preference as a way to understand neural circuits: circuit features may become more interpretable when connected to the kinds of functions the circuit readily learns and generalizes.

The authors build a neural network tool that meta-learns functions a target circuit finds easy to generalize. Their central idea is that these functions reveal the explanations the circuit tends to choose when data are incomplete. This provides a practical route from a circuit’s learning behavior to its inductive bias, a relationship that is otherwise difficult to derive.

The authors also extract biases from other supervised learners, including spiking neural networks, and describe how the method could be applied to animals. An application to recent connectomic data illustrates the intended use: interpreting structural circuit features through the learning preferences they produce.
summary.tldr: A meta-learning tool reveals neural circuits’ inductive biases by identifying functions they find easy to generalize.

title: Meta-Learning the Inductive Bias of Simple Neural Circuits

abstract: POMDPs capture a broad class of decision making problems, but hardness results suggest that learning is intractable even in simple settings due to the inherent partial observability. However, in many realistic problems, more information is either revealed or can be computed during some point of the learning process. Motivated by diverse applications ranging from robotics to data center scheduling, we formulate a Hindsight Observable Markov Decision Process (HOMDP) as a POMDP where the latent states are revealed to the learner in hindsight and only during training. We introduce new algorithms for the tabular and function approximation settings that are provably sample-efficient with hindsight observability, even in POMDPs that would otherwise be statistically intractable. We give a lower bound showing that the tabular algorithm is optimal in its dependence on latent state and observation cardinalities.

paragraphs: In a partially observable decision problem, an agent must act without directly seeing the underlying state. This hidden information can make learning statistically intractable even in otherwise simple settings. The paper asks what changes when the learner can obtain additional information after the fact, a situation motivated by applications including robotics and data center scheduling.

The authors define a hindsight observable MDP as a partially observable process whose latent states are revealed retrospectively during training. That assumption is central: the extra state information is available for learning, while the decision problem remains partially observable. They introduce algorithms for both tabular representations and settings that use function approximation.

The algorithms are provably sample-efficient with hindsight observability, including for some problems that would otherwise be statistically intractable. A lower bound also establishes that the tabular algorithm has optimal dependence on the numbers of latent states and observations. The result identifies a specific form of training-time information that can change learning difficulty, with an optimality claim tied to those two dimensions rather than every aspect of the algorithm.
summary.tldr: Revealing hidden states retrospectively during training enables provably sample-efficient learning in some otherwise statistically intractable partially observable problems.

title: Learning in POMDPs is Sample-Efficient with Hindsight Observability

abstract: We initiate the study of statistical inference and A/B testing for first-price pacing equilibria (FPPE). The FPPE model captures the dynamics resulting from large-scale first-price auction markets where buyers use pacing-based budget management. Such markets arise in the context of internet advertising, where budgets are prevalent. We propose a statistical framework for the FPPE model, in which a limit FPPE with a continuum of items models the long-run steady-state behavior of the auction platform, and an observable FPPE consisting of a finite number of items provides the data to estimate primitives of the limit FPPE, such as revenue, Nash social welfare (a fair metric of efficiency), and other parameters of interest. We develop central limit theorems and asymptotically valid confidence intervals. Furthermore, we establish the asymptotic local minimax optimality of our estimators. We then show that the theory can be used for conducting statistically valid A/B testing on auction platforms. Numerical simulations verify our central limit theorems, and empirical coverage rates for our confidence intervals agree with our theory.

paragraphs: In large first-price auction markets, buyers may manage budgets through pacing, creating market behavior described by first-price pacing equilibria. This paper develops statistical inference for that setting, motivated by advertising auctions. The goal is to estimate long-run market quantities and support statistically valid comparisons of changes to an auction platform.

The framework distinguishes a limiting market with a continuum of items from an observed market with finitely many items. The limiting equilibrium represents long-run steady-state behavior, while the finite equilibrium supplies data for estimation. Quantities of interest include revenue and Nash social welfare, an efficiency measure incorporating fairness.

The authors derive central limit theorems and confidence intervals that are valid asymptotically. They also establish asymptotic local minimax optimality of the estimators and show how the theory supports A/B testing. Numerical simulations agree with the predicted limiting distributions and confidence-interval coverage. The guarantees concern asymptotic inference, connecting finite observed auction data to estimates of the underlying long-run equilibrium.
summary.tldr: A statistical framework for budget-paced first-price auctions provides asymptotic confidence intervals and supports valid A/B testing.

title: Statistical Inference and A/B Testing for First-Price Pacing Equilibria

abstract: Multimodal learning is defined as learning over multiple heterogeneous input modalities such as video, audio, and text. In this work, we are concerned with understanding how models behave as the type of modalities differ between training and deployment, a situation that naturally arises in many applications of multimodal learning to hardware platforms. We present a multimodal robustness framework to provide a systematic analysis of common multimodal representation learning methods. Further, we identify robustness short-comings of these approaches and propose two intervention techniques leading to $1.5\times$-$4\times$ robustness improvements on three datasets, AudioSet, Kinetics-400 and ImageNet-Captions. Finally, we demonstrate that these interventions better utilize additional modalities, if present, to achieve competitive results of $44.2$ mAP on AudioSet 20K.

In this work, we are concerned with understanding how models behave as the type of modalities differ between training and deployment, a situation that naturally arises in many applications of multimodal learning to hardware platforms. paragraphs: Multimodal models learn from heterogeneous inputs such as video, audio, and text. Deployment can change which input types are available, especially across hardware platforms. This paper studies that mismatch between training and deployment, asking how well learned representations continue to work when the available modalities differ.

The authors introduce a robustness framework for systematically analyzing common multimodal representation-learning methods. Using it, they identify weaknesses in existing approaches and propose two interventions. The framework makes changing modality availability an explicit evaluation concern, so that a model’s use of several inputs can be assessed alongside its ability to cope with a different input combination.

Experiments on AudioSet, Kinetics-400, and ImageNet-Captions report robustness improvements ranging from 1.5 to 4 times. The interventions also make better use of additional modalities when they are available, achieving a competitive 44.2 mean average precision on AudioSet 20K. The findings therefore address two related deployment needs: maintaining performance under modality mismatch and benefiting from richer inputs when a platform can supply them.
summary.tldr: A modality-mismatch evaluation framework motivates two interventions that improve reported robustness and make better use of additional inputs.

title: Robustness in Multimodal Learning under Train-Test Modality Mismatch

abstract: We present Simplex Random Features (SimRFs), a new random feature (RF) mechanism for unbiased approximation of the softmax and Gaussian kernels by geometrical correlation of random projection vectors. We prove that SimRFs provide the smallest possible mean square error (MSE) on unbiased estimates of these kernels among the class of weight-independent geometrically-coupled positive random feature (PRF) mechanisms, substantially outperforming the previously most accurate Orthogonal Random Features (ORFs) at no observable extra cost. We present a more computationally expensive SimRFs+ variant, which we prove is asymptotically optimal in the broader family of weight-dependent geometrical coupling schemes (which permit correlations between random vector directions and norms). In extensive empirical studies, we show consistent gains provided by SimRFs in settings including pointwise kernel estimation, nonparametric classification and scalable Transformers.
