paragraphs: Random features approximate kernel computations using random projections. This paper asks how coordinating the geometry of those projections can improve approximation accuracy. Simplex Random Features, or SimRFs, correlate projection vectors geometrically while preserving unbiased estimates of the softmax and Gaussian kernels, meaning the estimates remain correct on average.

The authors prove that SimRFs achieve the lowest mean squared error within a specified family: positive random-feature mechanisms with weight-independent geometric coupling. Within that setting, they substantially outperform Orthogonal Random Features without observable additional cost. The scope of the theorem matters because it establishes optimality within this class of mechanisms, rather than among every possible kernel approximation.

A more expensive variant, SimRFs+, allows dependence between vector directions and norms. It is proved asymptotically optimal in that broader family of coupling schemes. Empirical studies report consistent gains in individual kernel estimates, nonparametric classification, and scalable Transformers. Together, the theory and experiments show that carefully arranged randomness can improve approximation quality and benefit downstream uses of the approximated kernels.
summary.tldr: SimRFs geometrically coordinate random projections to improve unbiased kernel approximation, with optimality guarantees within specified feature families.

title: Simplex Random Features

abstract: Semi-supervised semantic segmentation involves assigning pixel-wise labels to unlabeled images at training time. This is useful in a wide range of real-world applications where collecting pixel-wise labels is not feasible in time or cost. Current approaches to semi-supervised semantic segmentation work by predicting pseudo-labels for each pixel from a class-wise probability distribution output by a model. If this predicted probability distribution is incorrect, however, it leads to poor segmentation results which can have knock-on consequences in safety critical systems, like medical images or self-driving cars. It is, therefore, important to understand what a model does not know, which is mainly achieved by uncertainty quantification. Recently, neural processes (NPs) have been explored in semi-supervised image classification, and they have been a computationally efficient and effective method for uncertainty quantification. In this work, we move one step forward by adapting NPs to semi-supervised semantic segmentation, resulting in a new model called NP-SemiSeg. We experimentally evaluated NP-SemiSeg on the public benchmarks PASCAL VOC 2012 and Cityscapes, with different training settings, and the results verify its effectiveness.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns a category to every pixel in an image, making manual training labels expensive to collect. Semi-supervised methods also use unlabeled images, often assigning predicted labels to their pixels during training. When those predictions are unreliable, the resulting pseudo-labels can lead to poor segmentation.

NP-SemiSeg adapts neural processes to this setting to quantify uncertainty. Neural processes had previously been explored for semi-supervised image classification as an efficient approach to uncertainty estimation. Moving from classifying an entire image to labeling individual pixels brings that idea into a task where understanding uncertain predictions is especially relevant to the use of unlabeled training data.

The authors evaluate NP-SemiSeg on PASCAL VOC 2012 and Cityscapes under different training settings and report results supporting its effectiveness. The contribution is an adaptation of uncertainty-aware modeling to semi-supervised segmentation. Medical imaging and self-driving applications motivate the importance of unreliable pixel predictions in the paper; the stated experimental evidence comes from the two named public benchmarks.
summary.tldr: NP-SemiSeg adapts neural processes to quantify uncertainty in semi-supervised pixel labeling.

title: NP-SemiSeg: When Neural Processes meet Semi-Supervised Semantic Segmentation

abstract: In supervised learning, understanding an input’s proximity to the training data can help a model decide whether it has sufficient evidence for reaching a reliable prediction. While powerful probabilistic models such as Gaussian Processes naturally have this property, deep neural networks often lack it. In this paper, we introduce Distance Aware Bottleneck (DAB), i.e., a new method for enriching deep neural networks with this property. Building on prior information bottleneck approaches, our method learns a codebook that stores a compressed representation of all inputs seen during training. The distance of a new example from this codebook can serve as an uncertainty estimate for the example. The resulting model is simple to train and provides deterministic uncertainty estimates by a single forward pass. Finally, our method achieves better out-of-distribution (OOD) detection and misclassification prediction than prior methods, including expensive ensemble methods, deep kernel Gaussian Processes, and approaches based on the standard information bottleneck.

paragraphs: A prediction is easier to trust when the model has encountered relevant examples during training. Gaussian processes naturally connect uncertainty to proximity to observed data, but deep neural networks often lack this behavior. This paper introduces Distance Aware Bottleneck, or DAB, to give neural networks an explicit way to assess how closely a new input relates to their training experience.

DAB builds on information bottleneck methods by learning a codebook: a compressed representation of the inputs encountered during training. For a new example, its distance from that codebook serves as an uncertainty estimate. The codebook therefore connects uncertainty to a learned summary of the training data, while allowing the estimate to be computed deterministically in a single forward pass.

The authors report better detection of out-of-distribution inputs and better prediction of classification mistakes than the compared methods, including ensembles, deep kernel Gaussian processes, and standard information bottleneck approaches. These findings support the usefulness of compressed training-data representations for uncertainty estimation, alongside the practical benefit of obtaining that estimate without repeated model evaluations.
summary.tldr: Distance Aware Bottleneck estimates uncertainty from a learned training-data codebook, improving reported error and out-of-distribution detection with one forward pass.

title: A Rate-Distortion View of Uncertainty Quantification

abstract: In this study, we present $\text{aL\small{LM}4T\small{S}}$, an innovative framework that adapts Large Language Models (LLMs) for time-series representation learning. Central to our approach is that we reconceive time-series forecasting as a self-supervised, multi-patch prediction task, which, compared to traditional mask-and-reconstruction methods, captures temporal dynamics in patch representations more effectively. Our strategy encompasses two-stage training: (i). a causal continual pre-training phase on various time-series datasets, anchored on next patch prediction, effectively syncing LLM capabilities with the intricacies of time-series data; (ii). fine-tuning for multi-patch prediction in the targeted time-series context. A distinctive element of our framework is the patch-wise decoding layer, which departs from previous methods reliant on sequence-level decoding. Such a design directly transposes individual patches into temporal sequences, thereby significantly bolstering the model’s proficiency in mastering temporal patch-based representations. $\text{aL\small{LM}4T\small{S}}$ demonstrates superior performance in several downstream tasks, proving its effectiveness in deriving temporal representations with enhanced transferability and marking a pivotal advancement in the adaptation of LLMs for time-series analysis.

paragraphs: This paper introduces aLLM4TS, a framework for adapting large language models to learn representations of time series. It treats forecasting as self-supervised prediction of multiple patches, or segments of a sequence. The authors argue that this prediction task captures temporal dynamics in patch representations more effectively than masking parts of the data and reconstructing them.

Training proceeds in two stages. First, causal continual pretraining on multiple time-series datasets teaches next-patch prediction. Second, fine-tuning targets multi-patch prediction in the intended time-series setting. The framework also introduces a patch-wise decoding layer, which converts individual patch representations into temporal sequences instead of relying on decoding at the sequence level.

The reported results show superior performance across several downstream tasks and more transferable temporal representations. The methodological point is that adaptation involves both the training objective and the way representations are decoded. Together, next-patch pretraining, task-specific multi-patch learning, and patch-wise decoding are intended to make the language model’s learned representations capture the structure of temporal data more effectively.
summary.tldr: aLLM4TS adapts language models through next-patch pretraining, multi-patch fine-tuning, and patch-wise decoding to learn transferable time-series representations.

title: Multi-Patch Prediction: Adapting Language Models for Time Series Representation Learning

abstract: The current state-of-the-art theoretical analysis of Actor-Critic (AC) algorithms significantly lags in addressing the practical aspects of AC implementations. This crucial gap needs bridging to bring the analysis in line with practical implementations of AC. To address this, we advocate for considering the MMCLG criteria: Multi-layer neural network parametrization for actor/critic, Markovian sampling, Continuous state-action spaces, the performance of the Last iterate, and Global optimality. These aspects are practically significant and have been largely overlooked in existing theoretical analyses of AC algorithms. In this work, we address these gaps by providing the first comprehensive theoretical analysis of AC algorithms that encompasses all five crucial practical aspects (covers MMCLG criteria). We establish global convergence sample complexity bounds of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left( \epsilon^{-3} \right)$. We achieve this result through our novel use of the weak gradient domination property of MDP’s and our unique analysis of the error in critic estimation.

paragraphs: Actor-critic algorithms combine a policy-learning actor with a critic that estimates its performance. Their theoretical analyses often leave out features used in practical implementations. This paper organizes five such features into a joint target: multilayer neural networks for both components, Markovian sampling, continuous state and action spaces, guarantees for the final iterate, and global optimality.

Addressing these features together matters because they describe different parts of the same learning process. Markovian samples account for dependence along interactions with an environment. A last-iterate guarantee concerns the policy obtained at the end of training. Neural network parameterization and continuous spaces bring the analyzed setting closer to common actor-critic implementations.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis covering all five criteria and establish a global convergence sample complexity bound of approximately epsilon to the power of minus three, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Their argument uses a weak gradient domination property of Markov decision processes and an analysis of critic estimation error. The result links the quality of critic estimates to a global guarantee for the final policy.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes last-iterate global convergence bounds for actor-critic learning while jointly accounting for five practically relevant features.

title: Closing the Gap: Achieving Global Convergence (Last Iterate) of Actor-Critic under Markovian Sampling with Neural Network Parametrization

abstract: We present Code Reasoning, Understanding, and eXecution Evaluation, a benchmark consisting of 800 Python functions (3-13 lines). Each function comes with an input-output pair, leading to two natural tasks: input prediction and output prediction. First, we propose a general recipe for generating our execution benchmark by sampling from a model, which can be used for more challenging versions of the benchmark if needed. Second, we evaluate twenty code models on our benchmark and discover that many recent high-scoring models on HumanEval show no improvements on our benchmark. Third, we show that simple CoT and fine-tuning schemes can improve performance on our benchmark but remain far from solving it. The best setup, GPT-4 with chain of thought (CoT), achieves a pass@1 of 75% and 81% on input and output prediction, respectively. In contrast, Code Llama 34B achieves a pass@1 of 50% and 46% on input and output prediction. When it comes to reasoning about code, GPT-4 has a huge edge over other models but still fails consistently on some surprisingly simple Python programs.

paragraphs: CRUXEval tests whether a model can reason about what short Python programs do. It contains 800 functions, each three to thirteen lines long and paired with an input and output. The resulting tasks ask a model either to predict the output or to identify an input producing the given output.

The authors provide a model-sampling recipe for creating execution benchmarks, including potentially harder versions. They evaluate twenty code models and find that several recent models with strong HumanEval scores show no corresponding improvement on CRUXEval. This indicates that progress on one code benchmark need not translate into better reasoning about program execution.

Chain-of-thought prompting and fine-tuning improve results but do not solve the benchmark. GPT-4 with chain of thought achieves first-attempt success rates of 75% for input prediction and 81% for output prediction; Code Llama 34B reaches 50% and 46%. Even the strongest evaluated setup repeatedly fails on some simple programs, exposing specific weaknesses that aggregate code-generation performance can miss.
summary.tldr: CRUXEval reveals persistent weaknesses in reasoning about short Python programs, including among models that score highly on code-generation benchmarks.

title: CRUXEval: A Benchmark for Code Reasoning, Understanding and Execution

abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have been a large driver for AI breakthroughs in recent years, ranging from self-driving cars to intelligent assistants. However, these models have been getting increasingly large as they become more accurate and safe. This means that their training becomes increasingly costly and time-consuming, and typically yields a single model to fit all targets. To mitigate this, various techniques have been proposed in the literature, including pruning, sparsification or quantization of the model weights and updates. While achieving high compression rates, they often incur significant computational overheads at training or lead to non-negligible accuracy penalty. Alternatively, factorization methods have been leveraged for low-rank compression of DNNs. Similarly, such techniques (e.g., SVD) frequently rely on heavy iterative decompositions of layers and are potentially sub-optimal for non-linear models, such as DNNs. We take a further step in designing efficient low-rank models and propose Maestro, a framework for trainable low-rank layers. Instead of iteratively applying a priori decompositions, the low-rank structure is baked into the training process through LoD, a low-rank ordered decomposition. Not only is this the first time importance ordering via sampling is applied on the decomposed DNN structure, but it also allows selecting ranks at a layer granularity. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that LoD recovers the SVD decomposition of linear mapping on uniformly distributed data and PCA for linear autoencoders. Applied to DNNs, Maestro enables the extraction of lower footprint models that preserve performance. Simultaneously, it enables the graceful tradeoff between accuracy-latency for deployment to even more constrained devices, without retraining.
originalAbstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have been a large driver for AI breakthroughs in recent years, ranging from self-driving cars to intelligent assistants. However, these models have been getting increasingly large as they become more accurate and safe. This means that their training becomes increasingly costly and time-consuming, and typically yields a single model to fit all targets. To mitigate this, various techniques have been proposed in the literature, including pruning, sparsification or quantization of the model weights and updates. While achieving high compression rates, they often incur significant computational overheads at training or lead to non-negligible accuracy penalty. Alternatively, factorization methods have been leveraged for low-rank compression of DNNs. Similarly, such techniques (e.g., SVD) frequently rely on heavy iterative decompositions of layers and are potentially sub-optimal for non-linear models, such as DNNs. We take a further step in designing efficient low-rank models and propose Maestro, a framework for trainable low-rank layers. Instead of iteratively applying a priori decompositions, the low-rank structure is baked into the training process through LoD, a low-rank ordered decomposition. Not only is this the first time importance ordering via sampling is applied on the decomposed DNN structure, but it also allows selecting ranks at a layer granularity. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that LoD recovers the SVD decomposition of linear mapping on uniformly distributed data and PCA for linear autoencoders. Applied to DNNs, Maestro enables the extraction of lower footprint models that preserve performance. Simultaneously, it enables the graceful tradeoff between accuracy-latency for deployment to even more constrained devices, without retraining.

paragraphs: Compressing large neural networks can reduce deployment costs, but some methods add training overhead or sacrifice accuracy. Low-rank factorization offers another route, although repeated decompositions can be expensive and may be suboptimal for nonlinear networks. Maestro builds low-rank structure directly into training through trainable decomposed layers.

Its low-rank ordered decomposition, called LoD, uses sampling to establish an importance ordering within the decomposed network structure. This ordering allows ranks to be selected separately for individual layers. The theoretical analysis connects the procedure to familiar decompositions in specific linear settings: it recovers singular value decomposition for linear mappings on uniformly distributed data and principal component analysis for linear autoencoders.

For deep networks, the authors report that Maestro can produce smaller models while preserving performance. The same trained structure also supports trading accuracy for latency when deploying to more constrained devices, without retraining. This makes the contribution useful for obtaining different model sizes from a training process, with the exact decomposition equivalences established for the stated linear cases.
summary.tldr: Maestro learns ordered low-rank layers during training, enabling smaller models and deployment accuracy–latency trade-offs without retraining.

title: Maestro: Uncovering Low-Rank Structures via Trainable Decomposition

abstract: Modern information retrieval (IR) systems consists of multiple stages like retrieval and ranking, with Transformer-based models achieving state-of-the-art performance at each stage. In this paper, we challenge the tradition of using separate models for different stages and ask if a single Transformer encoder can provide relevance score needed in each stage. We present USTAD – a new unified approach to train a single network that can provide powerful ranking scores as a cross-encoder (CE) model as well as factorized embeddings for large-scale retrieval as a dual-encoder (DE) model. Empirically, we find a single USTAD model to be competitive to separate ranking CE and retrieval DE models. Furthermore, USTAD combines well with a novel embedding matching-based distillation, significantly improving CE to DE distillation. It further motivates novel asymmetric architectures for student models to ensure a better embedding alignment between the student and the teacher while ensuring small online inference cost. On standard benchmarks like MSMARCO, we demonstrate that USTAD with our proposed distillation method leads to asymmetric students with only 1/10th trainable parameter but retaining 95-97% of the teacher performance.

Retrieval benefits from independently computed embeddings, while ranking can use a cross-encoder to score a query and document together. USTAD asks whether one Transformer encoder can supply both forms of relevance information.

The proposed training approach produces a single network that works as a cross-encoder and also supplies factorized embeddings for dual-encoder retrieval. Empirically, this unified model is competitive with separate models for the two stages. USTAD also combines with an embedding-matching distillation method that improves the transfer from cross-encoder capabilities to dual-encoder students.

The findings support both sharing a model across retrieval stages and using that model to train smaller students with strong retained performance in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: USTAD trains one encoder for retrieval and ranking and supports compact students that retain 95–97% of teacher performance on reported benchmarks.

title: USTAD: Unified Single-model Training Achieving Diverse Scores for Information Retrieval

abstract: Modeling complex systems using standard neural ordinary differential equations (NODEs) often faces some essential challenges, including high computational costs and susceptibility to local optima. To address these challenges, we propose a simulation-free framework, called Fourier NODEs (FNODEs), that effectively trains NODEs by directly matching the target vector field based on Fourier analysis. Specifically, we employ the Fourier analysis to estimate temporal and potential high-order spatial gradients from noisy observational data. We then incorporate the estimated spatial gradients as additional inputs to a neural network. Furthermore, we utilize the estimated temporal gradient as the optimization objective for the output of the neural network. Later, the trained neural network generates more data points through an ODE solver without participating in the computational graph, facilitating more accurate estimations of gradients based on Fourier analysis. These two steps form a positive feedback loop, enabling accurate dynamics modeling in our framework. Consequently, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of training time, dynamics prediction, and robustness. Finally, we demonstrate the superior performance of our framework using a number of representative complex systems.

paragraphs: Neural ordinary differential equations model changing systems, but conventional training can be computationally expensive and susceptible to local optima. Fourier NODEs addresses these challenges by training the neural network to match an estimated vector field directly. This turns estimates of how observations change into explicit learning targets.

Fourier analysis estimates temporal derivatives and, when relevant, higher-order spatial derivatives from noisy observations. The spatial estimates become additional network inputs, while the temporal derivative becomes the desired output. The trained network then generates additional points through an ODE solver that stays outside the computational graph. Those points support improved Fourier-based derivative estimates in the next stage.

The alternating steps form a feedback loop between estimating derivatives and fitting dynamics. The framework is described as simulation-free training even though an ODE solver generates additional data outside the training graph. Across representative complex systems, the authors report improvements over state-of-the-art methods in training time, dynamics prediction, and robustness. These results support the approach of matching estimated local dynamics while refining the data used to estimate them.
summary.tldr: Fourier NODEs alternates derivative estimation and direct vector-field fitting to improve the speed and accuracy of dynamics modeling.

title: From Fourier to Neural ODEs: Flow Matching for Modeling Complex Systems

abstract: Gibbs sampling from continuous real-valued functions is a challenging problem of interest in machine learning. Here we leverage quantum Fourier transforms to build a quantum algorithm for this task when the function is periodic. We use the quantum algorithms for solving linear ordinary differential equations to solve the Fokker–Planck equation and prepare a quantum state encoding the Gibbs distribution. We show that the efficiency of interpolation and differentiation of these functions on a quantum computer depends on the rate of decay of the Fourier coefficients of the Fourier transform of the function. We view this property as a concentration of measure in the Fourier domain, and also provide functional analytic conditions for it. Our algorithm makes zeroeth order queries to a quantum oracle of the function and achieves polynomial quantum speedups in mean estimation in the Gibbs measure for generic non-convex periodic functions. At high temperatures the algorithm also allows for exponentially improved precision in sampling from Morse functions.

paragraphs: The paper develops a quantum approach to sampling from Gibbs distributions defined by continuous, periodic functions. These distributions associate probabilities with the values of a function, making them relevant to machine learning. The central computational goal is to prepare a quantum state that encodes the desired distribution.

The algorithm combines quantum Fourier transforms with quantum methods for solving linear ordinary differential equations. These tools are used to solve the Fokker–Planck equation. The authors show that efficient interpolation and differentiation depend on how quickly the function’s Fourier coefficients decay, and provide functional analytic conditions supporting this property.

Using a quantum oracle that supplies function values, the algorithm achieves polynomial quantum speedups for estimating averages under the Gibbs distribution of generic nonconvex periodic functions. A further result applies at high temperatures to Morse functions, where sampling precision can improve exponentially. These are distinct, qualified advantages: the general mean-estimation result concerns periodic potentials, while the stronger precision result additionally depends on temperature and the specified class of functions.
summary.tldr: A Fourier-based quantum algorithm offers polynomial speedups for Gibbs mean estimation with periodic potentials and stronger precision gains under additional conditions.

title: Gibbs Sampling of Continuous Potentials on a Quantum Computer

abstract: Many questions in science center around the fundamental problem of understanding causal relationships. However, most constraint-based causal discovery algorithms, including the well-celebrated PC algorithm, often incur an exponential number of conditional independence (CI) tests, posing limitations in various applications. Addressing this, our work focuses on characterizing what can be learned about the underlying causal graph with a reduced number of CI tests. We show that it is possible to a learn a coarser representation of the hidden causal graph with a polynomial number of tests. This coarser representation, named Causal Consistent Partition Graph (CCPG), comprises of a partition of the vertices and a directed graph defined over its components. CCPG satisfies consistency of orientations and additional constraints which favor finer partitions. Furthermore, it reduces to the underlying causal graph when the causal graph is identifiable. As a consequence, our results offer the first efficient algorithm for recovering the true causal graph with a polynomial number of tests, in special cases where the causal graph is fully identifiable through observational data and potentially additional interventions.

paragraphs: Constraint-based causal discovery uses conditional independence tests to infer relationships among variables. These tests ask whether two variables remain statistically related after accounting for others. Established algorithms can require exponentially many such tests, making the testing burden a central obstacle to learning causal structure.

The paper asks what structure can be recovered with only a polynomial number of tests. Its answer is the Causal Consistent Partition Graph, which groups variables into components and places directed relationships between those components. This representation preserves consistency of orientations and includes additional constraints that favor finer partitions, retaining more detail where the evidence permits.

The result gives an efficient route to a coarser causal description, with a stronger conclusion in identifiable cases. When the underlying causal graph is identifiable, the representation reduces to that graph. Consequently, the authors obtain polynomial-test recovery of the true graph in special cases where observational data, potentially supplemented by interventions, fully identify it. Exact recovery remains tied to that stated identifiability condition.
summary.tldr: A partition-based causal representation can be learned with polynomially many independence tests and recovers the full graph in identifiable cases.

title: Causal Discovery with Fewer Conditional Independence Tests

abstract: Real-world data generation often involves certain geometries (e.g., graphs) that induce instance-level interdependence. This characteristic makes the generalization of learning models more difficult due to the intricate interdependent patterns that impact data-generative distributions and can vary from training to testing. In this work, we propose a geometric diffusion model with learnable divergence fields for the challenging generalization problem with interdependent data. We generalize the diffusion equation with stochastic diffusivity at each time step, which aims to capture the multi-faceted information flows among interdependent data. Furthermore, we derive a new learning objective through causal inference, which can guide the model to learn generalizable patterns of interdependence that are insensitive across domains. Regarding practical implementation, we introduce three model instantiations that can be considered as the generalized versions of GCN, GAT, and Transformers, respectively, which possess advanced robustness against distribution shifts. We demonstrate their promising efficacy for out-of-distribution generalization on diverse real-world datasets. Source codes are available at https://github.com/fannie1208/GLIND.

paragraphs: Graph data contains dependencies between examples, and those dependencies can change between training and deployment. This makes generalization difficult because a model may learn patterns of interaction that are specific to its training distribution. The paper addresses this problem through a geometric diffusion model with learnable divergence fields.

The model generalizes the diffusion equation by making diffusivity stochastic at each time step. This is intended to capture multiple kinds of information flow among dependent data points. A learning objective derived through causal inference then guides the model toward interdependence patterns that remain insensitive to domain changes. The approach therefore addresses both how information moves and which movement patterns should be learned.

The authors implement three versions that generalize graph convolutional networks, graph attention networks, and Transformers. Evaluations on diverse real-world datasets demonstrate promising out-of-distribution performance and robustness to distribution shifts. The findings support this diffusion-based formulation as a way to improve several model families when the relationships among data points change across domains.
summary.tldr: A learnable diffusion framework helps graph models capture interdependence patterns that generalize across distribution shifts.

title: Learning Divergence Fields for Shift-Robust Graph Representations

abstract: Training neural networks requires optimizing a loss function that may be highly irregular, and in particular neither convex nor smooth. Popular training algorithms are based on stochastic gradient descent with momentum (SGDM), for which classical analysis applies only if the loss is either convex or smooth. We show that a very small modification to SGDM closes this gap: simply scale the update at each time point by an exponentially distributed random scalar. The resulting algorithm achieves optimal convergence guarantees. Intriguingly, this result is not derived by a specific analysis of SGDM: instead, it falls naturally out of a more general framework for converting online convex optimization algorithms to non-convex optimization algorithms.

paragraphs: Neural-network training can involve loss functions that are neither convex nor smooth. Stochastic gradient descent with momentum is widely used in that setting, but the classical analysis described in this paper requires at least one of those properties. The work addresses this mismatch between a practical training method and the conditions supporting its familiar theory.

The proposed change is small: multiply each momentum-based update by a random scalar drawn from an exponential distribution. This randomizes the update’s scale while retaining the underlying momentum method. The authors show that the resulting algorithm achieves optimal convergence guarantees for the nonsmooth, nonconvex optimization setting they study.

The guarantee emerges from a broader framework that converts online convex optimization algorithms into nonconvex optimization algorithms. This matters because the result is more than an isolated analysis of one modified optimizer: the conversion framework explains how the method arises. The stated contribution is a convergence result for irregular objectives, connecting a simple algorithmic change to a general theoretical construction.
summary.tldr: Exponentially distributed random scaling gives momentum SGD optimal convergence guarantees in the studied nonsmooth, nonconvex setting.

title: Random Scaling and Momentum for Non-smooth Non-convex Optimization

abstract: Machine learning (ML) datasets, often perceived as neutral, inherently encapsulate abstract and disputed social constructs. Dataset curators frequently employ value-laden terms such as diversity, bias, and quality to characterize datasets. Despite their prevalence, these terms lack clear definitions and validation. Our research explores the implications of this issue by analyzing "diversity" across 135 image and text datasets. Drawing from social sciences, we apply principles from measurement theory to identify considerations and offer recommendations for conceptualizing, operationalizing, and evaluating diversity in datasets. Our findings have broader implications for ML research, advocating for a more nuanced and precise approach to handling value-laden properties in dataset construction.

paragraphs: Calling a dataset diverse can sound like a straightforward description, but the term carries assumptions about what differences matter and how they should be represented. This position paper argues that dataset descriptions often use diversity, bias, and quality without clearly defining or validating those concepts. Such labels embed social judgments even when datasets are presented as neutral.

The authors examine how diversity is treated across 135 image and text datasets. Drawing on social-science measurement theory, they develop considerations and recommendations for three connected activities: defining the concept, turning that definition into something measurable, and evaluating whether the measurement captures the intended property. Each step makes the meaning of a diversity claim more explicit.

The paper’s contribution is guidance for reasoning carefully about dataset properties whose meanings are abstract and disputed. Its implications extend beyond the word diversity to other value-laden descriptions used in machine learning. The proposed direction is to support dataset claims with precise concepts and defensible measurement, making construction choices and their underlying assumptions easier to examine.
summary.tldr: An analysis of 135 datasets motivates clearer definitions, measurements, and validation for claims about dataset diversity.

title: Position: Measure Dataset Diversity, Don’t Just Claim It

abstract: Analyzing time series data is crucial to a wide spectrum of applications, including economics, online marketplaces, and human healthcare. In particular, time series classification plays an indispensable role in segmenting different phases in stock markets, predicting customer behavior, and classifying worker actions and engagement levels. These aspects contribute significantly to the advancement of automated decision-making and system optimization in real-world applications. However, there is a large consensus that time series data often suffers from domain shifts between training and test sets, which dramatically degrades the classification performance. Despite the success of (reversible) instance normalization in handling the domain shifts for time series regression tasks, its performance in classification is unsatisfactory. In this paper, we propose $\textit{FIC-TSC}$, a training framework for time series classification that leverages Fisher information as the constraint. We theoretically and empirically show this is an efficient and effective solution to guide the model converges toward flatter minima, which enhances its generalizability to distribution shifts. We rigorously evaluate our method on 30 UEA multivariate and 85 UCR univariate datasets. Our empirical results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method over 14 recent state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Time-series classifiers often encounter test data whose distribution differs from their training data, which can substantially reduce accuracy. Normalization methods that help time-series regression have been less satisfactory for classification. FIC-TSC addresses this challenge through a constraint on training, with the aim of improving generalization under distribution shifts.

The framework uses Fisher information as its constraint. The authors provide theoretical and empirical evidence that this guides optimization toward flatter minima: solutions in regions where changes to parameters have a less sharp effect on the training objective. Their analysis connects this training behavior to improved ability to handle changes in the data distribution.

Evaluation covers 30 multivariate datasets from UEA and 85 univariate datasets from UCR, with comparisons against 14 recent state-of-the-art methods. The reported results favor FIC-TSC across this evaluation. The contribution is a training framework that ties a specific information-based constraint to optimization geometry and then tests whether that connection translates into stronger time-series classification performance.
summary.tldr: FIC-TSC uses a Fisher-information constraint to encourage flatter solutions and improve time-series classification under distribution shifts.

title: FIC-TSC: Learning Time Series Classification with Fisher Information Constraint

abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) excel at fitting finetuning data, but often struggle on unseen examples. In order to teach models genuine reasoning abilities rather than superficial pattern matching, our work aims to better understand how the learning dynamics of LLM finetuning shapes downstream generalization. Our analysis focuses on reasoning tasks, whose problem structure allows us to distinguish between memorization (the exact replication of reasoning steps from the training data) and performance (the correctness of the final solution). We find that a model’s performance on test prompts can be effectively characterized by a training metric we call pre-memorization train accuracy: the accuracy of model samples on training queries before they begin to copy the exact reasoning steps from the training set. On the dataset level, this metric is able to almost perfectly predict test accuracy, achieving $R^2$ of $\geq 0.9$ across various models (Llama3 8B, Gemma2 9B), datasets (GSM8k, MATH), and training configurations. On a per-example level, this metric is also indicative of whether individual model predictions are robust to perturbations in the training query. By connecting a model’s learning dynamics to test performance, pre-memorization train accuracy can inform training decisions, such as the makeup of the training data. Our experiments on data curation show that prioritizing examples with low pre-memorization accuracy leads to 1.5-2x improvements in data efficiency compared to i.i.d. data scaling and other data scaling techniques.

This paper studies that distinction during mathematical finetuning by separating correct final answers from exact copying of training reasoning steps. summary.tldr: Accuracy before a model starts copying training reasoning strongly predicts test performance and guides more data-efficient mathematical finetuning.

title: What Do Learning Dynamics Reveal About Generalization in LLM Mathematical Reasoning?

abstract: Although it is well-known that humans commonly engage in risk-sensitive behaviors in the presence of stochasticity, most Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) models assume a risk-neutral agent. As such, beyond $(i)$ introducing model misspecification, $(ii)$ they do not permit direct inference of the risk attitude of the observed agent, which can be useful in many applications. In this paper, we propose a novel model of behavior to cope with these issues. By allowing for risk sensitivity, our model alleviates $(i)$, and by explicitly representing risk attitudes through (learnable) utility functions, it solves $(ii)$. Then, we characterize the partial identifiability of an agent’s utility under the new model and note that demonstrations from multiple environments mitigate the problem. We devise two provably-efficient algorithms for learning utilities in a finite-data regime, and we conclude with some proof-of-concept experiments to validate both our model and our algorithms.

paragraphs: People's choices under uncertainty often reflect attitudes toward risk, yet many inverse reinforcement learning models assume risk neutrality. That assumption can misrepresent observed behavior and prevents direct estimation of risk attitude. This paper introduces a behavioral model in which learnable utility functions explicitly represent how an agent responds to uncertain outcomes.

The authors analyze how much of an agent's utility can be identified from demonstrations. They establish partial identifiability, meaning the observations do not fully determine the utility in general. Demonstrations collected across multiple environments mitigate this ambiguity, giving the analysis a direct connection to the kinds of evidence available for learning.

The paper also develops two algorithms with provable efficiency guarantees in the finite-data setting. Proof-of-concept experiments provide support for both the behavioral model and the learning procedures. The contribution joins a more expressive account of risk-sensitive decisions with an analysis of what demonstrations can reveal. Its identifiability result is especially relevant when interpreting a learned utility as evidence about an observed agent's preferences.
summary.tldr: A risk-sensitive behavioral model and two efficient algorithms learn utility functions from demonstrations while characterizing their partial identifiability.

title: Learning Utilities from Demonstrations in Markov Decision Processes

abstract: Generalizing causal effects from Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs) to target populations across diverse environments is of significant practical importance, as RCTs are often costly and logistically complex to conduct. A key challenge is environmental shift, defined as changes in the distribution and availability of covariates between source and target environments. A common approach addressing this challenge is to identify a separating set–covariates that govern both treatment effect heterogeneity and environmental differences–and combine RCT samples with target populations matched on this set. However, this approach assumes that the separating set is fully observed and shared across datasets, an assumption often violated in practice. We propose a novel Two-Stage Doubly Robust (2SDR) method that relaxes this assumption by allowing the separating set to be observed in only one of the two datasets. 2SDR leverages shadow variables to impute missing components of the separating set and generalize treatment effects across environments in a two-stage procedure. We show the identification of causal effects in target environments under 2SDR and demonstrate its effectiveness through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: A randomized trial estimates treatment effects in its study setting, but applying those results elsewhere requires addressing differences between populations. Relevant covariates may change in distribution or may not be recorded in both datasets. A common transfer strategy matches trial and target samples using a separating set: covariates governing both differences in treatment effects and differences between environments.

That strategy usually assumes the entire separating set is observed in both datasets. The proposed Two-Stage Doubly Robust method, or 2SDR, relaxes this requirement so the set can be observed in only one. It uses shadow variables to impute missing separating-set components and then generalizes treatment effects through a two-stage procedure.

The paper establishes identification of target-environment causal effects under its framework and reports supportive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets. Its practical contribution is to address mismatched covariate availability, alongside ordinary distribution shift. The relaxed requirement expands the setting considered by the method while retaining the stated condition that the separating set is available in one of the two datasets.
summary.tldr: 2SDR transfers trial effects across environments when the separating covariates are fully observed in only one dataset.

title: Generalizing Causal Effects from Randomized Controlled Trials to Target Populations across Diverse Environments

abstract: Recent contributions of semantic information theory reveal the set-element relationship between semantic and syntactic information, represented as synonymous relationships. In this paper, we propose a synonymous variational inference (SVI) method based on this synonymity viewpoint to re-analyze the perceptual image compression problem. It takes perceptual similarity as a typical synonymous criterion to build an ideal synonymous set (Synset), and approximate the posterior of its latent synonymous representation with a parametric density by minimizing a partial semantic KL divergence. This analysis theoretically proves that the optimization direction of perception image compression follows a triple tradeoff that can cover the existing rate-distortion-perception schemes. Additionally, we introduce synonymous image compression (SIC), a new image compression scheme that corresponds to the analytical process of SVI, and implement a progressive SIC codec to fully leverage the model’s capabilities. Experimental results demonstrate comparable rate-distortion-perception performance using a single progressive SIC codec, thus verifying the effectiveness of our proposed analysis method.

paragraphs: Perceptual image compression must balance storage requirements, reconstruction error, and how the reconstructed image looks. This paper reexamines that problem through synonymity: different image representations can belong to the same set when they satisfy a perceptual-similarity criterion. The authors use this perspective to define an ideal synonymous set of images.

Synonymous variational inference approximates the posterior of a latent synonymous representation with a parameterized density. It learns that approximation by minimizing a partial semantic KL divergence. The resulting analysis proves a three-way tradeoff governing the optimization direction and provides a framework capable of covering existing rate–distortion–perception schemes.

The authors translate the analysis into synonymous image compression and implement a progressive codec. Experiments show that a single progressive codec achieves comparable rate–distortion–perception performance, supporting the usefulness of the proposed analysis. The contribution is both conceptual and operational: it connects sets of perceptually similar representations to a compression objective, then demonstrates a codec organized around that connection.
summary.tldr: Synonymous variational inference reframes perceptual compression around sets of similar images and yields a progressive codec with comparable reported performance.

title: Synonymous Variational Inference for Perceptual Image Compression

abstract: We study the repeated principal-agent bandit game, where the principal indirectly explores an unknown environment by incentivizing an agent to play arms. Unlike prior work that assumes a greedy agent with full knowledge of reward means, we consider a self-interested learning agent who iteratively updates reward estimates and may explore arbitrarily with some probability. As a warm-up, we first consider a self-interested learning agent without exploration. We propose algorithms for both i.i.d. and linear reward settings with bandit feedback in a finite horizon $T$, achieving regret bounds of $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ and $\widetilde{O}(T^{\frac{2}{3}})$, respectively. Specifically, these algorithms rely on a novel elimination framework coupled with new search algorithms which accommodate the uncertainty from the agent’s learning behavior. We then extend the framework to handle an exploratory learning agent and develop an algorithm to achieve a $\widetilde{O}(T^{\frac{2}{3}})$ regret bound in i.i.d. reward setup by enhancing the robustness of our elimination framework to the potential agent exploration. Finally, when our agent model reduces to that in (Dogan et al., 2023a), we propose an algorithm based on our robust framework, which achieves a $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret bound, significantly improving upon their $\widetilde{O}(T^{\frac{11}{12}})$ bound.

paragraphs: In a principal-agent bandit game, a principal learns about an unknown environment by rewarding an agent for taking actions. The agent has its own interests. This paper considers agents that also learn their reward estimates over time and may explore, making their responses harder to anticipate than those of fully informed greedy agents.

The authors develop an elimination framework with search procedures that account for uncertainty arising from the agent's learning. For a non-exploring learning agent, they obtain regret bounds scaling as the square root of the horizon in the independent, identically distributed reward setting and as the horizon to the two-thirds power in the linear setting, up to logarithmic factors.

A more robust version accommodates exploratory agents and obtains a two-thirds-power bound in the independent-reward setting. In a special case matching an earlier agent model, it improves the bound from an eleven-twelfths power to a square-root rate. These results distinguish the guarantees available under different reward and agent behaviors, showing how incentive design can accommodate an agent whose knowledge and actions evolve.
summary.tldr: New incentive algorithms provide regret guarantees when self-interested agents learn their rewards and may explore.

title: Principal-Agent Bandit Games with Self-Interested and Exploratory Learning Agents

abstract: Panoramic image outpainting acts as a pivotal role in immersive content generation, allowing for seamless restoration and completion of panoramic content. Given the fact that the majority of generative outpainting solutions operates on planar images, existing methods for panoramic images address the sphere nature by soft regularisation during the end-to-end learning, which still fails to fully exploit the spherical content. In this paper, we set out the first attempt to impose the sphere nature in the design of diffusion model, such that the panoramic format is intrinsically ensured during the learning procedure, named as spherical-nested diffusion (SpND) model. This is achieved by employing spherical noise in the diffusion process to address the structural prior, together with a newly proposed spherical deformable convolution (SDC) module to intrinsically learn the panoramic knowledge. Upon this, the proposed method is effectively integrated into a pre-trained diffusion model, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods for panoramic image outpainting. In particular, our SpND method reduces the FID values by more than 50% against the state-of-the-art PanoDiffusion method. Codes are publicly available at https://github.com/chronos123/SpND.

paragraphs: Panoramic image outpainting completes missing visual content for immersive scenes. Its geometry differs from ordinary planar images because the content represents a sphere. Existing panoramic approaches encourage spherical behavior through soft regularization during learning, but the paper argues that this does not fully use the structure of panoramic content.

Spherical-nested diffusion, or SpND, incorporates that geometry into the diffusion model’s design. Spherical noise supplies a structural prior during the diffusion process, and a spherical deformable convolution module learns panoramic information. These components make the spherical format part of the learning mechanism, and the resulting method can be integrated into a pretrained diffusion model.

The authors report outperforming existing panoramic outpainting methods, including an FID reduction of more than 50% relative to PanoDiffusion. This provides empirical support for building the target geometry into generation rather than depending only on a training penalty to encourage it. The contribution links a representation-specific model design with improved panoramic completion in the reported evaluation.
summary.tldr: SpND builds spherical structure into diffusion-based panoramic outpainting and reports more than a 50% FID reduction over PanoDiffusion.

title: Spherical-Nested Diffusion Model for Panoramic Image Outpainting

abstract: Accurate predictions rely on the expressiveness power of graph deep learning frameworks like graph neural networks and graph transformers, where a positional encoding mechanism has become much more indispensable in recent state-of-the-art (SOTA) works to record the canonical position information. However, the current positional encoding limits in three aspects, at least: (1) most positional encodings are pre-defined, and fixed functions, which are inadequate to adapt to the complex attributed graphs; (2) a few pioneering works propose the learnable positional encoding but still limited to the structural information, leaving the real-world time-evolving topological and feature information untouched; (3) most positional encodings should be equipped with transformer’s attention mechanism to fully release the power, where the dense or relational attention is often unaffordable on large-scale structured data. Hence, we study the possibility of Learnable Spatial-Temporal Positional Encoding in an effective and efficient manner and then propose a simple temporal link prediction model named L-STEP. Briefly, for L-STEP, we (1) prove the proposed positional learning scheme can preserve the graph property from the spatial-temporal spectral viewpoint, (2) verify that MLPs can fully exploit the expressiveness and reach Transformers’ performance on that encoding, (3) change different initial positional encoding inputs to show robustness, (4) analyze the theoretical complexity and obtain less empirical running time than SOTA, and (5) demonstrate its temporal link prediction out-performance on 13 classic datasets and with 10 algorithms in both transductive and inductive settings using 3 different sampling strategies. Also, L-STEP obtains the leading performance in the newest large-scale TGB benchmark.

paragraphs: Predicting future links in a changing graph requires useful representations of both structure and time. Fixed positional encodings may adapt poorly to complex attributed graphs, while learned encodings can still overlook evolving connections and features. L-STEP introduces a learnable spatial-temporal positional encoding designed to capture this changing information efficiently.

The authors prove that their positional learning scheme preserves graph properties from a spatial-temporal spectral perspective. They also show that multilayer perceptrons can exploit the resulting encoding and reach Transformer performance on it. This matters because dense or relational attention can be expensive on large graphs: a useful encoding can make simpler prediction machinery competitive.

Evaluation examines different initial positional encodings, theoretical complexity, and empirical runtime. L-STEP reports lower running time than state-of-the-art methods and superior temporal link prediction across 13 datasets against 10 algorithms, covering transductive and inductive settings with three sampling strategies. It also achieves leading performance on the large-scale TGB benchmark. Together, these findings support learning richer positional information as a route to both accurate and efficient temporal graph prediction.
summary.tldr: L-STEP learns spatial-temporal graph encodings that let simple multilayer perceptrons deliver strong, efficient temporal link prediction.

title: Learnable Spatial-Temporal Positional Encoding for Link Prediction

abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has shown promise in aligning large language models (LLMs). Yet its reliance on a singular reward model often overlooks the diversity of human preferences. Recent approaches address this limitation by leveraging multi-dimensional feedback to fine-tune corresponding reward models and train LLMs using reinforcement learning. However, the process is costly and unstable, especially given the competing and heterogeneous nature of human preferences. In this paper, we propose Mixing Preference Optimization (MPO), a post-processing framework for aggregating single-objective policies as an alternative to both multi-objective RLHF (MORLHF) and MaxMin-RLHF. MPO avoids alignment from scratch. Instead, it log-linearly combines existing policies into a unified one with the weight of each policy computed via a batch stochastic mirror descent. Empirical results demonstrate that MPO achieves balanced performance across diverse preferences, outperforming or matching existing models with significantly reduced computational costs.

paragraphs: Human preferences are diverse and can conflict, making alignment with a single reward model incomplete. Approaches that train with multiple reward dimensions can address this diversity, but their reinforcement-learning process can be expensive and unstable. Mixing Preference Optimization tackles the problem by combining policies that have already been aligned to individual objectives.

MPO is a post-processing framework that creates a unified policy through a log-linear combination of existing policies. It computes their mixing weights using batch stochastic mirror descent. The core decision is how much influence to assign to each available policy, allowing the method to reuse prior alignment work instead of performing alignment from scratch.

The paper presents MPO as an alternative to multi-objective RLHF and MaxMin-RLHF. Empirical results show balanced performance across different preferences, with performance that matches or exceeds existing models while substantially reducing computational costs. These findings support policy combination as an efficient way to handle competing preferences, with the reported balance arising from the tested mixtures and learned weights.
summary.tldr: MPO efficiently balances diverse preferences by learning how to combine existing single-objective policies after alignment.

title: MPO: An Efficient Post-Processing Framework for Mixing Diverse Preference Alignment

abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have manifested strong visual question answering capability. However, they still struggle with aligning the rationale and the generated answer, leading to inconsistent reasoning and incorrect responses. To this end, this paper introduces Self-Rationale Calibration (SRC) framework to iteratively calibrate the alignment between rationales and answers. SRC begins by employing a lightweight “rationale fine-tuning” approach, which modifies the model’s response format to require a rationale before deriving answer without explicit prompts. Next, SRC searches a diverse set of candidate responses from the fine-tuned LVLMs for each sample, followed by a proposed pairwise scoring strategy using a tailored scoring model, R-Scorer, to evaluate both rationale quality and factual consistency of candidates. Based on a confidence-weighted preference curation process, SRC decouples the alignment calibration into a preference fine-tuning manner, leading to significant improvements of LVLMs in perception, reasoning, and generalization across multiple benchmarks. Our results emphasize the rationale-oriented alignment in exploring the potential of LVLMs.

paragraphs: A vision-language model can produce a plausible explanation that does not support its own answer. Such misalignment contributes to inconsistent reasoning and incorrect visual question answering. Self-Rationale Calibration, or SRC, trains models to improve the relationship between the rationale they give and the answer they ultimately produce.

SRC first uses lightweight rationale fine-tuning so the model naturally generates a rationale before its answer, without needing an explicit prompt to request that format. It then searches for diverse candidate responses for each sample. A tailored model called R-Scorer evaluates pairs of candidates for rationale quality and factual consistency, and a confidence-weighted process turns those judgments into preference training data.

The framework iteratively calibrates alignment through preference fine-tuning. Across multiple benchmarks, the authors report significant improvements in perception, reasoning, and generalization. The contribution goes beyond requiring explanatory text: candidate rationales and their consistency help determine which responses the model learns to prefer. The reported results support treating rationale-answer alignment as a training objective that can improve broader visual-language performance.
summary.tldr: SRC scores and curates rationale-based preferences to improve consistency between vision-language models’ explanations and answers.

title: Towards Rationale-Answer Alignment of LVLMs via Self-Rationale Calibration

abstract: In this work, we explore a cost-effective framework for multilingual image generation. We find that, unlike models tuned on high-quality images with multilingual annotations, leveraging text encoders pre-trained on widely available, noisy Internet image-text pairs significantly enhances data efficiency in text-to-image (T2I) generation across multiple languages. Based on this insight, we introduce MuLan, Multi-Language adapter, a lightweight language adapter with fewer than 20M parameters, trained alongside a frozen text encoder and image diffusion model. Compared to previous multilingual T2I models, this framework offers: (1) Cost efficiency. Using readily accessible English data and off-the-shelf multilingual text encoders minimizes the training cost; (2) High performance. Achieving comparable generation capabilities in over 110 languages with CLIP similarity scores nearly matching those in English (39.57 for English vs. 39.61 for other languages); and (3) Broad applicability. Seamlessly integrating with compatible community tools like LoRA, LCM, ControlNet, and IP-Adapter, expanding its potential use cases.

paragraphs: MuLan aims to make multilingual text-to-image generation less expensive to train. The authors find that text encoders pretrained on noisy internet image-text pairs improve multilingual data efficiency compared with the described alternative of models tuned on high-quality images with multilingual annotations. This motivates reusing existing multilingual representations for image generation.

The proposed language adapter has fewer than 20 million parameters. It is trained while the text encoder and image diffusion model remain frozen, using readily available English data and an existing multilingual encoder. This focuses adaptation on a small connecting component, reducing the amount of model training needed to support prompts in many languages.

The authors report comparable generation capabilities across more than 110 languages, with CLIP similarity scores of 39.57 for English and 39.61 for other languages. MuLan also integrates with compatible tools including LoRA, LCM, ControlNet, and IP-Adapter. The findings indicate that multilingual support can be added efficiently while retaining access to a broader image-generation tool ecosystem.
summary.tldr: MuLan uses a small adapter and frozen pretrained components to support image generation in more than 110 languages using English training data.

title: MuLan: Adapting Multilingual Diffusion Models for Hundreds of Languages with Negligible Cost

abstract: Subgraph neural networks have recently gained prominence for various subgraph-level predictive tasks. However, existing methods either 1) apply simple standard pooling over graph convolutional networks, failing to capture essential subgraph properties, or 2) rely on rigid subgraph definitions, leading to suboptimal performance. Moreover, these approaches fail to model long-range dependencies both between and within subgraphs—a critical limitation, as many real-world networks contain subgraphs of varying sizes and connectivity patterns. In this paper, we propose a novel implicit subgraph neural network, the first of its kind, designed to capture dependencies across subgraphs. Our approach also integrates label-aware subgraph-level information. We formulate implicit subgraph learning as a bilevel optimization problem and develop a provably convergent algorithm that requires fewer gradient estimations than standard bilevel optimization methods. We evaluate our approach on real-world networks against state-of-the-art baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness and superiority.

paragraphs: Predicting properties of subgraphs requires representing groups of connected nodes whose sizes and connectivity can vary. Existing approaches can lose essential properties through simple pooling or depend on rigid definitions of what a subgraph must be. The paper also identifies inadequate modeling of long-range relationships within and across subgraphs as a significant weakness.

The proposed implicit subgraph neural network is designed to capture dependencies across subgraphs while incorporating label-aware information at the subgraph level. Its learning procedure is formulated as a bilevel optimization problem, linking two levels of optimization. This makes subgraph learning part of the model's optimization framework rather than relying only on a standard pooled graph representation.

The authors develop a provably convergent algorithm that uses fewer gradient estimations than standard bilevel optimization methods. Tests on real-world networks show stronger performance than the state-of-the-art baselines evaluated. The contribution therefore combines a richer approach to subgraph dependencies with an optimization procedure intended to make that learning more efficient.
summary.tldr: An implicit subgraph network learns cross-subgraph dependencies through bilevel optimization with a provably convergent, gradient-efficient algorithm.

title: Implicit Subgraph Neural Network

abstract: In existing works on population dynamics inference, there is a focus on flows arising from vector fields that are the gradients of scalar potentials. Among all admissible flows that are compatible with the population dynamic, gradient flows are optimal in a specific sense: they minimize kinetic energy. The selection of fields based on different criteria corresponds to a gauge freedom when determining population dynamics, which we leverage in this work. We propose Non-Gradient Inference Flows (NGIF), an algorithm to infer non-gradient population dynamics using a weak formulation of the continuity equation. This allows us to parameterize with general vector fields as well as choose other selection criteria beyond minimal energy. We demonstrate on a variety of low- and high-dimensional physics problems that this more general approach improves distributional accuracy over gradient-restricted baselines and better captures non-potential transport.

paragraphs: Inferring population dynamics means finding a flow consistent with how a distribution changes over time. More than one flow can explain the same population evolution. Existing approaches often select vector fields derived from scalar potentials; among admissible flows, these gradient flows minimize kinetic energy.

The paper treats this freedom to select among compatible flows as gauge freedom. Its Non-Gradient Inference Flows algorithm uses a weak formulation of the continuity equation, which expresses consistency between a vector field and population evolution. This allows general vector fields and selection criteria beyond minimum energy, expanding which dynamics the model can represent.

On a variety of low- and high-dimensional physics problems, the method improves distributional accuracy over gradient-restricted baselines and better captures transport that cannot be described by a potential. These results show why the selection criterion matters: choosing the minimum-energy explanation can restrict the inferred motion. The framework enables other choices while retaining consistency with the population dynamics being modeled.
summary.tldr: Non-Gradient Inference Flows broadens population-dynamics inference beyond minimum-energy gradient fields, improving distributional accuracy on tested physics problems.

title: Leveraging Gauge Freedom for Learning Non-Gradient Population Dynamics of Stochastic Systems

abstract: Many stochastic physical systems evolve smoothly over time in the sense that the distribution of states changes regularly with time. The precise transition from current to next state is often modeled as the interplay of a smooth map and an explicit source of randomness. Stochastic Lifting leverages this premise by attaching an independent, high-dimensional random label to each state transition in the training data and fitting a transition map from the current state and label to the next state using a standard regression loss. The labels act as auxiliary coordinates that let the model represent multiple plausible outcomes for similar current states, avoiding collapse to a mean prediction in the finite-sample size regime. At inference, drawing fresh labels and rolling the map forward generates diverse trajectories with a single network evaluation per time step, with the smoothness bias of the learned map supporting accurate sampling in practice.

paragraphs: A stochastic physical system can have several plausible next states from similar current states. A regression model may collapse these possibilities toward an average prediction. Stochastic Lifting addresses this problem by giving the transition model explicit random inputs alongside the current physical state.

During training, each observed transition receives an independent, high-dimensional random label. A model learns to predict the next state from the current state and this label using an ordinary regression loss. The labels provide auxiliary coordinates for representing distinct outcomes, helping avoid mean-prediction collapse in the finite-sample setting.

At inference, the method samples fresh labels and repeatedly applies the learned transition map to generate diverse trajectories. Each time step requires one network evaluation. The approach builds on the premise that many stochastic systems can be described through a smooth map combined with explicit randomness. The learned map's smoothness bias supports accurate sampling in practice, connecting a simple training objective with an efficient procedure for generating entire stochastic paths.
summary.tldr: Stochastic Lifting trains a transition regressor with random auxiliary labels to generate diverse physical trajectories using one network evaluation per step.

title: Stochastic Lifting for Generating Trajectories of Stochastic Physical Systems

abstract: Generating step-by-step "how-to" procedures is a key LLM capability: how-to advice is commonly requested in chatbots, and step-by-step planning is critical for complex reasoning tasks. Yet, measuring and improving procedural validity at scale on real-world tasks remains challenging and understudied. We introduce How2Everything, a scalable framework to evaluate and improve goal-conditioned procedure generation. Our pipeline How2Mine extracts and rewrites 351K procedures from 980K web pages across 14 topics, and can scale to larger corpora. From this pool we build How2Bench, a 7K-example evaluation set balanced across topics. We also introduce How2Score, an evaluation protocol that uses an LLM judge to detect whether a generation contains any critical failure that would prevent achieving the goal. For low-cost, reproducible evaluation, we distill a frontier judge into an open 8B model achieving 80.5% agreement with human annotators. How2Bench reveals clear scaling trends across model size and training stages, providing signal early in pretraining. Finally, RL using How2Score as a reward improves performance on How2Bench by $>$10 points across three base models without systematic regressions on standard benchmarks, with gains not primarily explained by source-document memorization or superficial format compliance. We release all code and data at https://github.com/lilakk/how2everything.

title: How2Everything: Mining the Web for How-to Procedures to Evaluate and Improve LLMs

abstract: Research has repeatedly demonstrated that intermediate hidden states extracted from large language models and speech audio models predict measured brain response to natural language stimuli. Yet, very little is known about the representation properties that enable this high prediction performance. Why is it the intermediate layers, and not the output layers, that are most effective for this unique and highly general transfer task? We give evidence that the correspondence between speech and language models and the brain derives from shared meaning abstraction and not their next-word prediction properties. In particular, models construct higher-order linguistic features in their middle layers, cued by a peak in the layerwise intrinsic dimension, a measure of feature complexity. We show that a layer’s intrinsic dimension strongly predicts how well it explains fMRI and ECoG signals; that the relation between intrinsic dimension and brain predictivity arises over model pre-training; and finetuning models to better predict the brain causally increases both representations’ intrinsic dimension and their semantic content. Results suggest that semantic richness, high intrinsic dimension, and brain predictivity mirror each other, and that the key driver of model-brain similarity is rich meaning abstraction of the inputs, where language modeling is a task sufficiently complex (but perhaps not the only) to require it.

They find that it peaks in middle layers where higher-order linguistic features develop, and that it strongly predicts how well a layer explains fMRI and ECoG measurements. Together, the findings suggest that semantic richness, representational complexity, and brain predictivity track one another. Language modeling appears sufficiently demanding to induce this abstraction, but the authors leave open whether other tasks could induce it too.
summary.tldr: The study links models’ ability to predict brain responses to rich meaning representations and high intrinsic dimension in intermediate layers.

title: Abstraction Induces the Brain Alignment of Language and Speech Models

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) struggle with numerical regression under longtailed target distributions. Token-level supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and point-wise regression rewards bias learning toward high-density regions, leading to regression-to-the-mean behavior and poor tail performance. We identify the lack of cross-sample relational supervision as a key limitation of existing MLLM training paradigms. To address it, we propose a distribution-aware reinforcement learning framework based on Group Relative Policy Optimization, which introduces batch-level comparison-based supervision via the Concordance Correlation Coefficient-based reward to align predicted and ground-truth distributions in terms of correlation, scale, and mean. The framework is plug-and-play, requiring no architectural modification. Experiments on a unified suite of long-tailed regression benchmarks show consistent improvements over SFT and existing MLLM regression methods, with particularly strong gains in medium- and few-shot regimes.
