paragraphs: Numerical prediction becomes difficult when target values follow a long-tailed distribution: common values dominate training while rare values receive less attention. The paper finds that multimodal language models trained with token-level supervision or rewards for individual predictions tend toward the mean and perform poorly in the tails. It identifies missing supervision about relationships between examples as a key contributor.

The proposed framework adds that relational information through reinforcement learning based on Group Relative Policy Optimization. Its reward uses the Concordance Correlation Coefficient to compare predictions and ground truth across a batch. This signal accounts for correlation, scale, and mean, encouraging the collection of predictions to match more of the target distribution’s structure.

The method requires no change to the model architecture, making the intervention a change in training supervision. On a unified collection of long-tailed regression benchmarks, it consistently improves over supervised fine-tuning and existing multimodal regression methods. Gains are particularly strong in medium- and few-shot regimes. The findings support evaluating predictions jointly across examples when isolated prediction rewards encourage excessive concentration around common targets.
summary.tldr: A batch-level distribution-aware reward improves multimodal numerical regression under long-tailed targets without changing model architecture.

title: Injecting Distributional Awareness into MLLMs via Reinforcement Learning for Deep Imbalanced Regression

abstract: Stability and robustness are critical for deploying Transformers in safety-sensitive settings. A principled way to enforce such behavior is to constrain the model’s Lipschitz constant. However, approximation-theoretic guarantees for architectures that explicitly preserve Lipschitz continuity have yet to be established. In this work, we bridge this gap by introducing a class of gradient-descent-type in-context Transformers that are Lipschitz-continuous by construction. We realize both MLP and attention blocks as explicit Euler steps of negative gradient flows, ensuring inherent stability without sacrificing expressivity. We prove a universal approximation theorem for this class within a Lipschitz-constrained function space. Crucially, our analysis adopts a measure-theoretic formalism, interpreting Transformers as operators on probability measures, to yield approximation guarantees independent of token count. These results provide a rigorous theoretical foundation for the design of robust, Lipschitz continuous Transformer architectures.

paragraphs: Constraining a Transformer’s Lipschitz constant limits how strongly its outputs can respond to changes in its inputs. This provides a principled route toward stability and robustness. The theoretical challenge is establishing that architectures built to obey such constraints can still represent the functions they need to learn.

The paper constructs in-context Transformers whose attention and multilayer perceptron blocks take the form of explicit Euler steps along negative gradient flows. This gives both kinds of block a shared dynamical interpretation and builds Lipschitz continuity into the architecture. The construction supports an analysis of stability together with expressive capacity.

The authors prove universal approximation within a Lipschitz-constrained function space. Their formulation treats Transformers as operators on probability measures, which makes the approximation guarantees independent of the number of tokens. The result establishes expressivity within the stated constrained space while preserving the architecture’s continuity properties. It supplies a theoretical foundation for designing stable Transformers without making token count the organizing variable of the guarantee.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs Lipschitz-continuous Transformers and proves token-count-independent universal approximation within a Lipschitz-constrained function space.

title: Approximation Theory for Lipschitz Continuous Transformers

abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) is a widely used approach for reducing the memory and compute costs of large language models (LLMs). Recent studies have shown that applying invertible transformations to activations can significantly improve quantization robustness by reducing activation outliers; however, existing approaches are largely restricted to rotation or Hadamard-based transformations. Moreover, most studies focused primarily on traditional quantization schemes, whereas modern hardware increasingly supports the microscaling (MX) data format. Attempts to combine both showed severe performance degradation, leading prior work to introduce assumptions on the transformations. In this work, we take a complementary perspective. First, we provide a theoretical analysis of transformations under MX quantization by deriving a bound on the quantization error. Our analysis emphasizes the importance of accounting for both the activation distribution and the underlying quantization structure. Building on this analysis, we propose LATMiX, a method that generalizes outlier reduction to learnable invertible affine transformations optimized using standard deep learning tools. Experiments show consistent improvements in average accuracy for MX low-bit quantization over strong baselines on a wide range of zero-shot benchmarks, across multiple model sizes.

paragraphs: Post-training quantization reduces the memory and computation needed by large language models by representing values with fewer bits. Transforming activations before quantization can reduce extreme values and improve robustness. However, much existing work uses rotations or Hadamard-based transformations and concentrates on traditional formats, while newer hardware increasingly supports microscaling formats.

The paper examines why transformations that seem useful elsewhere can perform poorly with microscaling quantization. Its theoretical analysis derives a quantization-error bound that accounts for both the activation distribution and the structure of the quantization format. This makes the transformation choice a joint problem involving the values being represented and the representation they must fit.

LATMiX uses that analysis to learn invertible affine transformations with standard deep-learning tools, expanding the options beyond the transformations commonly used previously. Across multiple model sizes and a wide range of zero-shot benchmarks, it consistently improves average accuracy over strong baselines for low-bit microscaling quantization. The findings support designing outlier-reduction transformations around the target numerical format rather than treating outlier reduction alone as sufficient.
summary.tldr: LATMiX learns invertible affine transformations tailored to microscaling quantization, improving reported average accuracy for low-bit language models.

title: LATMiX: Learnable Affine Transformations for Microscaling Quantization of LLMs

abstract: In deep learning for tabular data, efficient ensembles of multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) have recently emerged as effective and practical architectures. Existing methods of this kind use the same hyperparameters for all underlying MLPs, which requires hyperparameter tuning for achieving the best performance. In this work, we introduce TabPack, an efficient MLP ensemble with strong out-of-the-box performance and reduced reliance on traditional tuning. In a single run, TabPack samples and trains many MLPs with different hyperparameters efficiently in parallel and selects ensemble members on the fly during training. Thus, TabPack only requires specifying ranges from which to sample MLP hyperparameter rather than exact hyperparameter values, which naturally demands less precision for good performance. In experiments on medium-to-large public datasets, TabPack with default settings performs on par with extensively tuned prior methods, thus substantially reducing effort and compute resources needed to achieve competitive results on tabular tasks. Notably, running the default TabPack configuration on a modern MacBook took less time than tuning some baselines on an industry-grade GPU.

Finding good shared settings can require substantial tuning. TabPack moves variation in those settings inside the ensemble training process, aiming for strong performance with less preparatory search.

In one run, TabPack samples many MLPs with different hyperparameters and trains them efficiently in parallel. It also selects ensemble members during training. Users specify ranges of possible settings rather than choosing precise values for every setting. This reduces how accurately the configuration must be chosen in advance to obtain good results.

On medium-to-large public datasets, default TabPack performs on par with prior methods that receive extensive tuning. The reported benefit is therefore competitive accuracy with less tuning effort and computation. In one comparison, running the default configuration on a modern MacBook took less time than tuning some baselines on an industry-grade GPU. That comparison illustrates the potential savings from including hyperparameter diversity within a single training run.
summary.tldr: TabPack trains and selects MLPs with varied hyperparameters in one run, matching extensively tuned tabular methods with default settings.

title: TabPack: Efficient Hyperparameter Ensembles for Tabular Deep Learning

abstract: Standard softmax attention scales quadratically with sequence length, which makes long-context training and inference expensive. We introduce PLASH, an attention block whose cost grows linearly in the number of keys. PLASH compresses the original keys and values into $M$ learned prototypes, where $M\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is much smaller than the number of keys. The compressed prototypes are then enriched with randomized polynomial features that recover inter-token information lost to compression. The output is computed by exact scaled dot-product softmax attention from each query to the enriched prototypes, so PLASH preserves the standard attention interface.The construction applies to self- and cross-attention. We prove sketch-error bounds for the enrichment step, a per-input certificate that upper-bounds the deviation from standard softmax attention on each forward pass, and a runtime bound linear in the number of queries and keys. Experiments on long-context language modeling (Qwen3-4B on PG-19) and time-series forecasting (ETT, ECL, Weather) show competitive accuracy and favorable scaling against efficient-attention baselines.

paragraphs: Standard softmax attention becomes expensive on long sequences because its computation grows quadratically with sequence length. PLASH reduces this cost by compressing keys and values into a much smaller set of learned prototypes. Each query then attends to these prototypes, reducing the amount of information it must directly compare.

Compression can lose relationships between tokens, so PLASH enriches the prototypes with randomized polynomial features designed to recover such information. It computes exact scaled dot-product softmax attention over the enriched prototypes and preserves the usual attention interface. Exactness here refers to attention over those prototypes; the overall output can still differ from attention over the original keys and values.

The authors prove bounds on sketching error, linear runtime in the numbers of queries and keys, and a certificate bounding each forward pass’s deviation from standard attention. The construction supports both self-attention and cross-attention. Language-modeling and time-series experiments show competitive accuracy and favorable scaling against efficient-attention baselines, pairing empirical evaluation with explicit approximation bounds.
summary.tldr: PLASH combines learned prototypes and randomized feature enrichment to provide linear-time attention with explicit approximation-error bounds.

title: PLASH: Provably Linear-Time Attention with Selective Higher-Order Feature Sketching

abstract: Internet of Things (IoT) systems continuously collect heterogeneous sensing signals from ubiquitous sensors to support intelligent applications such as human activity analysis, emotion monitoring, and environmental perception. These signals are inherently non-stationary and multi-scale, posing unique challenges for standard tokenization techniques. This paper proposes Dywave, a dynamic tokenization framework for IoT sensing signals that constructs compact input representations aligned with intrinsic temporal structures and underlying physical events. Dywave leverages wavelet-based hierarchical decomposition, identifies meaningful temporal boundaries corresponding to underlying semantic events, and adaptively compresses redundant intervals while preserving temporal coherence. Extensive evaluations on five real-world IoT sensing datasets across activity recognition, stress assessment, and nearby object detection demonstrate that Dywave outperforms state-of-the-art methods by up to 12% in accuracy, while improving computational efficiency by reducing input token lengths by up to 75% across mainstream sequence models. Moreover, Dywave exhibits improved robustness to domain shifts and varying sequence lengths.

paragraphs: Sensor streams vary over time and contain patterns at different scales, making fixed tokenization inefficient or poorly aligned with meaningful events. Dywave builds adaptive representations for heterogeneous Internet-of-Things signals. Its goal is to preserve temporal structure while compressing intervals that contribute little new information.

The framework uses hierarchical wavelet decomposition to identify meaningful temporal boundaries. It then compresses redundant segments adaptively while maintaining coherence across the sequence. This makes token lengths respond to the signal’s own structure instead of imposing the same granularity on every interval.

Across five real-world datasets covering activity recognition, stress assessment, and nearby-object detection, Dywave improves accuracy by up to 12% and reduces input-token lengths by up to 75%. It also shows better robustness to domain shifts and changing sequence lengths. These are maximum reported gains across evaluated settings, rather than a guaranteed simultaneous improvement for every sensor or downstream model.
summary.tldr: Dywave aligns sensor tokens with temporal events, improving reported accuracy while substantially shortening input sequences.

title: Dywave: Event-Aligned Dynamic Tokenization for Heterogeneous IoT Sensing Signals

abstract: Vision-Language-Action models have recently shown promising progress in embodied robotic manipulation, yet their generalization to diverse open-ended embodied tasks is often hindered by execution failures. While prior work has explored failure handling, existing approaches still suffer from two fundamental limitations: coarse-grained failure correction and unreliable failure prevention. These limitations lead to brittle decision-making when VLA models are deployed in novel tasks and environments. To address them, we propose NeurVLA, a neural-symbolic framework that jointly addresses failure correction and prevention via neural-symbolic reasoning and further internalizes these failure-handling capabilities into VLA models. Experiments demonstrate that NeurVLA achieves strong performance and robust generalization across diverse tasks.

paragraphs: NeurVLA addresses execution failures in vision-language-action models used for robotic manipulation. These models have shown promise, but mistakes during action execution can hinder their transfer to varied, open-ended tasks. The paper identifies two weaknesses in existing failure handling: corrections that are too coarse and prevention that is insufficiently reliable.

The proposed framework uses neural-symbolic reasoning to address correction and prevention jointly. These are related but distinct responsibilities: correction responds to an execution failure, while prevention concerns avoiding failures before they occur. NeurVLA also internalizes these failure-handling capabilities into the vision-language-action model, making their incorporation into the action model part of the approach itself.

Experiments report strong performance and robust generalization across diverse tasks. The stated findings support the framework's combined treatment of failure response and prevention in the evaluated settings. Its broader significance is the focus on handling execution problems as part of embodied competence: successful transfer involves dealing with what goes wrong during action, alongside producing actions for the original task.
summary.tldr: NeurVLA combines neural-symbolic failure correction and prevention and incorporates those capabilities into robotic vision-language-action models.

title: NeurVLA: Unleashing Failure-Handling Capability of Vision-Language-Action Models via Neural-Symbolic Reasoning

abstract: Existing preference datasets for text-to-image models typically store only the final winner/loser images. This representation is insufficient for rectified flow (RF) models, whose generation is naturally indexed by a specific prior noise sample and follows a nearly straight denoising trajectory. In contrast, prior DPO-style alignment for diffusion models commonly estimates trajectories using an independent forward noising process, which can be mismatched to the true reverse dynamics and introduces unnecessary variance. We propose Prior Noise-Aware Preference Optimization (PNAPO), an off-policy alignment framework specialized for rectified flow. PNAPO augments preference data by retaining the paired prior noises used to generate each winner/loser image, turning the standard (prompt, winner, loser) triplet into a sextuple. Leveraging the straight-line property of RF, we estimate intermediate states via noise-image interpolation, which constrains the trajectory estimation space and yields a tighter surrogate objective for preference optimization. In addition, we introduce a dynamic regularization strategy that adapts the DPO regularization based on (i) the reward gap between winner and loser and (ii) training progress, improving stability and sample efficiency. Experiments on state-of-the-art RF T2I backbones show that PNAPO consistently improves preference metrics while substantially reducing training compute.

paragraphs: Preference datasets for image generation usually retain a prompt and the preferred and rejected images. For rectified-flow models, this leaves out information about the particular initial noise that generated each image. Estimating training trajectories through independent forward noising can then mismatch the generation dynamics and introduce avoidable variance.

PNAPO retains the paired prior noises alongside the preference examples. Because rectified-flow trajectories are nearly straight, it estimates intermediate states by interpolating between the recorded noise and its resulting image. This restricts the space of possible trajectory estimates and yields a tighter surrogate objective for learning from preferences. The approach is specialized to the structure of rectified flow.

The method also changes its regularization dynamically according to the reward difference between preferred and rejected outputs and the progress of training. This is intended to improve stability and sample efficiency. Experiments on state-of-the-art rectified-flow text-to-image backbones report consistent preference-metric improvements with substantially less training computation, supporting the value of retaining generation history in offline preference data.
summary.tldr: PNAPO records the initial noises behind image preference pairs to improve rectified-flow alignment while reducing training computation.

title: Offline Preference Optimization for Rectified Flow with Noise-Tracked Pairs

abstract: Direct preference optimization (DPO) has emerged as a promising approach for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences. However, the widespread reliance on the response-level Bradley-Terry (BT) model may limit its full potential, as the reference and learnable models are assumed to be autoregressive only after deriving the objective function. Motivated by this limitation, we revisit the theoretical foundations of DPO and propose a novel formulation that explicitly introduces the autoregressive assumption prior to applying the BT model. By reformulating and extending DPO, we derive a novel variant, termed Autoregressive DPO (ADPO), that explicitly integrates autoregressive modeling into the preference optimization framework. Without violating the theoretical foundations, the derived loss takes an elegant form: it shifts the summation operation in the DPO objective outside the log-sigmoid function. Furthermore, through theoretical analysis of ADPO, we show that there exist two length measures to be considered when designing DPO-based algorithms: the token length $\mu$ and the feedback length $\mu’$. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to explicitly distinguish these two measures and analyze their implications for preference optimization in LLMs.

However, the widespread reliance on the response-level Bradley-Terry (BT) model may limit its full potential, as the reference and learnable models are assumed to be autoregressive only after deriving the objective function. Motivated by this limitation, we revisit the theoretical foundations of DPO and propose a novel formulation that explicitly introduces the autoregressive assumption prior to applying the BT model. By reformulating and extending DPO, we derive a novel variant, termed Autoregressive DPO (ADPO), that explicitly integrates autoregressive modeling into the preference optimization framework. Without violating the theoretical foundations, the derived loss takes an elegant form: it shifts the summation operation in the DPO objective outside the log-sigmoid function. Furthermore, through theoretical analysis of ADPO, we show that there exist two length measures to be considered when designing DPO-based algorithms: the token length $\mu$ and the feedback length $\mu’$. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to explicitly distinguish these two measures and analyze their implications for preference optimization in LLMs.

paragraphs: Direct preference optimization trains language models using preferences between responses. This paper revisits the order of assumptions in its mathematical derivation. In the commonly used formulation, a response-level Bradley–Terry preference model comes first, and the reference and trainable language models are treated as autoregressive afterward. The authors argue that this ordering may restrict the framework.

Their alternative introduces autoregressive generation before applying the preference model. The resulting method, Autoregressive DPO, incorporates the sequential nature of text generation directly into the derivation. Its loss has a compact difference from standard DPO: the summation moves outside the log-sigmoid function. The authors derive this change while maintaining the theoretical foundations of the formulation.

The analysis also distinguishes token length from feedback length, identifying two separate length measures relevant to preference optimization. The paper's contribution is a theoretical reformulation and an account of these measures' implications. It gives designers another way to reason about how preference feedback interacts with autoregressive modeling when constructing DPO-based algorithms.
summary.tldr: ADPO derives preference optimization with autoregressive modeling built in from the start and distinguishes token length from feedback length.

title: Autoregressive Direct Preference Optimization

abstract: We introduce Debate2Create (D2C), a multi-agent LLM framework that formulates robot co-design as structured, iterative debate grounded in physics-based evaluation. A design agent and control agent engage in a thesis-antithesis-synthesis loop, while criterion-specific LLM judges provide multi-objective feedback to steer exploration. Across five MuJoCo locomotion benchmarks, D2C achieves the highest default-normalized score among the evaluated LLM-based and black-box baselines, with gains up to 3.2x on Ant and nearly 9x on Swimmer. Iterative debate yields 18-35% gains over compute-matched zero-shot generation, and D2C-generated rewards transfer to default morphologies in 4/5 tasks. These results suggest that structured, simulator-grounded multi-agent interaction is a useful mechanism for joint morphology-reward optimization under a fixed-topology, per-candidate-RL protocol. Project page: debate2create.github.io.

paragraphs: Robot co-design connects choices about a robot’s physical form with choices about how it learns to move. Debate2Create makes that joint search an iterative conversation between language-model agents, grounded in physics-based evaluation. A design agent and a control agent propose, challenge, and reconcile ideas, while judges focused on different criteria provide feedback across multiple objectives.

The debate structure creates repeated opportunities to revise morphology and reward design together. Simulation supplies the physical evaluation that anchors these exchanges. The study uses a fixed-topology protocol with reinforcement learning performed for each candidate, so its findings concern coordinated changes within that particular design and evaluation setup.

Across five MuJoCo locomotion benchmarks, Debate2Create achieves the highest default-normalized score among evaluated language-model and black-box baselines. Reported gains reach 3.2 times on Ant and nearly nine times on Swimmer. Debate improves results by 18–35% over compute-matched zero-shot generation, and generated rewards transfer to default morphologies in four of five tasks. These results suggest that structured interaction contributes useful refinement under the tested protocol.
summary.tldr: Debate2Create uses simulator-grounded debate between design and control agents to improve joint robot morphology and reward design.

title: Debate2Create: Robot Co-design via Multi-Agent LLM Debate

abstract: Behavior cloning (BC) is a practical offline imitation learning method, but it often fails when expert demonstrations are limited. Recent works have introduced a class of architectures named predictive inverse dynamics models (PIDMs) that combine a future-state predictor with an inverse dynamics model. While PIDMs often outperform BC, the reasons behind their benefits remain unclear. In this paper, we provide a theoretical explanation: PIDMs introduce a tradeoff. Conditioning the IDM on the predicted future state can significantly reduce variance, but the prediction itself introduces additional bias and variance. We establish conditions for PIDMs to achieve higher sample efficiency and lower prediction error than BC, with the gap widening when additional data sources are available. We validate the theoretical insights empirically in 2D navigation tasks, where BC requires up to five times (three times on average) more demonstrations than PIDM to reach comparable performance. Results are also illustrated in a complex 3D environment in a modern video game with high-dimensional visual inputs and stochastic transitions, where BC requires over 66% more samples than PIDM.

paragraphs: Behavior cloning learns to imitate expert actions from demonstrations, but limited data can make it unreliable. Predictive inverse dynamics models take a two-part approach: predict a future state, then use an inverse dynamics model to infer the action. This paper explains why that extra structure can improve imitation learning and when it is beneficial.

The theoretical account centers on a tradeoff. Conditioning action inference on a predicted future state can substantially reduce variance, but predicting that state introduces its own bias and variance. The authors establish conditions under which the overall balance yields greater sample efficiency and lower prediction error than behavior cloning. They also show that the advantage can grow when additional data sources are available.

Experiments in 2D navigation support the analysis: behavior cloning needs up to five times as many demonstrations, and three times as many on average, for comparable performance. In a complex 3D video-game environment with visual inputs and stochastic transitions, it requires over 66% more samples. These results illustrate the conditional benefits identified by the theory.
summary.tldr: Predictive inverse dynamics can outperform behavior cloning when reduced action-prediction variance outweighs the errors introduced by forecasting future states.

title: When Does Predictive Inverse Dynamics Outperform Behavior Cloning?

abstract: Multi-agent debate (MAD) systems improve LLM reasoning through iterative deliberation, but remain vulnerable to debate collapse, a failure type where final agent decisions are compromised on erroneous reasoning. Existing methods lack principled mechanisms to detect or prevent such failures. To address this gap, we first propose a hierarchical metric that quantifies behavioral uncertainty at three levels: intra-agent (individual reasoning uncertainty), inter-agent (interactive uncertainty), and system-level (output uncertainty). Empirical analysis across several benchmarks reveals that our proposed uncertainty quantification reliably indicates system failures, which demonstrates the validity of using them as diagnostic metrics to indicate the system failure. Subsequently, we propose a mitigation strategy by formulating an uncertainty-driven policy optimization to penalize self-contradiction, peer conflict, and low-confidence outputs in a dynamic debating environment. Experiments demonstrate that our proposed uncertainty-driven mitigation reliably calibrates the multi-agent system by consistently improving decision accuracy while reducing system disagreement.

paragraphs: Having several language-model agents debate an answer can improve reasoning, but the discussion can still end in decisions compromised by faulty reasoning. This paper calls that failure debate collapse and develops a way to diagnose it through behavioral uncertainty at several levels of the system.

The proposed hierarchical metric measures uncertainty within an individual agent’s reasoning, uncertainty arising between interacting agents, and uncertainty in the system’s final output. Empirical analysis across several benchmarks finds these measurements to be reliable indicators of system failures. They therefore provide a diagnostic signal connecting individual behavior, interactions, and collective outcomes.

The authors then use uncertainty to guide policy optimization in the evolving debate. Training penalizes self-contradiction, conflict among peers, and low-confidence outputs. Experiments report consistent improvements in decision accuracy alongside reduced system disagreement. The contribution joins failure detection with a mitigation strategy: the same kinds of behavioral signals that reveal unreliable debates also help shape more reliable collective decision-making.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical uncertainty measurements diagnose failures in multi-agent debates and guide training that improves accuracy while reducing disagreement.

title: The Value of Variance: Mitigating Debate Collapse in Multi-Agent Systems via Uncertainty-Driven Policy Optimization

abstract: Time series forecasting (TSF) plays a critical role in decision-making for many real-world applications. Recently, large language model (LLM)- based forecasters have made promising advancements. Despite their effectiveness, existing methods often lack explicit experience accumulation and continual evolution. In this work, we propose MemCast, a learning-to-memory framework that reformulates TSF as an experience-conditioned reasoning task. Specifically, we learn experience from the training set and organize it into a hierarchical memory. This is achieved by summarizing prediction results into historical patterns, distilling inference trajectories into reasoning wisdom, and inducing extracted temporal features into general laws. Furthermore, during inference, we leverage historical patterns to guide the reasoning process and utilize reasoning wisdom to select better trajectories, while general laws serve as criteria for reflective iteration. Additionally, to enable continual evolution, we design a dynamic confidence adaptation strategy that updates the confidence of individual entries without leaking the test set distribution. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate that MemCast consistently outperforms previous methods, validating the effectiveness of our approach. Our code is available at https://github.com/Xiaoyu-Tao/MemCast-TS.

paragraphs: MemCast treats time-series forecasting as reasoning informed by accumulated experience. The paper targets a gap in existing language-model forecasters: they can make effective predictions without explicitly organizing past experience or supporting continued evolution. Its learning-to-memory framework extracts reusable knowledge from the training set and stores it hierarchically.

The memory has three complementary forms. Prediction results become historical patterns, inference trajectories become guidance about reasoning, and temporal features become general laws. At inference time, patterns guide the reasoning process, reasoning guidance helps select trajectories, and general laws provide criteria for reflective revision. Across multiple datasets, the authors report consistent improvements over previous methods. The results support explicitly organized experience as a useful resource for forecasting, with adaptation occurring through confidence in remembered knowledge as well as its use during reasoning.
summary.tldr: MemCast improves time-series forecasting by organizing training experience into memories that guide, select, and revise reasoning.

title: MemCast: Memory-Driven Time Series Forecasting with Experience-Conditioned Reasoning

abstract: Real-world multimodal systems must be robust against low-quality data, such as sensor noise, incomplete multimodal data and conflicting inputs. However, existing trustworthy fusion methods rely on the model’s own prediction confidence to judge data quality. This creates a circular dependency: when a model is confident but wrong (overconfident), these methods fail to detect the error. To break this loop, we propose Geometry-based Multimodal Fusion (GMF). Instead of relying on predictions, we evaluate reliability by measuring the physical effort required to map input data back to the valid data manifold. We implement this using Diffusion Schrödinger Bridges with Rectified Flow, which allows us to calculate Transport Energy as a direct metric for quality. The logic is simple: valid data sits on the manifold (low energy), while noisy, incomplete data or conflicting data requires high energy to be restored. This geometric metric acts as an independent judge, effectively flagging unreliable inputs even when the classifier is fooled. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GMF significantly improves robustness against severe sensor noise and semantic conflicts compared to confidence-based baselines.

paragraphs: Multimodal systems must decide which inputs deserve trust when sensors are noisy, information is missing, or modalities conflict. Judging quality from a classifier’s confidence creates a circular dependency: a confidently wrong prediction can make an unreliable input appear trustworthy. Geometry-based Multimodal Fusion introduces a quality signal based on the input’s relationship to valid data.

GMF measures the effort needed to transport an input back toward the valid-data manifold. It implements this idea through Diffusion Schrödinger Bridges with Rectified Flow, calculating a quantity called Transport Energy. The method’s guiding premise is that valid inputs require little restoration, while corrupted, incomplete, or conflicting inputs require more.

This geometric score provides a reliability assessment separate from prediction confidence and can flag problematic inputs even when the classifier is fooled. Extensive experiments report significantly stronger robustness to severe sensor noise and semantic conflict than confidence-based baselines. The findings support restoration effort as a useful signal for deciding how much to trust multimodal evidence.
summary.tldr: GMF judges multimodal input reliability through geometric restoration effort, improving robustness when classifier confidence is misleading.

title: Geometry-based Schrödinger Bridges for Trustworthy Multimodal Fusion

abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has become a promising paradigm for scaling reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, the sparsity of binary verifier rewards often leads to low efficiency and optimization instability. To stabilize training, existing methods typically impose token-level constraints relative to a reference policy. We identify that such constraints penalize deviations indiscriminately; this can flip verifier-determined direction when the policy attempts to outperform the reference, thereby suppressing gains. To resolve this, we propose One-Way Policy Optimization (OWPO), a method based on the principle of decoupling optimization direction from update magnitude. In OWPO, the verifier dictates the update direction, while the reference policy serves only to adjust the magnitude. Specifically, OWPO applies asymmetric reweighting: it performs Accelerated Alignment for Inferior deviations (where the policy lags behind the reference) and Gain Locking for Superior deviations (where the policy surpasses the reference). Furthermore, by incorporating iterative reference updates, OWPO creates a “Ratchet Effect” that continuously consolidates gains. Experimental results demonstrate that OWPO outperforms strong baselines, including DAPO, OPD, and MOPD, breaking the bottleneck of fixed priors to enable continuous self-evolution without reliance on external reference models.

paragraphs: One-Way Policy Optimization addresses a tension in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. Reference-policy constraints can stabilize training, but the paper argues that they may penalize departures even when the verifier favors them. Such penalties can reverse the intended update direction when the current policy is trying to improve beyond its reference.

OWPO assigns the verifier and reference different responsibilities. The verifier determines the direction of learning, while the reference changes only the update’s magnitude. Its asymmetric weighting accelerates alignment for deviations where the policy falls behind the reference and locks in gains for deviations where it surpasses the reference. This design aims to retain stabilizing information without letting the reference overturn the reward’s direction.

The method also updates the reference iteratively, creating what the authors describe as a ratchet effect that consolidates progress. Experiments report improvements over DAPO, OPD, and MOPD, supporting continued self-improvement without external reference models. The key contribution is a training rule that treats reference guidance as a control on update size while leaving the verifier in charge of what to reinforce.
summary.tldr: OWPO lets verifier rewards determine learning direction while a changing reference policy controls update size and helps consolidate gains.

title: One-Way Policy Optimization for Self-Evolving LLMs

abstract: Social learning highlights that learning agents improve not in isolation, but through interaction and structured knowledge exchange with others. When introduced into machine learning, this principle gives rise to social machine learning (SML), where multiple agents collaboratively learn by sharing abstracted knowledge. Federated learning (FL) provides a natural collaboration substrate for this paradigm, yet existing heterogeneous FL approaches often rely on sharing model parameters or intermediate representations, which may expose sensitive information and incur additional overhead. In this work, we propose SoHip (Social Hippocampus Memory Learning), a memory-centric social machine learning framework that enables collaboration among heterogeneous agents via memory sharing rather than model sharing. SoHip abstracts each agent’s individual short-term memory from local representations, consolidates it into individual long-term memory through a hippocampus-inspired mechanism, and fuses it with collectively aggregated long-term memory to enhance local prediction. Throughout the process, raw data and local models remain on-device, while only lightweight memory are exchanged. We provide theoretical analysis on convergence and privacy preservation properties. Experiments on two benchmark datasets with seven baselines demonstrate that SoHip consistently outperforms existing methods, achieving up to 8.78% accuracy improvements. The code of SoHip is available at https://github.com/LipingYi/SoHip.

abstract: Mechanistic interpretability reveals that safety-critical behaviors (e.g., alignment, jailbreak, backdoor) in Large Language Models (LLMs) are grounded in specialized functional components. However, existing safety attribution methods struggle with generalization and reliability due to their reliance on heuristic, domain-specific metrics and search algorithms. To address this, we propose SafeSeek, a unified safety interpretability framework that identifies functionally complete safety circuits in LLMs via optimization. Unlike methods focusing on isolated heads or neurons, SafeSeek introduces differentiable binary masks to extract multi-granular circuits through gradient descent on safety datasets, while integrates Safety Circuit Tuning to utilize these sparse circuits for efficient safety fine-tuning. We validate SafeSeek in two key scenarios in LLM safety: (1) backdoor attacks, identifying a backdoor circuit with 0.42% sparsity, whose ablation eradicates the Attack Success Rate (ASR) from 100% $\to$ 0.4% while retaining over 99% general utility; (2) safety alignment, localizing an alignment circuit with 3.03% heads and 0.79% neurons, whose removal spikes ASR from 0.8% $\to$ 96.9%, whereas excluding this circuit during helpfulness fine-tuning maintains 96.5% safety retention.

paragraphs: Safety-related behaviors in language models can depend on specialized internal components. SafeSeek seeks to identify functionally complete circuits for these behaviors through a unified optimization framework. This addresses the generalization and reliability difficulties associated with attribution methods that rely on domain-specific heuristics or focus on isolated heads and neurons.

The method uses differentiable binary masks and gradient descent on safety datasets to extract circuits at multiple levels of granularity. It also introduces Safety Circuit Tuning to use these sparse circuits for efficient safety fine-tuning. summary.tldr: SafeSeek optimizes sparse masks to locate safety-relevant circuits and uses them to remove backdoors or preserve alignment during fine-tuning.

title: SafeSeek: Universal Attribution of Safety Circuits in Language Models

abstract: Algorithm extraction aims to synthesize executable programs directly from models trained on algorithmic tasks, enabling de novo recovery of executable mechanisms from weights without relying on human-written target programs. However, applying this paradigm to Transformer is complicated by representation entanglement (e.g., superposition), where features encoded in overlapping directions substantially hinder the recovery of symbolic expressions. We propose the Discrete Transformer, an architecture explicitly designed to bridge the gap between continuous representations and discrete symbolic logic. By injecting discreteness through temperature-annealed sampling, our framework effectively leverages hypothesis testing and symbolic regression to extract human-readable programs. Empirically, the Discrete Transformer achieves performance comparable to the RNN-based MIPS baseline on shared discrete tasks, while broadening extraction to tasks with continuous-valued intermediate computations. Finally, we show that architectural inductive biases provide fine-grained control over synthesized programs, establishing the Discrete Transformer as a controllable testbed for algorithm extraction and Transformer interpretability.

title: Weights to Code: Extracting Interpretable Algorithms from the Discrete Transformer

abstract: Self-supervised Continual Graph Learning (CGL) aims to successively learn from a graph sequence with different tasks without label supervision—a paradigm that has attracted widespread attention. Most existing self-supervised CGL methods rely on instance-level consistency objectives that enforce stability of individual node (or node-pair) embeddings. Due to optimizing nodes in isolation, these methods fail to maintain global relational structure, causing inter-node correspondences to progressively distort under continual learning. To this end, we propose a novel Structure-Aware Optimal Transport (SAOT) framework that explicitly captures and preserves relational structure within graph representations across sequential tasks. Specifically, SAOT leverages optimal transport theory to capture global inter-node correspondences, thereby facilitating and enhancing graph representation learning. Simultaneously, SAOT incorporates a cross-task knowledge distillation mechanism to preserve the previous structural knowledge. Extensive experiments on four CGL benchmark datasets demonstrate that SAOT outperforms existing self-supervised baselines. In particular, SAOT achieves significant performance gains, improving average accuracy by up to 5% on CoraFull-CL and over 15% on Products-CL compared with state-of-the-art methods in the Class-IL setting.

paragraphs: Self-supervised continual graph learning learns successive tasks from a sequence of graphs without label supervision. Maintaining individual node representations can help retain earlier knowledge, but the paper argues that this alone does not preserve the graph’s wider relational organization. Relationships among nodes can progressively distort even when learning objectives emphasize local consistency.

SAOT uses optimal transport to capture global correspondences among nodes across sequential tasks. This makes preservation of relational structure an explicit part of representation learning. A cross-task knowledge distillation mechanism also carries forward structural knowledge from earlier tasks. The two components connect learning the current graph with retaining the organization learned previously.

Experiments on four continual graph learning benchmarks report improvements over existing self-supervised methods. In the class-incremental setting, the abstract reports average-accuracy gains of up to 5% on CoraFull-CL and over 15% on Products-CL relative to state-of-the-art methods. These results support the value of preserving relationships across a graph, alongside individual representations, when learning continues through a changing sequence of tasks.
summary.tldr: SAOT improves self-supervised continual graph learning by preserving global node relationships through optimal transport and cross-task distillation.

title: SAOT: Self-Supervised Continual Graph Learning with Structure-Aware Optimal Transport

abstract: Offline meta-reinforcement learning (meta-RL) aims to train agents that can generalize to unseen tasks using pre-collected data from related tasks. Recent approaches leverage the scalability of transformer architectures to model behavior sequences and support task adaptation using target task demonstrations. However, such data is often unavailable in real-world settings, where the task objective may be known but cannot be easily demonstrated. In contrast, humans routinely interpret and perform new tasks based solely on natural language instructions. In this work, we explore the potential of using natural language task descriptions to enable zero-shot task adaptation in offline meta-RL without requiring any data from the target task. We propose the Text-Guided Decision Transformer (TG-DT), a framework that enables zero-shot generalization by grounding policy learning in natural language. TG-DT learns a shared embedding space between task descriptions and behavioral trajectories via a dual contrastive and matching-based objective, ensuring robust alignment. A transformer-based policy is then conditioned on these aligned representations to generate task-appropriate actions. At test time, TG-DT synthesizes policies for unseen tasks using only their text descriptions and can optionally leverage a description-guided data sharing strategy to enhance adaptation. Experiments on standard offline meta-RL benchmarks, including MuJoCo and Meta-World, demonstrate that TG-DT achieves strong generalization to unseen tasks.

The Text-Guided Decision Transformer, or TG-DT, explores adaptation using only a natural-language description of the new task.

Experiments on MuJoCo and Meta-World benchmarks report strong generalization to unseen tasks. summary.tldr: TG-DT aligns task descriptions with behavioral trajectories so an offline-trained agent can tackle unseen tasks from text alone.

title: Decision Transformers As Zero-Shot Learners via Text-Behavior Alignment

abstract: Federated stochastic multi-level compositional minimax optimization supports a growing number of machine learning applications. However, the interplay of multi-level compositional structure and minimax formulation in federated learning setting poses significant optimization challenges, resulting in slow convergence rates for existing algorithms. In this paper, we propose a novel federated learning algorithm, LS$^2$MC-GDA, that leverages smoothing techniques and variance-reduced stochastic compositional gradients. To support our theoretical analysis, we introduce a stage-wise extension of LS$^2$MC-GDA, which serves to bridge the gap between different stationarity measures. We establish that our algorithm achieves a sample complexity of $O(\kappa^{3/2}/N\epsilon^3)$ and a communication complexity of $O(\kappa/\epsilon^2)$, substantially improving existing theoretical results in terms of the condition number $\kappa$ and the solution accuracy $\epsilon$ and achieving a linear speedup with respect to the number of workers $N$. Finally, experimental results validate the effectiveness of our algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper studies federated optimization problems that combine nested functions with competing minimization and maximization objectives. Their difficulty comes from the interaction of these structures while training is spread across workers. Existing algorithms converge slowly in this setting, motivating a method that improves both the amount of sampled information and the communication needed.

LS²MC-GDA combines smoothing with stochastic compositional gradients whose variance is reduced. For the theoretical analysis, the authors also introduce a stage-wise extension that bridges different ways of measuring stationarity. This extension connects the algorithm’s progress to the solution criteria used in the complexity results.

The stated sample complexity is O(κ^(3/2)/(Nε³)), and communication complexity is O(κ/ε²), where κ is the condition number, ε is the requested accuracy, and N is the worker count. These bounds improve prior theoretical dependence on conditioning and accuracy. The sample bound also gives linear speedup with worker count. Experiments support the algorithm’s effectiveness alongside these theoretical improvements.
summary.tldr: LS²MC-GDA combines smoothing and variance reduction to improve theoretical sample and communication complexity for federated compositional minimax optimization.

title: LS$^2$MC-GDA: A Smoothed Algorithm for Federated Stochastic Multi-Level Compositional Minimax Optimization

abstract: Brain network classification is pivotal for diagnosing neurological disorders, yet identifying interpretable functional biomarkers fundamentally relies on precise parcellation. Unfortunately, conventional deep graph encoders applied to brain networks suffer from a critical theoretical limitation termed Spectral Unreachability. Through graph spectral analysis, this paper demonstrates that standard coupled encoder-pooling architectures inevitably oversmooth node representations, corrupting the high-frequency topological signals strictly required to delineate sharp module boundaries. To provide a structural remedy, the Hierarchical Spectral Parcellation Network (HiSP-Net) is proposed, which structurally decouples partition learning from feature smoothing via a project-then-align paradigm. Specifically, HiSP-Net maps representations directly into a partition space using a topology-agnostic projection block to preserve all-frequency details, while a Topology-Aware Alignment regularizer subsequently enforces spatial coherence. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that HiSP-Net consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in classification, while successfully extracting stable and structurally coherent functional biomarkers. Source code is available at https://github.com/Kevin-916/HiSP-Net-demo/.

paragraphs: Brain-network classification also seeks interpretable functional regions, whose boundaries depend on precise partitioning. The paper identifies a theoretical problem in standard architectures that couple graph encoding with pooling: smoothing node representations corrupts the high-frequency topological information needed to distinguish sharp boundaries. It names this limitation Spectral Unreachability.

HiSP-Net addresses the problem by separating partition learning from feature smoothing. Its project-then-align design first uses a topology-agnostic projection to map representations directly into partition space, preserving information across frequencies. A topology-aware alignment regularizer subsequently encourages spatial coherence. This ordering separates the preservation of boundary detail from the enforcement of a structurally coherent partition.

The reported evaluations show consistent classification improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, alongside stable and structurally coherent functional biomarkers. The contribution therefore links an architectural limitation to a structural remedy, rather than treating partition quality only as an empirical tuning problem. Its findings support learning partitions in a space that retains fine topological detail before imposing coherence.
summary.tldr: HiSP-Net separates brain-network partition learning from smoothing to preserve boundary information and improve classification and biomarker extraction.

title: On the Spectral Unreachability of Brain Graph Learning

abstract: The machine learning community has focused on computational efficiency, often leveraging lower-precision formats such as FP16, rather than the standard FP32. In contrast, little attention has been paid to higher-precision formats, such as FP64, despite their critical role in scientific domains like materials science, where even small numerical differences can lead to significant inaccuracies in physicochemical properties. This need for high precision extends to the emerging field of machine learning for scientific tasks, yet it has not been thoroughly investigated. According to several studies and our experiments, models trained with FP32 and FP64 can yield different scientific conclusions, yet this discrepancy is currently underreported, indicating that numerical precision is also a critical factor in scientific machine learning, as in traditional scientific computing. This precision issue limits the potential of scientific machine learning to serve as a reliable alternative or complement to traditional scientific computing in practical research. Our position paper not only highlights these precision-related issues but also recommends reporting comparisons between FP32 and FP64 results, encouraging the release of FP64 models. We believe that these efforts can enable machine learning to contribute meaningfully to the natural sciences, ensuring both scientific reliability and practical applicability.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that numerical precision deserves more attention in machine learning used for science. Much of the field emphasizes cheaper computation through lower-precision formats. Scientific applications can have different demands: in areas such as materials science, small numerical differences can produce substantial inaccuracies in the physical or chemical properties being studied.

Drawing on prior studies and their own experiments, the authors report that models trained using FP32 and FP64 can lead to different scientific conclusions. The concern therefore reaches beyond minor changes in prediction values. They argue that these discrepancies are underreported, leaving precision insufficiently examined as a factor in scientific reliability.

The paper recommends reporting comparisons between FP32 and FP64 results and making FP64 models available. These steps would help researchers assess whether numerical representation changes the conclusions drawn from a model. The authors present improved precision reporting and model availability as ways to strengthen machine learning's practical role as an alternative or complement to traditional scientific computing.
summary.tldr: FP32 and FP64 training can yield different scientific conclusions, motivating explicit precision comparisons and the release of FP64 models.

abstract: Topic models such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) and Correlated Topic Model (CTM) have recently emerged as powerful statistical tools for text document modeling. In this paper, we improve upon CTM and propose Independent Factor Topic Models (IFTM) which use linear latent variable models to uncover the hidden sources of correlation between topics. There are 2 main contributions of this work. First, by using a sparse source prior model, we can directly visualize sparse patterns of topic correlations. Secondly, the conditional independence assumption implied in the use of latent source variables allows the objective function to factorize, leading to a fast Newton-Ralphson based variational inference algorithm. Experimental results on synthetic and real data show that IFTM runs on average 3-5 times faster than CTM, while giving competitive performance as measured by perplexity and log-likelihood of held-out data.

In this paper, we improve upon CTM and propose Independent Factor Topic Models (IFTM) which use linear latent variable models to uncover the hidden sources of correlation between topics. There are 2 main contributions of this work. First, by using a sparse source prior model, we can directly visualize sparse patterns of topic correlations. Secondly, the conditional independence assumption implied in the use of latent source variables allows the objective function to factorize, leading to a fast Newton-Ralphson based variational inference algorithm. paragraphs: Topics in a document collection can be correlated, and understanding those relationships is part of modeling the text. Independent Factor Topic Models extend the Correlated Topic Model by introducing linear latent variable models for the hidden sources of topic correlation. These sources provide an additional level of explanation for why topics vary together.

A sparse prior over the sources makes sparse patterns of topic relationships directly visualizable. The source variables also imply a conditional independence assumption that lets the objective separate into factors. The authors use this structure to develop a fast variational inference algorithm based on Newton-Raphson optimization. Thus, the latent-source formulation serves both interpretation and computation.

Experiments on synthetic and real data show average runtimes three to five times faster than the Correlated Topic Model, while maintaining competitive held-out perplexity and log-likelihood. The reported benefit is a substantial speed improvement alongside competitive predictive performance. The model also offers a way to inspect the sparse sources underlying topic correlations, connecting efficiency with a more interpretable representation.
summary.tldr: Independent Factor Topic Models expose sparse sources of topic correlation and run three to five times faster on average than CTM in reported experiments.

title: Independent factor topic models
